ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS, 1891. TO THE OWNERS AND RATEPAYERS OF RUNCORN. LAMBS AND GeNTLEMEN.—In response to an appeal from a considerable and influential section of the :electors of the district, I have consented to become a candidate for the office of Commissioner, and therefore beg to solicit your support at the forthcoming election. Ido so with some degree of confidence, inasmuch as I have resided in the town over ten years, a fact which entitles me to say that I am thoroughly conversant with the wants and requirements of its inhabi- tants.

In my opinion, it is essential that a representative of the People upon your Local Governing 13ody should have time at his disposal to devote to the service of those whose interests he is pledged -to promote ; I claim that I am in thir position, and having in no small degree the welfare and prosperity of the town at heart, and being very closely in touch with the Masses, I appeal hopefully for general support. If I have the honour to be.elect3d, such energy, ability and knowledge, as Ti possess will be,unreservedly applied in promoting and furthering such objects as are most closely associated (with the advancement of the town and its retidents. ,While it would be my endeavour to keep down the expendi- ture of the Board within a reasonable compass, I shall never- theless. advocate thorough efficiency in all departments affecting the Sanitary arrangements of the town. whichare at present susceptible of much improvement. Being convinced of the advantage of Publ:c Baths in any populous district, I should strongly support any movement havingfor.its object the ,establishnsent of sueh a necessary and desirable institution.

Another important element which &serves consideration in a district so rapidly increasing, is the possession of some suitable place for Public Recreation, arid anytlarg in this direction will receive my hearty Sapport. Being of opinisn that great advantage and convenience would result from a better conne,etion between Runcorn and Widnes, I view with satisfaction and pleasure the scheme which has been mooted of connecting the two towns by means of a Bridge which would provide both vehicular and pedestrian paths, and will use my best endeavours to 'further the scheme and Assist in bringing about its adoption. In conclusion I appeal for your suffrages on the ground that my principal object will be at all times the safeguarding of theimerests of the ratepayeez, and the securing of the com- fort Axisj happiness of ,all my fellow townspeople. I remain Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours respeefully, ISAAC STUBBS.

"TENTH SOCIETY SIFTATE ": A Social Brochure. _ -By ALEXANDER WADDELL.

Hxcerpts from some if the many Press opinions : " The writer urges the necessity and the pleasure of spiritual intercourse with Gon."—Liverpool Mercury, April 15, 1891. "Mr. Waddell writes in a pleasant and earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various parts of the country with a view to presenting something to the reader which is well worth considering,"—Warrington Examiner, June 27th, 1891.

"The papers are written from a remarkable knowledge of Scripture, and recommend themselves by their quiet earnest- ness of style."—Scotsman, March 23rd. 1891. "With this key to the character of the work, the pages which follow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and appreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in stones, books in the running brooks, and good in everything."—Preston herald, April 4th, 1891. "A deep religious tone pervades the book, and as the writer has evidently travelled far and near, his anecdotes and description of places are both telling and interesting."— The Isle of Wight Times, May 7th, 1891. " 'The Tenth Society Siftate' deserves, and should have, a wide circulation."—Northampton Herald, May 2nd, 1891. "There is the ring of sound common sense in all the writer says. He sets up before young men a high ideal of life. * * * It is bright and interesting and in many parts, especially the first chapter, it is humorons."— Christian Union,April 18,1891. Extract from letter received by the author from his friend, the Rev. J. Lewellyn Roberts, M.A., vicar of Spratton, and Hon. Canon of Peterborough, March 22nd, 1891.—" There is something so chattyand cheerful, so kindly and friendly, that one takes up the book and lays it down again, and dips in here and dips in there, and finds that one has learned a good deal, or received many a happy suggestion, all by way of a pleasant talk." "It is dot often that an unprofessional author writes with such tact and skill, with such ease and grace, and vet with such masterly force as the author of the Tenth :,4ociety Siftate. The treatise has in it all the traits of that originality and piquancy that makes a social brochure popular and fasein- ating."— The Christian Union (2ndll'tice) Juue Zath, 1891.

Wife (next morning): "I wish you'd help with the washing machine work." Husband: "Do you wish me tc break my back, Sarah? Go and get some washer- woman to do it."

A GOOD old homespun old lady, who had attended for some time a church in which the service was intoned, met the vicar in the street one day, and said to him, "Mr. Pasture, I hey a little favour to ask of ye; I've bin a-sayin' my prayers in F now for nigh on to five years, and I would reely like to say them in E for awhile. I'm gettin' so husky in F now that I ean't jine in as I used to do." "Do you think, my dear," said Ethel, "I should allow M.r.Jeffray to kiss me twice in the play we are doing for Mrs. St. Claies charity 7" "Certainly not, -my dear," replied her mamma. "What can you be thinking of ?" "But I heard," answered Ethel, "that he is very wealthy, mamma." " Ah, why did you not say so before? Yes, dear, you may allow him; it is for sweet charity's sake, you know." HERE are two very amusing instances of cata- loguer's and binder's mistakes. It seems fit, but very harrowing, that Heine's poems snould be indexed as "Hen's Lays." A ben clucking over its egg quite realises a poet's condition after producing the offspring of his genius. In the other case, a French binder labelled two volumes of "Uncle Tom's Cabin" as "L'Oncle, Tome I." and " L'Oncle, Tome II."

"Mu. DICKSON, are you not a member of the African Church ?" "Not die year, sir. I jined that church in good faith. I give ten dollars to de preaching of the gospel the fast year, and the church people call me 'Brudder Dickson.' De second year, my business was not so good, and I only give five dollars. Dat year de people call me 'Mr. Dickson.' Well, sah, de third year, I feel very poor, sickness in de family, and I didn't gib nuffin fir the preachin'. Well, sah, arter that they called me 'Ole Nigger Dickson,' an' I left 'ern." QUANTITY strikes the eye at once. It is told that a certain king ordered his treasurer to give an artist a thousand pounds for some work which his faithful Minister knew would be most liberally paid for with half that gam. The treasurer therefore gave instructions to have five hundred pounds laid on a table in a room which he knew that His Majesty would pass through with him. On seeing the pile of silver, the king exclaimed, "What's all that money for?" "Sire," said the treasurer, "It is half the sum which your Majesty commanded 1218 to give the artist." "Is that so'?" said the king. "A deal of money—a deal of money; half of it will do!"

I CONFESS I am sometimes sorely perplexed, said the father, with a heavy sigh, "when I think of the future of my boys. It is a great responsi- bility to have the choosing of a calling in life for them." Through the open window came the voices of two of the lads at play. "Look here 2" loudly exclaimed Johnny, "that isn't fair? You've divided these marbles so as to get all the best ones in your own bag." " Did'nt I have the trouble of dividing 'em 2" retorted Willie, hotly. "Think I am going to spend my time at such jobs for nothing?" "So far as Willie is concerned," resumed the father, after a pause, "the task of vocation is not difficult. I shall make a lawyer of him."

In an old LararkFifire kirk, long ago, the minister was accustomed, in connection with "the occasion," to enumerate in detail different classes of offenders. "Leddy Betty," an elderly spinster, eat erect in her family pew, and in the pew reKt to that of her ladyship sat s certain 010 bacuelor laird, a neigh- bour and acquaintance. When the minister made mention of "eard players and gamblers," the laird used politely, but wlckedlv, to offer his snuff-box across to the fair Leddy Betty, hoping that "her leddyship was hearin'." TheN, when the minister, in due course, came to "profane swearers,"&c., Leddy Betty quietly leant over, and, tapping the' laird with her fan, said, " Ye're no sleepin', I hope, laird?" Why are sheep the most dissipated of animals? Because they gambol in their youth, pass their life upon the turf, the best of them are blacklegs, and they all are fleeced at last.

Few burglars possess such manners as the one of New York who lately visited the residence of Mr. Kemble, an artist employed on "The Century Magazine." Though he tOOK Mr. Kemble's revolver, gold watch, and sixteen dollars, he returned Mrs. Kemble's watch with a bow when she told him that it had been given her by a relative now dead.

The Prince of Wales's youngest daughter, Prin- cess Maud, is this year absent from the royal Danish family party at Copenhagen. This young lady, accordkg to the account of those who have the pleasure of her acquaintance, is lively and witty, with a very decided will of her own. The Princess is spending the autumn at the houses of various friends in the country under the incognita of Miss Mills.

Here is an interesting story about M. Renati. He formerly lived in a large house in the Rue de Fournon, opposite to a hairdresser's shop. One morning M. Renan went across the road to get a shave, and was asked by the barber to provide him with a legend to have painted on the shop-front. After a moment's reflection, Renan wrote on a card a Greek sentence, which may be translated as fol- io :—" I shave quickly, and my tongue keeps pace with the razor."

Taking the census in the wilds of Western Australia has a spice of exciting adventure about it, and involves a practical contemplation of magni- ficent distances. One sub-enumerator had to cross three flooded rivers to collect his schedules, and he only succeeded after three horses had been swept from under him. It is recorded that fifteen sub- enumerators travelled ten thousand miles between them. In one immense district the census had to be taken over again, all the schedules having been swept away by a flood.

" I never knew before," writes a correspondent, "that Oujda' was claimed as an Irishwoman. Such, howaver, is the fact. An interesting Dublin publication, the Lady of the House, recently asked its readers to name the most distinguished literary Irishwoman now living, and several of the replies bore the name of the Canadian authoress. No doubt the error arose from the fact that Ouida 'passed several years of her early womanhood in the Emer- ald Isle, where she acted in the capacity of gover- ness to the daughters of the Hon. Mrs. Herbert, of Muckross."

At the conference of the Institute of Journalists on Saturday it was proposed to establish a fund for the benefit of the orphan children of members. A resolution to that effect was seconded by Miss Drew, for many years connected with the London and provincial Press. She proposed that the lady journalists in each district should in a special manner be charged with the care of the orphans, and her very neat and purposeful little speech was much applauded. Miss Drew is a Belfast woman, the daughter of a clergyman, and sister to Mr. Drew, a prominent member of the Royal Hibernian Academy.

There was some amusing heckling during the late general election in New South Wales. To fully appreciate this little anecdote it must be remem- bered that the chronic impecuniosity of the Premier, Sir Henry Parkes, has passed into a proverb all over Australia. " Why did you desert Parkes when you were in Parliament before ?" an irate elector furiously inquired. "Because," replied the candidate placidly, "he was perpetually borrowing half-crowns from me.' Hereupon uproarious laughter, capped by the chairman with the conclusive observation, • And a very good reason too."

No man knew or cared less for Welsh aspirations than Mr. Raikes. He, however, married a Flint- shire bride, Miss Roper, of Plas Teg, and although he was not a rich man, he had a very happy home. lli daughters are deservedly popular in their neighbourhood, where they are enthusiastic Prim- rose Leaguers. One of them was married last year. Although a Philistine on Celtic subjects, Mr. Raikes had literary tastes, and after a hard day's work he delighted to take up a volume of Swift or Boswell's "Life of Johnson." In all Church matters he took a warm interest, and was an enthusiastic Church Congress man.

Mr. Raikes came of the stock of the "Sunday school" Raikes. Be went to Shrewsbury school and was undoubtedly a clever boy, for he climbed to the top of the scholastic ladder at an unprece- dented early age. He was naturally a favourite pupil of the great Dr. Kennedy, then head master of Shrewsbury, and their friendship lasted through life. At school Raikes not only got to the top, but also won athletic prizes, which, to the last, he showed with pride, and started a school debating society. Old Ben Kennedy was a warm-hearted and genial man, but he had not the knack of impart- ing these qualities to his pupils.

When the late Postmaster-General first contested Chester in 1865 he was in appearance very much the counterpart of Mr. Balfour of to-day. His grandfather was Chancellor of the diocese of Chester, and lived to a great age, finding more diffi- culty in defining the duties of his office than in performing them. In his walks about the city of Chester, the old gentleman was invariably accom- panied by a huge mastiff, which looked as old as its master. This dog bore a disreputable character, even for a Church dignitary, as he seldom passed a child on its way to school without first taking it gently by the front of its dress, laying it very care- fully on its back, and taking from its hands the bread and butter children so frequently munch on the way to school.

Miss Maud Guinness, who is to be married on Saturday in St. Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, to Cap- tain Henry Anstruther Kinloch, is the only child of Mr. Reginald Guinness, first cousin to Lord Ardi- laun and Lord Iveagh and brother to Lady Iveagh who, it will be remembered, was a Miss Guinness. The bridegroom-elect is a captain in the 60th Rifles, and second son of Sir Alexander Kinlock, of Glimer- ton, East Lothian, and is now in his thirty-sixth year. Miss Guinness is very tall, with exquisite complexion and perfectly marked eyebrows. Many people think she strongly remembles the Duchess of Portland. She is a fortunata young lady in every way, for besides being engaged to one of the hand- somest men in Dublin, she has a fortune of £20,000. Lady Iveagh's wedding gift to her neice will be a cheque for £15,000. Lord Ardilaun is heaping dia- monds upon her, and her trousseau has cost £l,OOO.

An ingenious evasion of the Free Education Act has been suggested in a county near London in the interests of the voluntary schools and of "religious education." The school managers are counselled to proclaim themselves free and so entitle themselves to the fee grant; but as there are many districts where the Church people would not like to think their children were going to a free school the matter is to be squared in this way. It is to be pointed out to them that they can practically pay for their children's schooling by becoming subscri- bers to the amount of five or ten shillings per annum, as the case may be, and the school managers are to make a point of obtaining as many of these small subscriptions as possible. The next thing we shall hear will be that parents unable to pay a sub- scription in a lump may give it in weekly instal— ments to the school managers, only taking care not. to call the instalments school pence.

The Rev. G. S. Raney, who recently proclaimed to the world "Why I Left Congregationalism" (a book, by the way,that has already passed through six editions), is now quartered as junior curate in a quiet country church at Bickley, where he has been sketched and interviewed by a representative of the "Christian Commonwealth." He is delighted with his new surroundings, and feels more keenly than ever, he says, "the grave and serious errors of Con- gregationalism." One of these "grave and serious errors" aspear to exist in the matter of pulpit supply. The practice amongst Nonconformist ministers of receiving fees for serving other churches while in receipt of regullir salary from their own churches has a tendency, Mr. Reaney thinks, to de- velop a mercenary spirit and to make a commercial transaction of what should be an intensely spiritual act. By the way, the rev, gentleman is writing another book entitled "The Creed of the Common People," which he hopes to publish in November.

A clatter-day Knox has arisen, in the person of the Rev. Jacob Primmer, a minister of the Estab- lished Kirk of Scotland, who has for some time back made it his special business to denounce, by written and spoken word, what he conceives to be the "prelatical and Popish" tendencies of modern Presbyterianism. Amongst other eminent back- sliders tackled by the Reverend Jacob is no less a personage than the Duke of Argyll,with whom he re- cently conducted a highly amusing correspondence on the subject of his Grace's degenerate principles

and practice in matters ecclesiastical. At present Mr. Primmer is stumping the Highlands "to pro- test," in his own words, " against liturgies, the mass, Popish images, blessing bells, teaching of Popish error and superstitition, reimposing patron- age, and setting up prelacy in the Church of Scot- land." An autumn tour among the lochs and glens is, no doubt, an agreeable, if somewhat expensive, form of recreation; but it is not explained how our new crusader's parish gets along during his absence.

plicity ; but, as he would be the first to acknowledge, while he is at home in the dialect, he is not, like his brother, graceful and free in ordinary English. Richard Rawcliffe's poem," Idyls by the Hearth," though not free from minor defects, is fit to be classed amongst the most charming pieces of verse in the English language. Take, for instance, the following stanza:— Blushingly the clover glanceth Upwards, saying, " Can'st thou love me, Beauteous butterfly that danceth Up above me ?" Then the butterfly alighteth, At these love-words spoke in bliss, And the clover he requiteth With a kiss!

How playful and innocent the fancy, and how feli- citously expressed! And so all through. The " Idyls " are really the recollections of a factory worker in the town of the sweet sights and sounds of his early life in the country. They are pebbles from the Ribbleside which have been brilliantly polished and set as gems. Richard Rawcliffe was fond of birds,and especially of the robin. How suggestive of his own hard lot are the lines in the first epistle to the robin And when the sun has lost its glow; And when thy spirit sinketh low, I love thee most, for then I know, 'Tis hard to sing, Red Robin. ”Vizarn.••••

div.head: "PEBBLES FROM RIBBLESIDE."
div.p: "PEBBLES FROM RIBBLESIDE."
THE POEMS OF TWO BROTHERS.
(From "The Blackburn Times.")

A new volume has recently been added to the stores of local literature under the above title. It has been printed at this office, and is issued by Mr. John Rawcliffe, a local poet who made his first con- tribution to literature so recently as 1888, through the medium of the "Blackburn Times." It is in- tended as a tribute to the memory of his late brother, Richard Rawcliffe, whose poem and prose writings alike will be remembered by our readers. " Dick " was one of the old school of Blackburn poets,—a boon companion of "Jack" Baron,William Billington, and others who, like himself, have gone to their rest. Ills poems occupy the foremost place in the book, and an interesting introductory and biographical note, from the pen of his friend, Mr. John Walker, formerly sub-editor and manager of the "Blackburn Times," is given by way of preface. We take the liberty of quoting this introduction in extenso, as we feel sure it will be read with interest !oy many of our readers, and if it st ould induce some of them to secure a copy of Richard and John Rawcliffe's poems, all the better. .Mr. Walker writes :

Blackburn, it is safe to say, has produced more weavers of calico and of verse than any other town in the United Kingdom. Not that there is any relation between the two; but the fact is there nevertheless, and should be taken into account by the gentle south, when, as sometimes happens, it grows harsh in its criticism of " the Northern barbarian." This taste for verse-making is surely indicative of a delicate striving after higher and better things; and that it has not been in vain is shown by the high level of excellence which tas been attained during the past twenty years by at least a dozen of these wooers of the Muses. To what are we to attribute this un- doubted tendency? To a common inclination to follow in a track once made? Or is it" something in the air "and the scenery ? It is not improbable that all three factor l have operated as formative influences. Blackburn, rude, grimy, and smoke- smitten though it be, is certainly happily situated with regard to its surroundings. Within a mile from its busy centre the workman can gain heights from which he may catch " glimpses which will make him less forlorn "of moorland and moun- tain, and valley and plain. There is grand old Pendle and Bleasedale Fells, and Clitheroe Castle— a rocky islet in a sea of verdure—and the broad pleasant valley of the Ribble leading the eye by many a smiling mead until it reaches Preston, and widens to the sea. Need we wonder that such scenes have attuned the soul of harmony, and that, the tender emotion which has been stirred has oc- casionally found fitting expression in song? The late Richard Rawcliffe, whose poems (issued by his brother along with his own) have the first place in this volume, was an ardent lover of nature, and as a lover was a keen observer of her ever- varying moods. He was born in Ribchester on the 19th November, 1839, and was a son of John and Martha Rawcliffe. Like his parents, Richard was early taught to earn a scanty living as a hand-loom weaver, but the power-loom having gradually superseded the hand-loom, he removed to Black- burn in August, 1853, and in his nineteenth year became a weaver in a cotton mill. In 1860 he mar- ried his first wife Esther Robinson who bore him three children ; and it was during tliafirst stay in Blackburn that he found his way into the "Poet's Corner" of local and other journals, and became a member of the Blackburn Literary Club. In 1864 he returned to Ribchester, having been offered the post of everlooker at Ribblesdale Mill. Here for a short period he was truly happy. He had made a step in advance; he was in his native village amongst people who knew him and liked him, and, as he himself expressed it, he was— Away from smoke, to where the breezes free Do kiss the flowery mead and craggy steep.

But death stepped in and snatched the cup from his lips; his wife died in November,lB6s; and soon afterwards he returned to Blackburn to take a post as overlooker at Peel Mill, which he held for five or six years. It was whilst working here that he married again. The maiden name of his second wife was Alice Formby, and she bore him five chil- dren. He was afterwards employed in a respon- sible position at Moorgate Mill; and became president of the Blackburn Overlookers Association. The death of one of his sons from consumption was a great blow to him. Whether his constant nursing of the sick lad resulted in infection, or whether it simply developed seeds within of the dread malady must ever be a matter of conjecture. But it was not long after the death of his son that it was seen that he too was stricken. He bore up bravely, and kept at work as long as he could. But the time came when he was unequal to the daily task, and, with his savings melting away,. the prospect before him was indeed a dreary one. Still,, he rallied occasionally; and, like other consumptives, he was ever hopeful of a favourable turn. He was advised at length that the only chance for him was to go to Australia. lie had relatives living in the- country awide of Melbourne; but, as his means were ex- hausted, a number of his friends and well-wishers subscribed something more than was sufficient for the voyage out. The experiment was, however, made too late. tie left England for Australia by the" Garonne" (Orient Line), on the let of Sept., 1886, and arrived at Melbourne on the 16t-h October, reaching his new home early next morning. He was warmly received by his relatives; and wrote a glowing description of his surroundings;;the scenery, the constant sunshine, and the wealth of fruit and flowers being like a new birth to-him.. He was still hopeful, and yet the- end was near. He had pre- served a descriptive record of the journey out which he had promised-to send me for publication. That record reached me; it was a bulky letter; I opened it with a glow of pleasure, but what a shoek I received. A brief note accompanied the diary. It was in an unfamiliar hand, and it announced that " Dick " had died somewhat suddenly on the night of the 11th Decembsr, in the same year, 1386. He had sat up somewhat later than, usual to finish his writing. Soon-after he retired he had a surere fit of coughing, which was followed by hemorrhage of the-lungs. The," fell aergeant. Death," had sum- moned him; and before daylight,,he had obeyed the summons and was gone._

It would be out of place to make more than a brief mention of John Rawcliffe, seeing that his book's issued by him as a tribute, in some measure,: to the memory of his brother;: but it may be fitt- ingly stated that he was born, in Ribchestar on the 10th of February, 18414, He left his native dale in 1868, about a fortnight after his brother, having as a boy been bobbin-winder, and then hand- loom weaver. He went to. Blackburn to become a power-loon a weaver; and was married to Eleanor hispresent wife, in,186;7. Singular to sta.te, his first essay in verse was made whilst suffering from a tumour in 1888—when he was forty-four years of age. It is a literal; if somewhat grotesve, illustration of Shelley's saying that—
Most wretched men Are cradled into poetry by wrong; They learn it sufferik I, what they taach in song.

The portrait of him, which is given in the volume, is in every respect satisfactory. The portrait of Richard Rawcliffe, which prefaces his poems, scarcely doea him justice. It is repro- duced from a photograph taken when the effects of consumption were beginning to show themselves. ' The features are somewhat too angular, and the ex- pression is lacking in that repose which was ordi- narily characteristic of him. There was nothing pretentious about him—quita the reverse; yet his bearing and manner were dignified and manly. Be- neath an unassuming aspect, there was confidence in himself, and marked firmness of character, It went ill, as a rule, with anyone who tried a game of bluff with him. He had a quick eye for weak points, and his cool sarcastic shafts yvent straight to the mark. Although not possessed of what is termed the "gift o' th' gab," he was exceedingly ready at what Lancashire people call " hullocking ;" and he knew when it was lair to begin and when it was merciful to stop. His brother John had much less confidence in himself; and this striking difference in the brothers is seen in the:fact that, while Richard took to poetising before he was out of his teens, it is only within the past few:years—since, in fact, his brother's death—that John has discovered that he

is possessed of a faculty for expression in verse. That he has worked the vein freely since be struck it is obvious from the contents of this volume. Ile is not lacking in genuine humour and artful sim-

div.head: While lush and song, above the rill, Rears up the yellow daffodil!
div.p: While lush and song, above the rill, Rears up the yellow daffodil!
The thrifty bees, with constant hum, That tell us Summcr time has come.
And—

To hear again, through sunny rain, The lively skylark sing ; So full of joy in heaven's blue, As if he knew not what to do. There is nothing strained or far-fetched in anything that Richard Rawcliffe wrote, He "piped but as the linnets do "—that is to say, he sang more to please himself and to express his feelings than with any thought of others, for he was free from the vanity of authorship. Perhaps it would have been better if he had had ambition in this direction ; for in that case his admirers would not have been left to regret that his poems are so few. But regret there is ; and that, alter all, is the best compliment that could be paid to him as a writer.
THE PRINCE OF WALFS SPEAKS ON HEALTH.

In his able and timely remarks at the opening of the International Congress of Hygiene, at St. James's Hall, London, Augurt 10th, 1891, the President, the Prince of Wales, said :—" The highest possible prosperity is when rich and poor alike can do such useful' work as they are fit for, and to this end it is essential that they shonld enjoy the best possible health and vigour." Very true, but how can the public health be best pro- moted ? Clearly by such preventive measures as the Congress Meets to consider, and by reliable remedies so long as certain diseases continue to prevail. We submit an example of the latter necessity in the form of a statement which cannot fail to convince the minds of all who may read it. [coPY.] _

I, Margaret Morland, of Throstle Nest Farm, Elaya Park, near Knaresboro', Yorkshire,, do solemnly and sincerely declare as:follows "I have suffered all my life from a weak stomach, indigestion, and liver complaint. I was never properly well but always ailing and never seemed to gain strength. I had a bad taste in the mouth and a strange sinking feeling at the pit of my stomach. I haelalwaye pain after eating, no matter how simple the food was. My appetite was poor and what little Late did not seem to give me strength. I had great pain at the chest and sides and felt as if I was held or bound round my waist. I was much, troubled with sickness and very often found no ease until 1 vomited all the food I had taken. I felt low,, weak and ds- pressed, as if something was hanging over me. 1 could not sleep at night, and got sofbad that 'I even3dreaded going to bed, for I would lie awake for hours together,. and on rising in the morning I felt worse tiredthan when I went to, bed. As years went on I became a bad colour,. my skin and particularly the whites of my eyes were tinged of a yellowish color, and at times I was as yellow as a sovereign. In August, 1880, my stomach became very irritable and everything that F took turned sour on my stomach,. and I was constantly vomiting a foul bitter fluid or gas. I took little or no nourish- ment, and after each morsel of even liquid food I strained and vomited as if my poor inside ,would come out. The pain at my heart now became so severe that I became alarmed and sent for our doctor, who attended me for ten or twelve- weeksebut all the medicine he gave me did no good.' The doctor seemed puzzled with my complaint and changed the medicine over and over again,but still I got worse instead of better. At :est I lost all faith in physic and gave up taking it. Now better, now worse, I continued until July, 1/188, when my kidneys became affected. I had dreadful pain in the back and could not void my. water. My skin was dry and hot, my lips parched and feverish. After a time, the water lodged so bad that I: thought I should have died. I grew weaker and weaker every day,. and felt that if a change did not soon take place my conditioe would be critical for the pain was more than I could bear. I could. not even bide to lie- in bed, and' had to get out of bed and walk about the room. I took all kinds o-Zi medicines but nothing gave me more than temporary relief, arid I dragged: on in this miserable state until December, ; 1838, when Mr. Day, the chemist,. at Knaresboro,' sent me-a book telling. of a medicine called Mother Seigel's curative Syrup, and I read of a case similar to mine-having been cured by this. medicine. I deter- mined. W, try it, and sent to Mr. Day and procured a large bottle of the Syrup and commence& taking it. I soon began to find relief, my food digested better and gave me strength, ail pains ia any back and sides left me. 11 could now sleep better and gradually gained strength every day, and by the time I had taken a 45.6 d. bottle I was better than ever I was im any life, and by taking an occasional dose I have since kept in good health. I! may mention that I paid over she pounds to one doctor and did not receive any benefit whatever. I feel very, grateful for the great benefit I have.';received from Seigers7Syrup,lnand I wish others to know of it. I have recomMended the medicine to many peoplc,in this district with great bone- 'fit. My daughter, Mrs.. Ware, living at York, was cured of severe dyspepsia after every other means had failed. If by publishing this statement others may be benefited I shall be very glad, and I hereby give permission to the proprietors.of Seigel's Syrup to. make any use they may think fit of this testimonialond I make this solemn de- claration conscientiously believing tho same to be true. Mr. William, Morland, the husband of this lady, is a farmer, well-known and highly respected. He has lived on his present farm at Throstle Nest, Haya Park, seven- teen years, and in the district all his Life. He was present at Leeds when the foregoing declaration by his wife was read, and vouched for its accuracy and truth. Mrs. Morland's malady, indigestion and dyspepsia, is suffi- ciently common and fatal to make it a duty to give the widest publicity to any remedy that will cure it. Hence our mention of the above case in connection with the work of the society of which His Royal Highness is Presi- dent.

A DARING IMPOSTOR:
THR STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER ONE HT/NDRED AND TWENTY-EIGHT PINE-PLACE

The gates of the gloomy prison closed behind the ex-convict, and the great, wide, bright world of freedom and untried possibilities opened up before him. Yet, strange though it may seem le looked back at the gates with a sigh of regret, and lost sight of the encircling walls with much the feeling of the exile who sees the shore of his native land sinking down the horizon's rim, while before him lies the tempest-tossed world of waters. Allen made his way to the address given in the last letter received from his sister, but his family was not there, nor did any of the occupants of the dingy, swarming tenement know whither they had gone. He met an old acquaintance, who told him the family—so he had heard—had moved to Brooklyn, but an examination of the directory failed to show their name.

While vainly searching, he realised that his little stock of money was running low, and that he must get work or starve. It is an easy matter to advise an unfortunate man to "get work," when every avenue swarms with applicants well recommended, and eager to be employed; when every employer wants to know the antecedents of those he hires; and when every department of labour is organised, and arbitrarily refuses to associate with those unable or unwilling to be members.

Allen Lee dare not go to old acquaintances anti ask them for work, for he had a little spirit left, and he desired to hold himself aloof from those who thought him guilty. It is nonsense to say that the man or woman who serves a term of imprisonment for crime thereby expiates the offence. Whether guilty or innocent,. the man once convicted by the law, though he walk the earth a free man, is to society a criminal. Through all the years of life he is burdened by an unfor- given sin, and starved into misanthropy and rebellion for the want of a little charity, or may be, a word of encouragement and sympathy. Too often the very machinery of the law—ma- chinery that cannot be said to be perfect, so long as children are raised in degradation and innocent women go to prison, and innocent men to the gallows—so long as this machinery tends to give publicity to every offence, so long will society be uncharitable and unforgiving. Allen Lee was an innocent man, a man who worked for his dear.vones from a high sense of duty, made pleasant by an internal feeling of love. But his life had been blasted ; its best years spent In a prison; his family were dead or hiding in dis- grace; and he—he who had never knowingly done a wrong—was an outcast in the city of his birth, begging, as a pauper begs a crust, for leave to work, and not daring to apply under a name which the law had disgraced, but which in the sight of the Eternal Judge, had suffered no stain.. With his last few cents he had bought a ticket on the hvat to Long Branch, for he had read that the a:l' of his ruin was there, but we dare not look motives that stirred him as, desperate and -zt zi.- he made his way to the city of fashion by th 4.

This is the story of Allen Lee.up to this time. It is necessarily brief in its outline; but before 1113 lies the duty of showing how this. man was received by the world that had so cruelly-wronged him. Poor though he was; he would have spurned the money offered by Mr. Lefferts; for, though he had never seen that gentleman, his son Frank and his associates were the meu who had sworn him into prison. But the fifty dollars, was a boon at this time, for it would enable him to keep up the search for his family, till he had found them, or was forced by want and failure to give up the search.

128 Pine Place was certainly an explicit enough direction to have been easily found; that is, if Pine Place had been marked on the map of the city of Brooklyn. The ex-conviet walked und inquired for hours the night of his rot um from Long Branch, but no one could tell him %-%. ire \Pine Place was, though all agreed that if it ,xisted at all, it had received its name very lately, .*t
That night Allen stopped at a cheap lodging. house, and the next morning be began the search _ _

About dark the foliovring evening, he found him- self in a dingy labyrinth oistreets to the south-east of Hamilton F erry. Between these streets and the Atlantic Basin there are itnmense lumber yards, au - on a bit of board nailed to.a post, Allen read "Pine Place," and an index hand:pointed in the direction of the water.
n4t

Down through top-heavy piles of lumber, that looked as if the least push from behind would send them crashing into the, narrow roadway, Allen hurried, and after two hundred yards of winding he came upon the shore, where there was a cluster of shanties surrounded by goats, tin-cans, and ragged children.

"Is this Pine Place r 'asked Allen, addressing the oldest of aqroup of children, who gathered to look at him, with the savage curiosity of a lot of Fijians. " S'poshe it is Pine Place," said the girl, with a coltish toss of her sunburned hair. "What do you want I"
"I want to know iti a family named Lee lives here."

"No, they don't," said the girl. "What is them folks like 7" asked a boy whose trousers were turnettup, so high and so tight as to threaten the circulation of blood and to account for the.mottled appearance of his legs. Allen described his father, mother, and sister as, he reraerabered them 4 and the boy said: "There's an old man an' woman, down there in that id shanty, an' they have agl as sews. The old man's a dying, so they say, but the name ain't Lee," said the boy, very confidently.

"What is the name "I can't think; :but it's funny; lanyrate, I never heerd the like before." Allen thanked the children and went down to the cabin, in thcksing/e visible window of which a light burned. He was abonti to peep in, to,assure himself that be was on the right track at last; but ashamed of the very suggestion of acting like a spy, he knocked at the door.

It was opened in response, and the figure of a slender young, woman, whose face was in shadow, appeared before him. He tried to speak, but the words he -would utter refused to pass his lips. He was brought back to self-possession by the question of the young woman: "What can I do for you), sir 7" With a choking voice he replied: "Florie 1. Flom 1 Have you indeed forgctten me 7"
" Allem!! Allen! my brother 1" cried the young woman ;:and she totte.Ted forwani and was caught in his arms, .

The noise at the or brought an old white- haired woman from a. little, back room, and as she advanced she asked, in the whisper peculiar to pro- fessional nurses and those much with the sick and nervous.
"What is it, Flo3l'e7_What 1a it, my child 7"
Before Florence could reply Allen advanced till the light from tho lamp on the pine table shone- full on his face, and stretching out his arm, he faltered:
"Oh, mother! has your boy so changed 7"
" Allen I Allen I"

The words were whispered with an effort and she would have sunk to the floor had he not thrown his arms about her and pressed her to his heart. Allen laid his mother on an old-fashioned settle, that looked as if it answered for a box at night, and Florence bathed her face and hands till she showed signs of reviving, "Free again I Free again, my boy 1" cried Mrs. Lee, when she saw the pale, careworn face of her son bending over her. He kissea her tenderly, and as he did so the tears fell on her shrunken cheeks, and he whisoered the one wo,rd : "Father 7"

"Praying for death to spare mm till he sees you again." And Mrs. Lee rose to her feet and pointed to the little room from which she had come. l'And he is here 2" "He is here, Allen. Come with me, said Florence, as she took up the light and led the way into the room. Allen followed, supporting his mother, and they came and stood by a bed on which rested the worn frame of an old man, whose deathly face was nearly concealed by its setting of long white hair and beard. The man's eyes were closed, and only the slightest rise and fall of the breast told that he still lived. "There lies father," said Florence, holding the light so that it fell full upon the dying man. Suppressing the cry that rose to his lips, Allen ciropped, upou_his k4pes_ beside the bed, and taking

one .of the-cold hands between his own warm but trembling palms, he sobbed as if his heart were breaking. Slowly the old man's eyes opened, and more slowly he turned his head till he could see the young man bending over his head. Then, without any other show of feeling than the grateful light that flashed f®i a moment in his sunken eyes, he said, in a voice that seemed the ghost of a whisper: "I have prayed God—that I might live till—till my eyes could rest again—on my innocent boy. Now, oh, Lord, let Thy servant depart in peace!" -‘ Father! father! lam back again! lam here to love and care for you! I am free ! " cried Allen.
The old man raised his eyes to the low ceilintz above his bed, and echoed the wore
" Free 1"

The mother and her two children bent for 013 bed, but the fixed gazes, the unmistakable pallor, and the sunken but never-rising breast told that the supreme moment for which he had battled with deatix had come, and the object won, life ceased.
In stupefied horror Allen looked fi:om the face of the dead to the faces of his mother and sister.
Pale, worn and care-lined they were, but there was no change in their expression to indicate a sense of bereavement.

It was not a want of love or sympathy for the dead marr ; it was simply that years of sore trial had so exhausted their capacity of expressing emotion that they could not give utterance to the horror at their hearts.

With mingled feelings of hate, sorrow and rebellion in his breast, Allen closed the eyes and composed his father's limbs for their long, last rest; and then taking the light from Florence, he supported his mother with one arm and went into the other room.
"It is well for him, that he is gone; it would be better for me if I could go with him," said Mrs. Lee, as she dropped into a chair and covered her face with her hands.

"Do not say that, mother," said Florence, kneel- ing beside her and taking her hand, "Allen is back, and there is much to live for. I have faith in Heaven; and kneeling beside you here, as at an altar, I believe that justice will be done my brother and us in God's good time." Allen had now a good chance to see his sister's face. Pale and wan it was, but its lines and ex- pression were rarely beautiful, even angelic, and the form, set off by by the close-fitting calico dress, was exquisite in its proportions. That night she told her brother of their sore trials, and how they had taken their mother's name. "Gilbert," in order to secure work from houses that had become prejudiced against the name Lee. They had come to Pine Place a year before "to be out of the world," she said, and here she brought. the sewing, on the proceeds of which she had barely managed to keep soul and body together. Allen had money enough for the humble funeral expenses, but as he could not buy a burial lot, it was decided to leave the body in the receiving vault at Greenwood, till such time as he could afford to purchase a grave. Mrs. Lee was too much broken down to, attend the funeral, but the shanty dwellers at Pine Place, though poor, had kind hearts, and they hired a car- riage amongt them, and four of them followed the hack, in which Allen and his sister rode behind the hearse.

The simple services were over and the doors of the vault locked, and Allen and his sister were standing near the drive, thiaking about going back on foot, when a fine, open carriage, with a liveried driver, came to a sudden stop near them. Allen looked up and .saw, standing- in the back seat of the open carriage, a superbly beautiful young woman whose-face was more familiar to him than his own, and yet he could not recall where he had seen it before.
Half raising her arms mid letting therm fall again, she asked, in tremulous accents: "Is not this Mr. Allen Gilbert 7" "I will answer to that name," 'said Allen, raising his hat.
"Do you not know me, Mr. Gilbert?" As she said this she sprang from the carriage, and with flushed face, open lips, and extended hands approached him and his sister.
"My memory," he. stammered, "has-ever been good for names. Pardon me, but I have forgotten yours." "I am Irene Lefferts," she said, "and. I we my life to you."
CHAPTER IV. IRE. LEPPERT&

•Allem Cilbert--let us- give him the fume be gave himself—stood uncovered; and for the first time in many years the blood from his heavy heart rushed to his white cheeks, and a light, not born of indig- nation, glowed in his great dark eyes. As he took Irene's daintily gloved hand, he said :

"I chanced to be the first in a thousand who stood ready to help you, Miss Lefferts. If I had not succeeded, someone else would,. Pardon me, but this is my sister, Florence." And he took Florences arm and brought her forward. Florence, with the black calico dress, the black, threadbare shawl about her shoulders, and the little black bonnet on her head, looked as much the lady as if the blood of ten generations of earls ran in her veins.

She bowed without moving from where she stood, while an expression of wonder, which she could not conceal, came into her large grey eyes•as she glanced from her brother to the lady who claimed that she owed her life to him.

"I am sorry to see you here, Miss Gilbert," said Irene, with a quick glance after the retreating hearse • adding, with a sigh: "This is the anniver- sary of, my mother's death, and it always finds me in Greenwood. I sincerely hope. ywa have had no such affliction."

"My. brother and myself are. I.4ere to-day," said Florence, "sole mourners at our father's funerah Our mother still lives, but she was not able to come with us. But, while loving the dead, the poor do not look on earth as a foe.. Why should_ they r

"It is as sad as death to hear you talk in-this way, Miss Gilbert. May I come to see you." And as Irene Lefferts said this her beautiful eyes looked largqr for the rings of moist= that surrounded them.

Florence, Gilbert had not heard of her brother's adventure- at Long Branch, but she did know of Irene Lefferts and of the part her brother had played in Allen's downfall, She would have been less than human if all the memory of those years of wrong and disgrace could have been blotted out by the utterance of a kind word. Still she would have Leen less of an angel if she had not been deeply touched by the earnestness and honesty of the beautiful girl standing before her. "I thank you, Miss Lefferts," she said, grat- itude for the present struggling in her heart with indignation for the past-; "but the worst of our trials is- over. If we can see how you can help us in the future, I shalt go to you." ' "Pardon my making the suggestion," said Irene, taking a card from her case and handing it to Florence, "hut I did not think to pain you with my offer. It is natural, when we feel deeply indebted 'to any one, to hail with pleasure-the opportunity of showing our gratitude. And I may add that here in this city of the dead the heart is more apt to be touched by the duty we owe to the living.' Then, addressing Allen she continued; "To your bravery I owe my life. Command ma if you think I can be of service."

"I did for you what I would havo done as readily for the meanest of God's creatures. It is I who should feel thankful that an opportunity was given me to provertirat I oould be useful to some one," said Allen; and as he spoke his eyes fell before her wondering gaze. "You, do not look like one capable of an ignoble act. I ask to know no more of your life, than you choese to, tell; and beforeleaving, I will add that my father is quite as eager as myself to show his appreciation of the man who saved his daughter's life. And now good-bye, but not farewell." Irene Lefferts shook hands with the brother and sister. Then, with trembling lips and tear-dimmed eyes, she entered her carriage and was driven away. . The mission that had taken her to the cemetery was not of a nature to make her cheerful;. but even if it had been, the meeting with Allen and his sister, and particularly her reception by them would have weighed heavily on. her breast. Irene Lefferts had on her side youth, beauty, wealth, and the swarms of friends and admirers these possessions always bring, and she was corres- pondingly happy. The serious thought her frivolous, her suit ors thought her heartless, her few intimate friends loved her for the sweetness of a character known only to themselves, and the world ad; large envied her for what it had not. When out, helplessly struggling with the tide, she east one look at the crowded shore then turned her eyes to heaven, with the feeling that another itcstant and all of earth would be over. felt_ hersel I sinking, s:s one sink 4 in a drearn_;

like a rude awakening. ,:he was brought bacg 1.0 life, with the sun flashiLf lown again, and a pair -{ brave ~:yea, set in a pale awl heroic face, looking hers, wij„le in a voice low, clear and inspiring, awe the words : "Courage, and I will save you r

Ever since that moment those wards had been sounding in her ears, and even in her sleep she ,:kr(l them, and the eyes and the face were before :.er, clothed by her imagination into the semblance 03 ,11 angel's. The fact. that she had remained heart-whole till her twentieth year certainly proved that Irene ,efferts was not unusually impressible, and it may I,e that it was the excitement due to the ordeal through which she had passed that kept the words of her rescuer ever ringing in her ears, and the bnive, pale face as distinct as a living picture before hr mind.

When she saw Allen in the cemetery, she could hardly credit her senses—he looked so much like the image in her mind. She had imagined herself thanking him for what he had done, and some warmth in his- manner, as in a manly way he tried to under-estimate his own heroism. And so she was quite unprepared for the reception she met with at the bands of this remarkable young man and his more remarkable sister.

As she was being driven to her home in Lexing- ton Avenue, New York, every detail of that strange meeting at Greenwood went whirling through her brain; but, though looked at from every side, she was unable to account for the cold- ness with which her well-meant advances were received.

She was convinced, though the attire of Allen and his sister told of poverty, that they were people of breeding and culture, quite the equals— if, indeed, they were not the superiors —of those with whom she was daily brought into con- tact.

That there was some mystery about these people, she felt assured ; and, although this did not pique her curiosity, it made her the more resolved to get into their confidence, that she might be the better able to assist them.
On reaching home, she told the driver to wait for her, as she was only going to stay at the house —which was closed for the summer—till her father came to take her to their cottage at Long Branch.

On entering the library, Irene was not a little surprised—though she was too well-bred to show it—at seeing Mott Reybold seated in an easy-chair and so absorbed in a book that he did not hear her till she stood before him.

"Oh, pardon me l" he cried, springing to his feet. "This is hardly the way to receive one for whom I. have been anxiously waiting." "I thought to find my father here," said Irene, glancing about the room, as if to make sure that he was not present. "I am here, Miss Lefferts, to say that your father will be detained in the city until late, and to offer you my escort to the Branch." Here Mott Reybold glanced at his watch, and added, hurriedly: "By starting at once we can make the four o'clock, and save a wait here or at the station."
"As father •is not coming," replied Irene, "there is nothing to detain me. The carriage h outside." _

She led the way out, and, entering the carriage, they were driven to the ferry. Until they were seated side by side in tho car, and the train was in motion, but little was said by either Irene or her escort, though from his nervous, constrained manner, she—with her fine tact—saw that there was something on his mind, and that he would endeavour to get rid of it before their journey was finished. In this surmise she was not mistaken. "I have been longing for a chance to speak with you, Miss Irene, when there was no third person present," Mott Reyfiold began, after a good deal of preliminary coughing. "Oh," she said, with a light laugh, "you are be- coming:SS mysterious ash f you had a great secret to oommunicate. I dislike secrets very much; so, pray, don't tell me any." "What 1 have to say," he responded, "is neither a secret to-myself nor to the world that knows me, and if it should be a secret to you, then there can be nothing in my manner to indicate my thoughts or feelings." "In this day of artificial things, there rarely is anything in one's manner to indicate one's actual feelings, and I must confess," said Irene, with another laugh, "I am sorry for it." "When men begin to feel desperate, they are nob apt to consider forms- -at least they cannot palm off a pretence of feeling for the genuine thing— " Not unless they are very good actors, Mr. Rey. bold," interrupted Irene. "To that accomplishment I can lay no claim," he said, with a flushed face and a nervous stroking of his black moustache. Then, with an effort, he said in a lower tone: "That I love you may be folly— it surely is not a fault." "No, it is a folly, and like most other weaknesses. time will correct it—" "Do not laugh at me, Irene." . _ . _
" What ! Lori, at your confeasion "
" No."

" What, then ? " "Treat it with the sincerity due to a strong man's love. lam not a speech-maker. I never could deal in compliments or fine phrases. I love you. Tell me, at least, that my love does not offend you," he said, passionately. " Offend ? No, it pains me—" "But you have guessed it ? " "Why should I guess in such a matter?" "You had no reason to, surely, only that I hoped you might have seen, lightly, at least, what I have Long felt so deeply and keenly. Do not speak. I Fear to hear your answer now. I spoke hastily, perhaps, but I wanted you to know from this time nn the relationship on which my heart is set." "And you have, of course,. spoken to my father shout this ? ' she said, with forced calmness. "There was no need of that," he replied.

"But why not?" "Because, ever since you were born, and I was five years old, it was understood between your Father and mine—they were school-mates and life-long friends -that you and I should marry when we reached a proper age. Even on his death bed, six years ago, my father spoke about that to. Mr. Lefferts, who has ever treated me as a son. Why, then, should I ask him for a consent that has already been given 1" And Mott Reybold waved his hand, to intimate that this subject was at an: and, but Irene refused to think it so. "It has always struck me as absurd," she said,. "that men, otherwise sensible enough, should pledge their children in marriage before those children are old enough to have an opinion of their awn. Such conduct may be admissible, for state policy, between kings or great aristooratic houses ; but as I take pride in being an American, ' very naturally, rebel against having my personalinde- pendence interfered with, particularly when that interference threatens the happiness of all my Future life." "Then you think I could make you unhappy?' "I did not say that." "What, then, am .I to inter? "That, while I. am anxious to proem love am! obedience to my father—who, as the best and, noblest of men, I am eager to please—still, in the matter of marriage, I shall be ruled wholly by my own choice. Now, you understand me?" she said, and she turned and looked frankly and fearlessly into his black eyes. _ _ _

"Then," he stammered, with another and a mere nervous tug at his moustache, while his eyes sought the floor, "you cast me off?" "To cast you off would imply that there had been an actual or an assumed attachment, on my part, at least, No, Mr. Reybold, we remain just as we were,

"And you give me no hope ? ' "Do not press me for an answer. See we are being noticed, and may be overheard. I shall speak with my father about this; and, more than. that, I shall consult my own heart." Then she adroitly changed the subject, and he replied in monosyllablea till the train rolled into the station at Long Branch. • Here they found another carriage awaiting them, and they were driven to Mr. Lefferts's beautiful dwelling that looked out on the sea, not from the place wb.ere Allen Gilbert had shown that the heart of a hero beat under his shabby garb. Strange indeed it is that Irene Lefferts should keep repeating to herself, during all the pleading of her escort, the words she heard out in the midst of those waves, "Courage and I will save you I' How could this poor, pale-faced, sad-eyed man influence for weal or woe the life be had so bravely rescued? Why, as she was whirled down the shore road should, She lose sight of the crowds, the gay equip- ages, the flecks of sail on the far-off-blue, and the clonds crimsoning overhead, and see only the lathe form of the swimmer as he rose over the breakers ? Music, laughter, and the clatter of wheels on every hand, yet to her all scunds made up the words ; Courage and I will save you." (To be continua.)
