div.head: BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: THE BREWSTER SESSIONS.
WARRINGTON.

The Annual Brewster Sessions for the borough of Warrington, were held at the Police Court, on Tues- day, and judging both by attendance of magistrates and the public, there appeared to be a good deal ol interest taken in the proceedings. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb), presided over .the bench, and the other magistrates present were-Aldermen Burgess, Chandley, Sutton, Harrison, Holmes, and Wright, and Messrs. John Fairclough, E. M. Cros- field, Robert Garnett, F. Monks, E. J. Guest, James Fairclough, L. Voisey, John 'White, and Captain Ridgway. The Licensing Committee consists of the Mayor and Messrs. Burgess, Chandley, Holmes, F. Monks, John Fairclough and Captain Ridgway. Amongst those present in the body of the Court were the Revs. J. J. Langham, John Yonge, J. Davies, John Gunnell, Thomas Ross, Edward Moore, W. Thornley, arid J. Warnock; Councillors henry Roberts, J. Hepherd, and William B•Aton ; and Messrs. W. Diggle, William Roberts, John Gandy, Warlow and Drury. The solicitors present were Messrs. Robert Davies, Spencer Wellhead, Arthur Browne (who represented the Warrington Temper- ance Federation), and W. J. Forshaw. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. The following is the .annual report of the Chief Constable presented to the licensing justices :-" The present number of license holders are :-Licensed victuallers 88, beerhouse keepers 48, and off-licensed shopkeepers 73, total 209. The extension of the borough has added one licensed victualler and four off-licensed shopkeepers, whilst one of the latter class has declined to renew his license; thus there are four more license holders this than last year. The transfers during the year were 18 licensed victuallers' houses, 5 beerhouses, and 12 off-licensed shops. Proceedings have not been taken against any license holder dnring the past year, and the number of persons brought up for drunkenness is less by 33 than the preceding year. *Looking as far back as 1866, when there were no off-licenses, publicans and beerhouse-keepers numbered '135, and the drunkenness was 536' in 1871, under same conditions, drunkenness was 762; in 1876 31 off-licenses were created, milting 166 license holders, the drunken- ness being 1,033; in 1881 off-licenses reached 88, making 223 license holders, but 'drunkenness was only 706; in 1886 off-licenses had been reduced to 71, other licenses remaining the same, and drunkenness fell to 574. This year there are 88 licensed victuallers, 48 beerhouse- keepers, and 73 off-license holders, being an increase of 4on last year's total, and the drunkenness is 773. The gross number of cases of drunkenness' during 5 years ended 1871 was 3,567; 5 years ended 1878 was 4,242; 5 years ended 1881 was 4,025; 5 years ended 1886 was 3,557; and for the five years ended at Brewster Sessions, 1891, is 3,682. The annual average for drunkenness during the last 25 years is therefore 763. It would ap- pear from these figures that the number of licensed houses has no material influence either in increasing or decreasing drunkenness; therefore other causes must be in operation, the principal of which must be ascribed to the goodness or badness of trade, and the consequent ability or inability of the people to purchase drink." The report of the Chief Constable also contains some statistics with reference to the number of licensed victuallers and beerhouse keepers and shopkeepers, and the convictions for drunkenness. The report is as follows :-1882; licensed victuallers.' houses 87, convicted four, discharged two; 1883, houses 87, convicted 4, discharged 2; 1884, houses 87, con- victed 1, discharged 2; 1885, houses, 87, coavicted 5; 1886, houses 87, convicted 1 ' • 1887, houses 87, convicted 2; discharged 2; 1888, houses 87, dis- charged 2; 1889, houses 87, convicted 3; 1890, houses 87, convicted 2; 1891, houses 88, no convic- tion. Beerhouse keepers: 1882, houses 48, convicted 2 • 1883, houses 48, convicted 5; discharged 1; 1884, 114;uses 48, convicted 2, discharged 1 ; 1885, houses 48, convicted 1 ; 1886. houses 48, convicted 1 1887, houses 48, convicted 2; 1:•:8, houses 48, convicted 1, discharged 1; 1889, houses 48; 1890, houses 48; 1891, houses 48. - _

The following shows the number of persons charged with drunkenness between August 23rd, 1890, and Aug. 22nd, 1891 : PHRSONS CHARGED WITH DRUNKENNESS. Convicted. Discharged. Male. Female. Male. Female. Total.
1889 1890-.-. 537 1891 513 166 - 773 APPLICATIONS FOR NEW LICENSES.

Joseph Houghton Clarke applied for a provisional license for a new hotel to be built in Battersby- lane, and George Pilling made ~a similar application in respect to a new hotel to be built in Catherine- st. Mr. Robert Davies, who appeared for the applicants, asked the bench to adjourn the applications to the next licensing sessions, September 22nd. There had been an agreement, to which he need not further allude, about those applications, and it was possible that they might not be made at all. ' Mr. Spencer Wallhead, on behalf of William Bolton, who applied for a full ale-house license for the off-licensed premises 112 and 114, Batteriby-lane, asked for a similar adjournment as did Mr. Forshaw,on behalf of Mrs. Susan Lawton, who applied for a full ale-house license for the Grove House, Bewsey-road. Henry Corney applied for an off-license to sell beer and cider at 173, Orford-lane. He handed in a petition which he said had been signed by the inhabitants of the upper end of Orford-lane. This was the fourth time he had applied for an outdoor license. He was leaving the army after serving for 38 years, having served in the Crimean and other wars, and he hoped the Bench would give him a chance to mainfkin is wife and family. Mr. Arthur Browne said that he was instructed to oppose the application. It might be the fact that Mr. -Gurney was a man of the very best character, but he asked the Bench to adjourn until the next licensing day the consideration of the application. He bad underobood that the application was to be adjourned by consent, and ' was, therefore, not prepared with any serious opposition at the present time. The Licensing Committee retired for consultation,and .on their return the Mayor announced that they had de- cided to adjourn the whole of the applications until the 22nd of September. OPPOSITION TO RENEWALS. The Magistrates' Clerk having asked if there was any opposition to the renewal of alehouse licenses, Mr. BROWNE said it would be within the recollection of the bench that since the last licensing day a most important cue lad been decided. Mr. 11. DAVIES, interrupting, saidbe should like to ask their worships if they intended to bear any statement otherwise than evidence on oath. Mr. BROWNE said he was going to call evidence on oath. Mr. R. DAVIES : My friend has no locus stanchi Mr. BROWNE admitted that he had no locus standi un- less he brought evidence on oath. But he should ask his friend what locus stand; he had. Mr. R. DAVIES : None except to object. Mr. BROWNE: You have no right at all. Mr. R. Devlvs said if Mr. Browne made a statement he should claim the right to reply. He had been in hopes that there would have been no opposition. The object of their not pressing the applications for new licenses, after consultation together, was that they might, for one year at all events, cause peace to reign in Warrington. He hoped there would be similar forbearance on the part of their friends. If not they reserved their rights and if Mr. Browne made a statement he should ask their wor- ships to hear him on the other side. Mr. BROWNE said he was speaking on behalf of an ob- jector, who would be sworn. Mr. DAVIES said he would call the attention of their worships to the fact that their worships had had no notices of objection, and he should ask whether Mr. Browne bad any locus standi at all. Mr. BROWNE referred the Bench to the 42nd section of the Licensing Act, of 1872, and having read the section, be asked that the consideration of certain licenses to which he objected should be adjourned to a future day. They would remember that on the last occasion he took the same course. He brought two objectors into court, and made objection to the renewal of the licenses of cer- tain public-houses in town, and thereupon they decided under the section that they had the right and power to adjourn those applications for renewals until the ad- journed day. He was going to repeat that application, and it was well known that an advocate had a right to open his case to the Bench before he called his evidence. He had a locus .standi, because he should call before them an inhabitant of the town who, on oath, would object to licenses Since the last licensing day a very important case had been decided, the case of Sharpe v. Wakefield, in the House of Lords, and it gave their Worships abso- lute discretion as to the refusal of Ay renewal of the license of a public-house, it must be admitted on all hands that Warrington, and especially Buttermarket-st., was a place where there were so many licensed houses that it injured the trade of the street to a very great ex- ea, lie was going to object to the renewal of the

licenses of seven public-houses, to some on four grounds and to others on two grounds. The first public-house he objected to was the Bear's Paw, in Rutterinarket-st., and the grounds of the objection were these: that it was not required for the wants of the neighbourhood; that the premises were not structurally adapted to the pur- poses of a public-house ; that there was no accommodation for the convenience of travel- lers; and, fourthly, that there was no stabling accommodation. The next house he objected to was the Curriers' Arms, Buttermarket-St., and the same grounds applied to that ; and the next was the Fox, to which also the same grounds applied. These were the three in Buttermarket-st. they intended to oppose. The Bench would know that they were in immediate con- tiguity to each ot'aer, almost next door to each other, and therefore that there was no necessity for those houses to be there. The fourth house he would object to was the Green Dragon in Bridge-st.,to which he objected on the grounds that it was not required for the necessities of the neighbourhood, that it had no accommodation for the convenience of travellers, and, thirdly, that the police could not have proper supervision of the licensed premises owing to its being situated in an enclosed yard. The next was the Hop Pole, and: the objections were, first, that the place was not needed for the wants of the neighbourhood, and, second, that it had no bed accom- modation for travellers. He also objected to the Royal Exchange, kept by Mr. Wm. Bolton, on the four grounds he had mentioned in connection with the Bear's Paw and Curriers' Arms. The last house he objected to was "The Shakespeare" in Dolman's-lane on the same four grounds. He would draw the attention of the Bench to a resolution passed last week at a meeting of inhabit- ants, with only two dissentients— Mr. R. DAVIES : I object to this. Alderman SurroN also here made a remark, where- upon Mr. BROWNS said he should object to Mr. Sutton act- ing on the bench. Alderman SurroN : Why so? Mr. BROwNE : I understand you are interested in a license. _
Alderman SurroN : That is a mistake. Mr. BROWNE,: Then I beg leave to withdraw my objec- tion.
Alderman SuTToN said he had formerly an interest in a license but not now.

Mr. BROWSE: I know you did not act last time. Mr. Browne was then proceeding to read the resolution passed at the meeting referred to, when The MAYOR remarked that the magistrates had all already seen the resolution. Mr. BROWNX said he should, therefore, conclude his remarks and call the objector. He should ask the Bench to adjourn the whole of these seven applications until the adjourned licensing day for the purpose of taking into consideration the wants of the neighbour- hood ae decided by Sharpe v. Wakefield. the Bench using their judicial discretion as to the refusing or grant- ing of the renewal of the licenses. Mr. JOHN DRURY said he occupied a house and premises at 30, Orford-st. He objected to the renewal of the licenses of the public-houses mentioned by Mr. Browne on the grounds stated. Mr. R. DAVIES was proceeding to cross-examine Mr. Drury, when Mr. BROWSE objected, pointing out that that was only an application for an adjournment the applications for the renewals to be heard on the adjourned licensing day. Mr. It. DAVIES said that if Mr. Brown's argument was worth anything it was equally as forcible against his making a speech as against him (Mr. Davies) saying anything. He wanted to know who Mr. Drury was, whether he was a Warrington man, or where he came from, and, further, if he could give security for costs. Mr. BROWSE said he had no objection to Mr. Davies asking those questions. Mr. R. DAVIES said he represented a legitimate trade, and he had as much right to be heard as Mr. Browne or anybody else. Mr. BROWNS said he had no objection to questions being asked as to who Mr. Drury was; but as to paving costs their Clerk would advise them that they could not order costs. The MAYOR said the feeling of the bench was that Mr. Davies be allowed to put all reasonable questions. -- _ _

Mr. DAVIES (addresiing Mr. Drury) : Are you a War- ringtcn man, Mr. Drury, as I never heard the name in connection with Warrington ? I don't say this to in- sult you. Mr. DRURY : I am rather surprised that Mr. Davies does not know my name, as I think he has had it in his office. (Laughter.) • Mr. DAVIES : Are you a Warrington man? Mr. DRURY : No, Sir. Mr. DAVIES : Have you been through any of the houses of which you complain? Mr. DRURY : No; I have not. (Laughter.) Mr. Devlns : How then can you swear to what you have stated in Court to-day? Mr. DRURY : I can swear, because there is no earthly use for them.

'Mr. DAVIES: But you have sworn there is no accommo- dation. and you have sworn a number cf things in reply to your advocate, and now you tell me that you have not been through any of the houses. Is that so? Mr. DRURY : I have not been through them. Mr. DAVIES :\ Have you been in any of them? Mr. DRURY : No; I have not. (Laughter.) Mr. BROWNS said he should call the Rev. John Yonge, who would make the same objection. Mr. DAVIES asked if it was worth while to put the Rev. Mr. Yonge in the same position. They all had a great respect for Mr. Yonge, and he hoped Mr. Browne would not put him in the position of being cross-examined by him (Mr. Davies.) The MAYOR: Perhaps Mr. Yong(' has been through some of the houses. The Rev. J. YONGE : lam glad to say I have net. The MAYOR: There would be no harm done by going through them. The Rev. J. YONGE : By the courtesy of the owners. —Mr. Yonge then said that he objected to the licenses named on the ground that they were not wanted for the necessities of the neighbourhood. That was the only objection which he could personally take, and he took it very strongly. The MAYOR: That is quite right. Mr.Dsvms Why do you object to these houses more than any others ? I have a number of others in my eye which are exactly open to the same objection, and why have you selected these, or why has anyone selected these? _

--- Mr. BROWNE objected to that question being put. Mr. DAVIES : Are there not many other houses equally objectionable in your eyes, Mr. Yonge ? The Rev. J. YONGE : They are nearly all objection- able in my eyes. (Laughter and some applause.) ' Mr. DAVIES, addressing the Bench,said the temperance party had come upon them that day with a surprise after the attempt which had been made by" the trade" to hold out the olive branch. With respect to Mr. Drury he was sorry his friends had put him in such a position. He had sworn that there was no accommodation in cer- tain houses, and yet he had never been in any of them. What did the magistrates think of that? Could the magis- trates adjourn the consideration of the renewal of the licenses upon such evidence as that ? It must be in their worships/ ksowledge that these objections applied to, perhaps 29 out of every 30 licensed houses in Warring- ton. If stabling or bed-room accommodation was not wanted it was not provided. He took it that there were many restaurants and hotels in London, and other cities and large towns, and to these equally every one of the objections which had been named would apply. What he had to do was to ask their worships to reject the evidence as it had utterly broken down. They could all respect the feelings which had brought the temper- ance party to the court. They thought the brewers and publicans were really the people who caused most of the drunkenness which, unfortunately, disgraced this king- dom, but he contended that until they could mend the drinking habits of the population they would do very little good indeed. However, he would not argue points like that that morning, and he put it to the Bench that there was no evidence before them upon which they could adjourn the eases to which reference had been made. The only evidence which had been given was by a man who had sworn to things about which he knew nothing, and a statement which had been made by his friend Mr. Yonge, who would equally object to almost every house in Warrington. Therefore he centended that the Bench could not go out of their way to object to these particular houses on such evidence as had been brought before them.

Mr. WALLHEAD, on behalf of the tenant of the Royal Exchange said it must be apparent to everyone in court that the objections to the applicatians could not be sus- tained, as there was no evidence before the Court. The Bench retired from the court,and after an absence of about 20 minutes they returned. The MAYOR: The Bench have decided not to adjourn the seven licenses, and consequently the whole of them will be renewed. (Applause.) The DE•PIITY-CLERE : That extends to beerhouses and off-licenses?
ne MAYOR: All except the applications for new Licenses. •

Mr. BROWN : The responsibility must, of course, rest upon the magistrates, and not upon those persons wish- ing the welfare and temperance of the town. Mr. DAVIES : I must certainly object to these observa- tions. The MAYOR: They don't affect us. . Alderman CHANDLEY : It is rather an uncourteous re- mark on the parlhiof Mr. Browne, and quite uncalled for. We are quite aware of our responsibility.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.
The Brewster Sessions for Daresbury Petty Sessional Division Were held on Tuesday, the magistrates present beinp Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman) W. Long and H. Neild.
THE SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.

Police-Superintendent Large submitted the tcllosiing report :--4' Cheshire Constabulary, 25th August, 1891. Gentlemen, I have the honour to submit my annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed vic- tuallers and beer retailers in the division during the past year. There are 23 licensed victuallers, 2 beersellers, and 4 others who sell off the premises; total 29, which gives an average of 326 of the population to each license. 2 licensed victuallers hays been proceeded against dur- ing the year, both of whom were convicted,aa compared

with one proceeded against and not convicted in the preceding year. No beersellers have been proceeded against, as compared with one in the preceding year,not convicted. 60 persons have been convicted of drunken- ness durinc, the year as compared with 62 in the preced- ing year. I have the honour to be, gentlemen, your obedient servant, Nathan Large, superintendent. To the magistrates assembled in Petty Sessions at Dares- bury, 25th August, 1891."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 29, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 29, 1891.
APPLICATIONS_ FOR LICENSES,

There were no applications for new licenses. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor for the firm of Jenkins and Unswortle, Warrington, applied, on behalf of Wm. Long Greaves, for a renewal of the license of the old Red Lion beer- house, Stretton. He statel that the house was an old established one and that there was no other licensed house within a mile on eitherhside and there had been no complaint against the house during the past year. Mr. John Darbyshire, farmer, of Summit Cottage, Lower Stretton, opposed the application on the ground that such a house was not required in the neighbourhood and that thoe existence of such a house contributed largely to the use of profane and immoral language. At the same time he admitted that he had no objection to the manner in which the house was conducted.—Mr.Jenkies said an ex parte statement that excessive drinking took place, without proof, could not for one moment be entertained,especially in the face of the Superintendent's report that the beerhouses of the district had been well conducted. The Chairman (to Mr. Darbyshire) : You are prepared to call evidence to substantiate your statements Mr. Darby-shire: I don't in- tend to call any evidence whatever. The Chairman said the magistrates could not consider his statement unless he brought evidence to prove it.—Mr. Darby- shire: I have not come here with any organised opposi- tion, but simply to make a plain truthful statement. I hope the magistrates will take into consideration as much as they can the law of God in such a matter as this.—The Chairman said they were bound to follow a certain line of procedure, and could not accept ex parte statements from anybody as to the conduct of public- houses without any evidence to support them.—The application was acceded to. All the other old licenses were renewed, except that the consideration of the applications of Thomas Bower, Bridge Inn, Little a fully licensed house and Wm. Beswick, Ship Inn. Walton Superior, also a fully licensed house, was ad- journed.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

The annual licensing sessions for the Runcorn Petty Sessional Division took place at the Runcorn Police Court on Monday morning. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. John Brundrit (chairman), Major Hazlehurst, Mr. A. Thomas, Mr. Henry Rey- molds, Mr. James Reynolds, Mr. Jas. landley.

div.head: THRATRE ROYAL
div.p: THE THRATRE ROYAL

Mr. E. W. Humphreys, on behalf of Mr. Henry Cad- dick, applied for a renewal of the theatrical license to the Theatre Royal. For two years Mr. Caddick had practically managed the theatre, and was fully qualified to take control of the place on his own behalf. The re- gulations under which the place were carried on were very stringent and there was no complaint on the part of the police. Supt. Large would say that the theatre was remarkably well conducted. The character of the en- tertainment was very much higher than at any previous time.—Supt. Large corroborated this statement and said he had no objections :to offer. The license was granted and Mr. frenry Coward and Mr. John J. Water- worth became sureties with Mr. Caddick for the proper carrying out of the license.

The ahairman-Waid-ice-Understood there were several memorials to be presented on the licensing question, and after the Supt. had read his report the bench would be glad to receive them and they should receive their con- sideration. But there must not be any speeches •, they were not allowed to receive any evidence except upon sworn testimony.

div.head: SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.
div.p: THE SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.

Superintendent Large read the following report :- "Gentlemen,—! have the honour to submit my annual roport with reference to the conduct of the licensed 1 victuallers and beer retailers in this division during the past year. There are 44 licensed victuallers, 53 beer- sellers, and 4 others who sell eff the premises. total 101 ; which gives an average of 251 of the population to each license. Two licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year, of whom one was convicted, as compared with one proceeded against and convicted in the preceding year. Five beersellers had been proceeded against and three convicted, as compared with four pro- ceeded against and two convicted in the preceding year. 492 persons have been convicted of drunkenness during the year, as compared with 539 in the preceding year. Of the former number 232 were non-residents, most!, of the tramp and navvy class. I also beg to inform you that the whole of the licensed houses are frequently visited, almost daily, by the police, and every breach of the licence that has been detected has been brought to the notice of the Bench. I desire to draw your attention to the convictions against the following licenses, and on an intimation that you do not consider them proper persons to be entrusted with the management of licensed houses I will serve them with notice of objection to the renewal of the licenses at the adjourned Licensing Ses- sions, viz. James Taylor, Thomas Pendlebury, and Sarah Priss. I also desire to bring to your notice that on the 10th March last, I received a complaint in writing against Mrs. Rigby (now Jones), licensee of the London and North-Western Hotel, for refusing to accommodate travellers,viz.,Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Duff, of Bedford Leigh. Compaint was also received against A. H. Brookes, licensee of the Castle Hotel, Halton, of permitting gaming on his licensed premises on the 20th Juno. In each of these instances the licensee was cautioned by the police. The list of publicans and beersellers proceeded against for the year ended 31st July, 1891, is as follows: Thos. Finegan, Boathouse Inn, permitting drunkenness and selling to a drunken person, dismissed; James Woods, Bridge Inn, similar charge dismissed; Thomas Wolsten- croft, Castle Hotel, Halton, opening during prohibited hours, fined 40s. and costs, drunk on his licensed premises, fined 10s. and costs (tenant changed) ; James Taylor, Rose and Crown, permitting drunkenness, fined 40s. and costs, selling to a drunken person. dismissed; Thomas Pendlebury, Royal Oak, selling to a drunken person, fined 10s. and costs, permitting drunkenness, dismissed; Sarah Prigs. Rutter's 'faults, selling to a drunken person, fined 20s. and costs, charge of permit- ting drunkenness, dismissed; Elizabeth Pegg, Sloope Inn, selling to a drunken person, dismissed.
MEMORIALS AGAINST LICENSES.-NO SPEECHES ALLOWED.

—The Rev. Canon Wood (vicar) was about to read a memorial, when the Chairman said they could not hear him.—The Rev. H. Burson: The reading will take but two or three minutes.—Mr. A. Fletcher (Northwich) said he appeared for the Licensed Victuallers' Association and if anything was said he should have a right to reply. He pointed out that it was an improper proceeding altogether. —The Chairman: I have already stated that we cannot allow any speeches. We are not allowed by law. Unless you have sworn evidence we cannot hear you. If you like to present the memorials we will retire into the next room and read them.--Mr. Burson": Will you allow us to read the document ?—The Chairman: No; if its objected to we cannot.—Mr. James Handley: Seeing that the Superintendent has been allowed to make statements that are not supported by sworn evidence we are in duty bound to allow the memorials to be read.—Mr. Fletcher: He is bound to report to carry out your directions. Under section 42 of the Licensing Act if your worships after hearing that statement decide that it is necessary

for the licensee to appear in person to have this matter gone into, then the Superintendent and the Clerk to the Bench could give notice requiring the attendance of the licensee at the adjourned sessions.—Mr. Handley: But this statonent having been allowed. Mr. Fletcher : It is bound to be allowed. It is part of the Act of Pariament part of your mode of administration.—Mr. Handley : It would have been competent for the Superintendent to have given objection to-day.—Mr. Fletcher said the Superintendent was quite in order. It was for the licens- ing justices to say whether they required the attendance of the licensee at the next sessions.—Mr. Handley: Suppose we don't have, any adjourned sessions —Mr. Fletcher: You are bound to by Act of Parliament.—Mr. Johnson (the deputy magistrates' clerk) : No, no.—The Chairman (to the memorialists) : If you will hand in the memorials we will retire into our own room.—The Rey. Canon Wood then handed in a memorial on behalf of ths clergy and ministers of the town and neighbourhood.— The Rev. H. Burson (Superintendent Wesleyan) on behalf of the Wesleyan Quarterly meeting; Mr. D. Bisbrown, on behalf of the Sons of Temperance and Rechabitos ; and Mrs. Humphreys on behalf of the Women's Temperance Society.—The magistrates immediately retired and were absent half-an-hour.
ALL LICENSES RENEWED.

The Cbhirman said they had taken into consideration the various memorials presented, and they had decided to renew the licences of the whole of the houses. He wished to draw attention to one point. In the memorial it was stated the number of persons to each public- house. That was calculated on the census of 1881. The increase of population in the district during the last de- cade was 6,282, which made only one house for each 251 of the inhabitants.—The Rev. C. Finch replied that in the ministers' memorial the figures were 1 in 237.—The Chairman said in that case the difference was not very material. THE WATERLOO HOTEL AND BRIDGE IMPROVE- MENTS.

Mr. R. Davies, of Warrington, said he appeared to make an application on behalf of Messrs. Greenall Whitley and Co., the owners of Waterloo Inn. He did not ask for any favour for them or any increase of the licensing accommodation in the town. As their Wor- ships would recollect, in 1888, in consequence of the death of Miss Stelfox, the Waterloo Hotel and other pro- perty came under the hammer, and at that time the Runcorn Board of Commissioners and Messrs. Greenall had an understanding that when the town was ready for it, Messrs. Greenall would not object to part of the hotel being taken for improving High-st., and doing away with the dangerous corner at Waterloo Bridge. The lln pro vement would be a very great one, and it was necessary to take part of the public-house down to carry it out. Although the house was old-fashioned in its accommodation inside it was not an old house and would have sufficed for many years,and had it not been for the Commissioners Messrs. Greenall would not have dreamt of comi ag to the magistrates for any order upon the sub- ject. But the time for making these improvements had arrived. He wished to submit plans carefully prepared by Mr. Owen, of Warrington, for their Worships' sanc- tion. The new house would be higher and more con- venient but the accommodation for drinking had not in- creased at all. There had been a commercial room and some bedrooms added at one end, in the hope that they would prove necessary with the increase of population, and the convenient position the house held in regard to the Docks and the Railway Station and the Ship Canal. The alteration would entail an outlay of £3,000 without any corresponding advantage to Messrs. Greenall, exccept a somewhat better house, but con- sidering the business they had in the town they thought they ought to do something for the benefit and improvement of the town. The Com- missioners had been interviewed by himself, and they approved of the plan. If the Bench could not see their way to sign their approval of the plans for Messrs. Greenall, of course the matter dropped through, but it was very undesirable for the sake of Runcorn that it should.—The Chairman : What Dower have we to go into this matter P—Mr. Davies said it was always done at Northwich and Warrington. It was quite within the province of the magistrates to approve of the plans. He knew that they could not pledge any future Bench of magistrates, but at the same time if he could show their approval, Messrs. Greenall would have no fear in carrying out the improvement.—The magistrates then consulted together.—Mr. Davies said he understood that one of the magistrates held that notice of a provisional application should be made. If that were the case, the matter would entirely drop through, because Messrs. Greenall were not prepared to go to Quarter Sessions and have all the wrangle and unpleasantness connected with such an application. There was no reason for them to rebuild this house except the wish of the Commissioners. After a brief discussion between Mr. Handley and Mr. Davies, Mr. Lake said the Board of Commissioners had pressed Messrs.Greenall to make this alteration,and they were do- ing so in compliance with the wish of the Commissioners. The approach to Waterloo Bridge would be wonderfully improved. The road would be widened from about 24 feet to 32 feet, and the gradient would be reduced from about 1 in 10 to 1 in 15.—Mr. James Reynolds: They are desirous to have this alteration.—Mr. Lake: Strongly.—Mr. M. Barker (surveyor) also described the improvement.—The Chairman said the magistrates were unanimously of opinion that this would be a boon to the town and were in favour of the extension. They were speaking as individuals, as they could not bind the bench from one year to another. They did not wish to sign the plans as a Bench of magis- trates.—Mr. Davies said if the magistrates did not see their way to sign these plans that improvement would never be done because he must have something to show, that they approved of what was proposed. They did not bind anyone.—Mr. Handley: I shall not sign it.—The Clerk: But you don't object, Mr. Handley.—Mr. Handley: No, but I hold that there is no need for the application to-day.—Mr. Brundrit then signed the plans.
THE TEMPERANCE MEMORIALS. The following are the memorials presented to the magistrates :
FROM THE CLERGY.

"To the Justices of the Runcorn Petty Sessional Divi- sion. Gentlemen,—We the undersigned ministers of religion of the town and neighbourhood of Runcorn, desire to approach your worshipful bench, upon a sub- ject of urgent local interest at the present time. By .a return, familiar to yourselves, it appears that in the town of Runcorn, there ià one licensed house to every hundred and eighty inhabitants, and in, the licensing district one to every 197 inhabitants, or, corrected to the population of the census of the present year, one to every 239, and in the licensing distriet about the same prvortion. Whilst congratulating your Bench on the fact that, notwithstanding the large increase of popula- tion, there has been no increase in the number of public- houses during the past ten years, we venture to point out that of the 82 licensed houses in the town, about 70 are for merely drinking purposes. That of the same 82 licensed houses, 43 have more than one entrance, afford- ing, in many cases, opportunities for evading legitimate police control. That during the years 1888, 1889, 1890, the number of convictions of publicans has been as fol- lovis :-1888, 9 ; 1889, 8; 1890, 4; whilst on the other hand, the number of persons convicted for drunkenness and disorderly conduct has been :-1888, 388 ; 1889,523; 0573 ; We are glad to know that the decision in the claBs9, eof Sharpe v. Wakefield has made it plain that the magistrates have a large discretion in the renewal or transference of licenses, and believing, as we do, that your Bench has the welfare of the town and neighbour-

hood at heart, and that their moral and material welfare will largely depend upon the control exercised by you over licensing, we beg to assure you that if you should see fit to refuse licenses attaching to premises where deliberate and flagrant violations of the law have been proved, or to diminish the number of houses in neigh- bourhoods where they are thickly clustered, you would have our sincerest gratitude. We are, gentlemen, your obedient servants, A. Maitland Wood, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, Hon. Canon of Chester, R.D., of Frodsham. W. Preston, D.D., vicar of Holy Trinity; Herbert Burson, superintendent Wesleyan minister; Henry Sanderson, curate of Holy Trinity; John Baptist Gastaldi, D.D., Charles Finch, superintendent Primitive Methodist minister; John Simpson, Congregational minister ; Joseph Holden, assistant curate of Runcorn; John Judson, Wesleyan minister, Halton; Arthur J. Jameson, M.A., assistant curate of Parish Church ; George Daniel Wray, M.A., vicar of Halton; G. H. Seelay, assistant curate of Runcorn; William Bendrew, Wesleyan minister, Halton-road; James Martin. Free Church minister ; J. Pulford Williams, Presbyterian minister ; J. H. Wilcockson, M.A. incumbent of Weston Point."
FROM THE SONS OF TEMPERANCE AND RECHABITES.

"To the Worshipful Bench of Licensing Magistrates of the licensing division of Runcorn. We, the Sons of temperance and Independent Order of Rechabites of this town and neighbourhood, present this memorial to your worshipful bench, as the constituted authority to whom is committed the weighty responsibility of safeguarding the interest of the public, under the admitted dangers attending the sale and the public consumption of intoxi- cating liquors. We are deeply convinced that the exist- ing number of licenses in Runcorn is much in excess of the requirements of the town; and we are con- firmed in our opinion by observing that in almost all the larger districts in the county the: proportionate number of licensed houses to population is considerably less. We believe that such an excess in the houses authorized to sell an article which the law recognizes as requiring special check and restraint, is a source of many moral evils, hinders the work of temperance reformation, impairs the effective supervision by the police is con- trary to the spirit of the existing laws, and should, there- fore, on these and many other grounds be diminished. We appeal, therefore, with respect and confidence to your worshipful bench to use the discretionary power which the recent decision of the House of Lords conclu- sively proves to be in your hands, and at the ensuing licensing sessions to effect a reduction of houses by refusing to renew the licenses in such cases as shall, on their merits, commend themselves to your judgment as most suitable for the purpose. Your memoralists feel sute that in this course you will have the sympathy and approval of the majority of the inhabitants of the town. —Signed on behalf of the two said orders, Edward Key, chairman; Robert W. Harrop, James Lea, vice-chair- men ; D. Bisbrown and Thomas Lea and Thos. Cooke and George Leadstone, secretaries." PROM THE WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.

"To the licensing magistrates of the Runcorn Brew- ster Sessions. Gentlemen,—At the quarterly meeting of the Wesleyan Methodists of the Runcorn circuit, held June 29th, 1891, in the Brunswick vestry, Runcorn. Present—The Rev. H. Burson (superintendent of the circuit) in the chair, the Revs. W. Kendrew and J. Judson, with Messrs. T. Simister and S. Pope (circuit stewards), also the office bearers and official representa- tives of Wesleyan Methodism from St. Paul's, Halton- road, Camden, Halton, and Weston. The following resolutions were unanimously adopted :-1. That this meeting of the representatives of the Wesleyan Method- ist Churches of the town and neighbourhood of Runcorn rejoices in the manifest growing public opinion as to ,the necessity for the further restriction of the issuing of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquor, and respectfully urges upon the magistrates the importance of exercising their powers in the interests of temperance and morality. 11. That a copy of the resolution be presented to the magistrates at the forthcoming brewster sessions, to be held in Run- corn during the month of August.—Signed for and on behalf of the meeting. Herbert Burson, chairman; Ed. Taylor, secretary of the circuit quarterly meeting. Aug. 24th, 1891."

div.head: WOMEN'S _TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.
div.p: WOMEN'S _TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.

"To the worshipful magistrates of the Runcorn licen- sing division of the county of Chester. The humble memorial of the Runcorn Women's Temperance Associa- tion, showeth :—That your memorialists, being deeply sensible of the gigantic evils and widespread misery arising from the indulgence in intoxicating liquors, and being convinced of the intimate connection between the facilities for the supply of drink in any locality and an increase of drunkenness, respectfully urge your worships to give effect to the recent decision of the House of Lords, by refusing to renew such licenses as may seem to your worships to be unnecessary for the requirements of any particular district.—And your memorialists will ever pray,&c. Signed on behalf of the Runcorn Women's Temperance Association, president, Kate Williams, or- ganising secretary, H. T. Wynne-Humphreys."

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

The annual licensing sessions for the Prescot Petty sessional Division, which includes the townships of Prescot, Widnes, Rainhill, Eccleston, Knowsley, Whiston, Huyton-with-Roby, Cronton, and Dittcn, were held at Prescot Police Court, on Wednesday, before Colonel W. W. Pilkington (chairman), Dr. E. P. Twyford, Mr. H. R. d'A. Willis, Mr. A. Eccles, and Mr. F. Stapleton-Bretherton. Superintendent Barker reported that there were at present doing business in the Prescot district 43 licensed victuallers, 22 beersellers for consumption on the premises, and six other license- holders; total, 71. The population was 16,343, averaging one license for every 230 persons. Durimg the past year the licensed persons had con- ducted their houses fairly well, one only, a publican, having been convicted, and another tenant now occupied the house. He was smry to report that there had been an increase of 42 in the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness. There was only one new application. The returns for the respective townships were as follows— Inn- Beer- Off- Other Popula- keepers, sellers. licens's. licens. Total. tion. Prescot Eecleston Whiston TArbock Huyton Roby Knowsley Croxteth Park 0 ...... 0 .......0 0 -- Total... 43 22 2 4 71 16,343

Superintendent Noblett (Widnes) reported that in the portion of the Widnes police division in the Prescot petty sessional divison there were 121 licensed houses viz., 73 public-houses, 37 beerhouses for sale on the premises, six off-license holders, and five other license. holders. One publican:had been convicted of selling intoxicating liquors dunng prohibited hours, and one of selling adulterated whisky. The number of persons proceeded against for offences'against the Licensing Acts Was 630, a decrease of 117 as compared with last year. The population in 1891 was 35,072, giving an average of 289 persons to each licensed house. There were no new applications. The persons proceeded against during the year numbered as follows ;—Drunkenness : Summoned 252, last year 282; apprehended 378, last year 465 ; total, 630 last year 747. All offences : Summoned 1,145, last year 2,99; apprehended 712 last year 688 ; total 1,857; last year, 1,987. The township statistics *were asunder—

Total ... 73 ... 37 ... 6 ... 5 ...121 35,072 There were no objections to any of the old license- holders, and all the licenses were renewed. The only new application was one by Mr. Thomas Davies, jun., car proprietor, for a provisional grant in respect to premises proposed to be erected on the side of two cottages known as Cauter's Cottages, corner of St. John's-road, Huyton. Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, anpeared for the applicant; and Mr. A. G. Steel, barrister, Liverpool, instructed by Mr. J. E. Eccles, St. Helens, opposed the application cn behalf of the Rev. E. M. Sanderson, vicar of Huyton ; the Rev. A. W. Carter, Congregational minister, Huyton ; and the owners of the surrounding property. In answer to Mr. Swift, Mr. Steel stated that the owners of property he represented were Messrs. Samuel Leyland, E. Lightfoot, Charles H. Fairclough, John Miller, George Fletcher, John Gore, and Miss Annie Saunders. The occupiers for whom he appeared were Messrs. Geo. Barton, Peter J. M. Brown, and Alfred A. Russell.—Mr. Swift stated that there was a great deal of traffic along the roads near the site of the , proposed house, and within the last few years there , had been considerable building operations going on. Within a circle of 150 yards there was a population of between 400 and 500 people, and they required more licensed house accommodation. The plans for the house had been prepared by Mr. Prescot, of Liverpool, and an expenditure of about £l,OOO would be required.—Mr. Davies, the applicant, then gave evidence, and in reply to Mr. Steel said he had not got the money himself with which the house would be built. He intended to borrow the money. Messrs. Burton and Bell, the brewers, had promised to lend him any money he might require.—Mr James Prescot, architect and surveyor, handed in the plans and proved their accuracy.—Mr. A. G. Steel said he had been instructed to strenuously oppose the applica- tion, but the opposition was not made in any fanatical spirit. A good many of those by whom he was instructed were not teetotallers, but owned and occupied houses in the immediate vicinity of the site, and they all said it would be an extremely bad thing for the neighbourhood if the proposed public-house was allowed. He submitted that the house was net required in the district, and that there were sufficient facilities for obtaining whatever drink was wanted.—The bench, after a short consulta- tion, refused to grant the application. Mr. J. 0. Swift applied to the bench for the approval of plans of the proposed alterations to the Red Lion Inn, Market-st., Prescot, on behalf of Mr. Dingsdale. The bench inti- mated that they had no objection to the plans.

ST. HELENS (COUNTY.)

The annual licensing session's for'the St.Helens County Petty Sessional Division were held at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday. before Colonel W. W. Pilkington and Dr. E. P. Twyford. Superintendent Barker, of the Pres- cot section, reported that on the 31st ult. there were do- ing business in the district 26 licensed victuallers, 15 beersellers for consumption on the premises,and two off- license holders; total, 43. The population was 8,354, being a license to every 194 persons. During the past year the licensed persons had conducted their houses well, none having been proceeded against. There had been a decrease of three in the number of persons proceeded against for drunkenness.—Super- intendent Noblett, of the Widnes section of the division, reported that the district contained four licensed houses, viz., three public-houses and one beerhouse. No proceedings had been taken either this year or last year against any license holder. The number of persons pro- ceeded against for drunkenness this year was 11, an in- crease of sas compared with last.year. The population in 1891 was 947, giving an average of 236 persons to each licensed house. There were no applications for new licenses.—The Chairman (Col. Pilkington) remarked that those who had the licensed houses at present appeared to be on their good behaviour, and he hoped they would 'continue in the same state of mind for many years to come.—Mr. J. 0. Swift applied for magisterial approval of plans of proposed alterations to the old Abbey Inn, Windle, near the St. Helens Cemetery. lie stated that he appeared on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., the owners, and Mr. John Almond, the present tenant of the house. The Abbey Inn, according to tradi- tion, had been built and licensed for something over 300 years. Mr. Almond had occupied it for the last 17 years, and his wife's mother had formerly been the tenant for a period of 30 years. The increase in the size of the building would be about 25 per cent.—The Chairman stated that the bench could see no objection to the altera- tions.

div.head: "TIED HOUSES" IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: "TIED HOUSES" IN CHESHIRE.
THE REPLY OF THE BREWERS TO THE JUSTICES'
REPORT.

Mr. J. L. Kemp, chairman of the Cheshire, Shrop- shire, and North Wales Brewers' Association, has sent, on behalf of the association, a long letter to every magistrate in Cheshire with reference to the late report of the Special Committee of the Cheshire Quarter Sessions regarding the licensing question. In the course of the document the writer says :—" Two opinions seem to stand out prominently—namely (a) a reduction in the number of public-houses without compensation to the holders of licenses; (b) a condemnation of the system of tied houses.' As regards the first head I may perhaps be permitted to say that the magistrates of days gone by are in the main responsible for the present (perhaps) excessive number of alehouse licenses. If the Legisla- ture thinks it ought to pass a measure for the reduction in the number of public-houses we should welcome it, provided the just claims of license-holders to compensa- tion were considered. The report. upon the subject of tied houses' and those conducted `by managers seemed to be rather confused; but let me at the outset state boldly that the Legislature does not prohibit tied houses, nor does it prohibit houses conducted by managers. The most valuable licensed premises in the ciounty are owned by companies or corporations, and such com- panies or corporations carry on upon such premises the business of retailing wine, beer, and spirits by managers or secretaries to whom the license is granted. We are prepared to challenge many of the statements contained in the 13th section of the report as to tied houses and houses conducted by managers and we should welcome an opportunity of doing so. We maintain, and are pre- parrd to prove, that tied houses and houses conducted by managers are better conducted than the small so-called free houses.' In the former case the brewer or land- lord exercises for his own sake an overwhelming influence for good over the person in charge of the public-house ; whereas in the small free house, often held by persons without sufficient capital, there is no check whatever, and the so-called free tenants find it imperatively neces- sary, in order 'to make two ends meet,' to resort to questionable practices. We do not hesitate to denounce the statement contained in the latter part of section 23 of the report that the practice of dilution of beer with water would appear to be an almost inevitable incident of the tied-house system,' as utterly untrue and incap- able of proof.

"One of the Tied" writes as follows in a Liver- pool contemporary :—"Mr. J. L. Kemp, chairman of the Cheshire, Shropshire, and North Wales Brewers' Association, would try to make it appear that tied houses were more prosperous and better conducted than free houses—in short, that free houses were just crying to be tied, and pay all the way from 10s. to 15s. ner barrel more for their ale than the are in the habit of doing. Everyone who knows anything about tied houses knows that in many cases they are compelled to take the brewers' ale, and pay more for it than the same brewer would supply a free house for. My experience of it is this, that a publican who pays 428. per barrel for his beer cannot compete with another who gets his for 30s. per barrel; consequently he is obliged to resort to the questionable practices that Mr. J. L. Kemp speaks of, and runs more risk of running foul of the ' law in his endeavour to make both ends meet. My advice is this,diminish the number ot public-houses and it will be all the better for those who are left, because there will not be so much competition, and will make the publicans more independent,and less likely to serve the drunken men, who we all know are a nuisance and an anxiety to the publican and the public, who go for a quiet glass and smoke after their day's hard work. I agree that some compensation should be given to the publican who is deprived of his license, but care should be taken that it is he who should get it and not the brewer he is tied to."

div.head: THREATENED STRIKE IN CHATIIAII
div.p: THREATENED STRIKE IN CHATIIAII
DOCKYARD.

The Amalgamated Society of Engineers have given instructions to those members of the Chatham branch at work in the Dockyard who are receiving less than ss. Bd. per day to give one week's notice to the Dockyard authorities of their intention to come out on strike unless their wages are raised to the amount named, which is the minimum fixed by the Society. The matter affects the greater portion of the fitters in the Dockyard.

The severe gale which sprang up suddenly on Tuesday night raged for many hours, and was accompanied by tremendous torrents of rain. The visitation seems to have been general over the three kingdoms, and the damage done to the growing crops and the fruit orchards. is simply incalculable. ASSAULTS ON SALVATIONISTS AT EASTBOURNE.—The disturbances at Eastbourne in connection with the musi- cal processions of the Salvation Army were renewed on Sunday in an aggravated form. The processions were broken up by a crowd of residents, and several of the Salvationists were hurt. Some attempts, too, were made to storm the Army "citadel." The crowd numbered many thousand persons, and a good many of them were injured by stones and blows from sticks. "Jewellers. Stationers," &c., commencing. See Prospectus (post free), 186, Euston-rd.,London. Established 1886.-4drt.

div.head: SHIP CA.NAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CA.NAL.
ACCIDENTS ON THE CANAL.

Several accidents occured on Monday morning, on the Ship Canal, on the cton Grange, and Runcorn sections. Joseph Mucklow, a man about 50 years of age, was working in the Big Field, Runcorn, "clearing up" at the waggons which were standing near a steam navvy, when a piece of earth fell out of the bucket of the navvy upon him. The weight of the earth caused him to fall on the rails, and IR received serious injuries to his back and face.—Benjamin Baxter, a middle-aged man, was working at what is called a "sump," on the Acton Grange section, when the plank upon which he was • standing capsized, throwing him into the hole. He fell a distance of about 20 feet, alighting crosswise on a piece of timber, which was used as a support. He sus- tained injuries to his head and side.—Edward Jones, a man about 55 years of age, was at wprk on the Runcorn section of the Ship Canal, when, in passing through the locomotive shed, he fell into a pit, which is 41 t. 3in. deep. He received injuries of a serious character. In each case the injured man was removed to the hospital at Latch- ford, and medically attended.

div.head: MR. RELY AND MR. PARNELL.
div.p: MR. RELY AND MR. PARNELL.

At the National Federation meeting oa Wednesday, in Dublin, Mr. T. M. Healy, M.P., presided. He said that having recently spent some time in the North of Ireland he could tell them that at the next general election there was no doubt they would succeed in retaining the major- ity of the Ulster seats they had at present. There were 33 seats allotted to Ulster. The National party held 17, and the anti-National party held H. The city of Derry was absolutely safe for Mr. Justin M'Carthy, and West Belfast for Mr. Sexton. There was a kind of working arrangement between the Parnellites and the Tories to hand over South Dublin to the latter. He congratulated the Federation on the success achieved during the past six months. They had to thank their opponents for that. Their opponents were now getting ashamed of their leader, and they raised the cry of the principle of independent opposition. Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien had seen quite enough of independent opposition in their time. They had now got the Liberal 'Arty into that state of mind in which they were going to concede to Ireland that principle which was the fruit of independent opposition. In his opinion it would b. an unfortunate thing for Ireland if one man of Mr. ParnelPs following was returned again to the House of Commons. They had waited long enough for signs of repentance on Mr. Parnell's part. He said it with regret that so far as he was concerned he would do his best to put every man of them out of Parliament—(cheers),—and that he would be no party to any arrangement with traitors and pledge-breakers.—(Cheers.)—Mr. Kenny, M.P., Mr. D Sheehy, M.P., Mr. A. Webb, M.P., and the Rev. Dr. White (Kilrush) also spoke.

div.head: GALLANT ACT AT SEA.
div.p: GALLANT ACT AT SEA.

On the 20th July last the Cunard steamer Cephalonia, bound up channel from Boston, via Queenstown, saw a signal displayed from the Tuskar Lighthouse, signifying that medical aid was urgently required. Capt.Seacombe, without a moment's hesitation, immediately stoppel the ship and lowered a boat which was given in chaage of Mr. Turner, the second officer,to convey the surgeon. Dr. Giffen, to the rock. Mr. Warden, the company's pilot volunteered to accompany the boat as the weather was hazy, and in the event of losing sight of the Cephalonia his knowledge of the channel would be available in tak- ing the boat into the nearest port. On nearing the rock great care had to be exercised lest the boat should be stcve in, as there was considerable swell on, and Mr. I Turner, while holding the tiller hard over, and the rudder being struck by a sea, was suddenly thrown out of the boat, but being a good swim- mer, he immediately called out "never mind me, look after the boat." Mr. Warden, however, see- ing no absolute necessity for thus risking the life of a brave man, manceuvred the boat so as to reach Mr. Turner, who being a slightly built man was literally pitched into the boat again by the powerful arm of Mr. Warden. The wounded signaller, who without medical aid would soon have bled to death, was quickly got on board the Cephalonia,where his arm was skilfully ampu- tated by Dr. Giffen, and safely landed and lodged in the Bootle Hospital. Here the poor fellow received every calla, and eventually made a good recovery. It is gratify- ing to add that the Commissioners of Irish Lights, not satisfied with merely acknowledging the act at the time, have now forwarded through the Cunard Company a handsome cheque for Dr. Giffen, and also express their warm appreciation of Mr. Turner's bravery, and that of the.other persons concerned. In these day of supposed deterioration of our seamen, of imputation of inhuman- ity at sea, and reflections of heartlessness of public bodies, we have much pleasure in recording this incident which does so much credit to all concerned.

"JACK THE RIPPER" SCARE IN LONDON. ARREST OF AN ARMED " GENTLEMAN."

A sensation was caused in the notorious Buck's-row, Whitechapel, London, late yesterday week, when a gentleman drove up in a cab and alighted at the corner of Anne-street. He opened a conversation with a woman standing near by, and the wornanresentingthe intrusion called him "Jack the Ripper." He immediately became excited, drew a six-chambered revolver, and threatened to Ilre indiscriminately, upon the crowd which rapidly gathered. A police inspector and a sergeant who were near at hand immediately arrested him, and he was taken to Bethnal Green Police Station. Upon being searched a large bladed knife was found upon him. The prisoner was on Saturday brought up at the Wor- ship-st. Police Court. His name was given as Percy Greathead, aged twenty-nine, and he was described as a "gentleman," on the police sheet, living at Wood's Hotel, Furnival Inn, Holborn. He was charged with presenting a loaded revolver at Margaret 'Sweeney, slip. posed with intent to shoot her at Queer i Anne-st., White- chapel. There was a good deal of excitement n court, owing to a report having been spread that "Jack the Ripper" had been captured. The evidence showed that the accused went for a walk down Buck's-row, White- chapel, to see the scenes of the Whitechapel crimes. He had taken a cab to Whitechapel, and left the vehicle whilst he went down the street so painfully celebrated. He had in his possession a revolver, and passed the woman Margaret Sweeney, who stood at a door in a bye street. A man came towards him, and made some remark to Sweeney, who retorted, "Now, then big-head, go home. It's time you were in bed.' " Big-head " suggested " Greathead" (the prisoner's name), and caused him to think the woman was insulting him. He turned to her, and she seems to have remarked, "Here's Jack the Ripper." The prisoner produced his revolver, and immediately there was a scene. One or two men, being on the spot, raised an alarm, whilst the prisoner said they alse alarmed him, and were the cause of his producing the weapon. A constable appeared and took to the station, where to Inspector Wells he gave up a six-chambered revolver fully loaded.--The manager of Wood's Hotel said he had known the prisoner fourteen years, and he had travelled a great deal. He alwafs found him quiet.--Mr. Montagu Williams remanded the prisoner, and refused an application for bail.

icensing The ways of Warrington magistrates L Justices. are peculiar. Individually, they• admit that there are too many lieensed houses in the town ; collectively, they act as. if they did not believe anything of the kind. The town is drink-ridden; it has, been noted for half • a century for its "bad eminence" in this respect; and, judging from the inaction of the licensing .justicesi. it is likely to remain noted. So long as there wee a doubt about the law, the magistrates were in a position to nlead that they . weremot called upon to run unnecessary risks by reducing the number of licenses. But all doubt has been removed by the decision in the case of Sharp versus Wakefiekl ; and yet they have taken upon themselves to,renew every °misting license in Warrington. Thishaa been donertoo, after the strongest expression., of public opinion as to the necessity of lessening the number a drink-shops; and people are now asking—What does it mean Do the-magistrates really think they are conferring a benefit upon the public by renewing all the 'ficensesi ,or are the "blind as never bat was blind ?'! We notice that the Chief Constable in his Annual -Report says Proceedinga have not been taken against any license-hold or during the past year, and the number of persons brought up for drunkenness is lens by 33 than the-preceding year." As an item of information; this is exceedingly suggastive. No license-holder has been proceeded against, and fewer persons have been brought up for drunkenness. It might be inferred from this that the tows,is improving —that there are no breaches of the licensing laws, and the " drunk-and-disorderlies " are fewer! : But is that. so? Does it. accord with, eommon ob- - servation ? Not at all.. Strangers.: coming into Warrington are struck with the amount of drunken- - ness which they find in the principal streets— drunkenness which is tolerated so long asit does not result in -a. scene. It isnot many months since we published a letter from a Warrington man who had been. absent from his native town.. a...considerable number of years. Ho.was asham-,d• and appalled . on returning to find so many drunken persons in the streets on a Saturday night ;: and could not - but,contrast what he saw with Ile condition of thiags in Birmingham,where he lad been residing for some time. But the magistmiles of •Warrington apotear to be oblivio-as of all thif.'k. "Having eyes they see not, and ha7ing ears thay hear not;" and they may under the circumstanss be .fittingly re- - minded of Voltaire's saying that ,people are never so degraded as when they are urnonseions of their • degradation.

The Chief Constable in hiss Report goes back: as far as the year 16; . but lie does not say, as lie might have said‘,.that in that yeaE the law was : so strictly carrieol.out that:. as many as thirty- eight publicans awl beer-sellers were fined,-many ~ ,Of them heavily fued—for breaches of the Liens - ing Acts; while daring the year just closed not a single license-holder has bean proceeded against.— so "lamentably Itex:"—to cp.4ete the words,cg one magistrate—haa..been the staminiemkratiun va •jr.z,o- - tice. We put this broad, this startling contrast. bet- • tween 1866 ant:11891 to the most drink-favouring magistrate on the bench„and *we invite hire to,tell •, us what he thinks of it. Can he honestly say that. the absence alproceedings against:drink-sellers,re- - presents a really satisfactory state of thiags .?.- It :. would be . kiiterestingfalso to know what is the • opinion . of the Chief Oonstthle ; whether; them police have:been encouraged or disccuraged by:. 1 haring, laat year, their strongest canes ,agsinst i license-holAlers dismissed; aud whether theylfay.e, been encouraged ;or discouraged sines Councilor -SOLTON and Aldorman GRaltNALL—two pernons directly interested in "the trade"—were placed upon the Watzli Committee. The legislature, 'knowing. the weakness el human naturb,, has debarled any person from acting as a lidamaing magistrate who has an ilterest int " the txtde"— even when the interest -Is of the inanitesi=al kind which is represented 4 holding shares,ima Rail- way Company that. is possessed. a licensed rdreshment rooms. The legislature has not, however,. debarred brewers,, or distillers, or licensed-xictuallers kora being appointed members: ,of a Watch Committee. It does not seem to have :occurred to Parliament that any Corporation w,ould be so utterly foolish as to, set the cat to watch the cream.

In the course of the proceeding& in the Waning- ton, Court, on Tuesday, Mr. ROBSILT DAviEs,who appeared on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whatley, and Co., the principal brewers of the tow 4 con- tended that " until they could mend the drinking habits of the population they would do vary littl& good indeed." But we would ask him wbiether he: thinks it is calculated to mend drinking habits to add to the already excessive number of licensessa his clients are seeking to do; or Ivether that desirable end is not more likely to be accomplished by largely lessening the number. The rule is "the more drink shops the more drunkenness "—other things being equal—and that rule could have no better illustration than is afforded by the de- plorable condition of Butterraarket-st When a brewer's advocate, with his eye on a fresh site for a public-house, begins to talk of mending drinking habits, it is a reminder that the devil can quote scripture to suit his purpose. and the Rev. J. YONGE to take objection to houses which they had not inspected, nobody knows better than Mr. ROBERT DAVIES that there is nothing in the contention. Two years ago, these very houses were objected to by the magistrates' clerk on behalf of the ma- gistrates; and it is ridiculous to suppose that he had previously paid a visit to each house. The broad ground of objection is that so many licensed houses are not required in the interests of the inhabitants; and it is quite competent and per- fectly legitimate for the objectors to put forward other objections and sustain them by means of supporting witnesses. When Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. are seeking for power to set up a new drink-shop in a new district it is not consi- dered necessary to place Sir Gilbert Greenall in the box to give evidence as to the proposed new structure. That is done by other witnesses who can give technical evidence; and in.the same way other witnesses with technical knowledge could have testified to the deficiencies of the existing houses. But what matters P. When the adminis- tration of justice in a town is" lamentably lax," the publicans are likely to be taken care of whatever becomes of the public. There is little or no hope of Licensing Magistrates being equal to the task before them either at Warrington or elsewhere. Some there are with a high sense of duty, but they are in a minority. There are too many magis- trates throughout the country who hang—not on princes' but on brewers' favours; and it is often the case with them of "letting' I dare not 'wait upon' I would.'" They are not to be depended on; the hope of the people is not in them ; it is in Local Option, and for that they must now strive with might and main.
WE have taken signal vengeance Lord Cross and upon the authors of the massacre

Manipur. of the British officers at Manipur; but is has been a question from the first whether the Senapati was not more sinne(sl against than sinning ; and the latest Government paper on the subject does not remove the impression that Mr. Quinton was guilty—not only of a grave error of judgment, but of a grave wrong in arranging to arrest the Senapati at a durbar. In the letter which Lord Cross has forwarded, as Secretary of State for India, to the Governor-General of India, he is careful to say that he fully approves of the policy of the Indian Government in interfer- ing at Manipur. He says: "It was honourable; it asserted the rights of the Government of India; and it was calculated to give assurance to feudatory chiefs. Nor do I doubt that you were right in leaving to the discretion of the chief commissioner the details of the method of enforc- ing your decision." Referring, however, to Mr. Quinton's intention for causing the Senapati, should he not surrender, to be arrested in durbar, Lord Cross writes:—" I fully concur with you that nothing like treachery can be imputed to Mr. Quinton in this matter; but care should be taken that persons summoned to attend durbars—which -are almost universally understood to be held for ceremonial purposes—should not be subjected therein to measures of personal restraint." This goes as near condemnation of the action of Mr. quinton as a Secretary of State could be expected to go. He has to consider what will be the effect Of his words upon native princes, and be careful .not to weaken the authority of British officials. But we at home are under no such obligation. In a ease of this kind we ought to do more than hint we should speak out. It seems to us, now that all the facts of the case may be said to have been made public, that Mr. QUINTON committed a blunder in taking such a small force to Manipur, and the penality of that blunder he has paid with his life. But it was worse than a blunder—it was in the nature of a crime to invite the Senapati to a durbar, after making arrangements for his arrest in case of his refusing to surrender. Durbars, as Lord CROSS states, are "understood to be held for ceremonial purposes," and as such they should be regarded as sacred. It is true that Mr. QUINTON did not carry out his intention, and cannot there- fore be said to have been actually guilty of treachery; but it was not that the spirit was unwilling, but because the flesh was weak. The Senapati suspected foul play, and declined to walk into the trap. Afterwards, his suspi- cions were from his point of view justified, for , he was called upon to give himself up as a pris- oner. He refused to yield, and turned the tables upon his enemies by leading them into a trap, and being party to their massacre. Nothing could justify the Senapati's treachery, for two wrongs do not make one right, but, whilst condemning this Eastern chief,it is but just that we should acknow- ledge that, in the first instance, wrong was done on our own side. Lord CROSS has put it on record that when a prince, or chief, is invited to a durbar he is not to be arrested. It would be well if this intimation went the length and breadth of India; for we may be quite sure that if there is any doubt upon the subject the durbar will become the means of sowing seeds of discord rather than of concord. Our right to govern India is based on the convic- tion that we can be of service to India, but we can only be of service to India and her tributaries by pursuing that policy of righteousness which ex- alteth a nation.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Letters have been received from Laurence Flood, "P. D. Pease," and "A Radical Shareholder."

The filesmiths of Warrington are pressing for an advance of ten per cent.; and as wages have gone up in other branches of the tool trade, they are likely to succeed in their demand. It would be a good thing if men in the tool trade generally could organise and settle prices. It is bad alike for employers and employed when there is no standard list.

A right of way has been asserted at Braemar in Scotland by publicly pulling down some 500 yards of palisading which had been put up to shut off access. Hundreds of public paths have been lost through lack of such public spirit as Scotchmen are showing in this matter. The Corporation of Warrington have a right of way question in hand; and it is just possible that it would prove the cheapest and best mode of asserting the right tc take a leaf from the Braemar book.

"The Pope he leads a happy life," but not where pensions are concerned. "The Commission of Cardinals has discovered that for many years pensions have been ostensibly paid by the Holy See to persons who are long since dead. In future no pension will be paid except on the production of a certificate from the Municipality that the person is still living." And quite right too. The pension system is at the best unsatisfactory ; "it is not and it cannot come to good."

At Widnes, on Monday, two boys were ordered to be birched for stealing coats from the lobbies of dwelling-hous3s and pledging them. The money they obtained in this way they spent in cigarettes. The Chairman said he had a very strong opinion that the pawnbrokers ought not to take things in pledge from children except for their own parents; and most people will agree with him. div.p: scribing speeches, namely, " When in doubt, leave out."

Warrington Primrose Leaguers seem to have had a good time at Grappenhall Reyes on Satur- day, considering the weather. Mr. J. W. D. Barron, of Manchester, was the leading speaker, and the principal part of his speech was in the statement that, "they should be satisfied with the conditions under which they. laboured, and remember the party which had honestly done their best to benefit them." Just so; it is a prose version of the ancient Tory doctrine as originally expressed in rhyme : Bless the Squire and his relations, And keep us in our proper stations.

Councillor Muir had a word in,and it was to the effect that "the moral philosophy of the present Government had done a lot to tone down and modify politics of the present day." One might ask what Councillor Muir meant by this ; but that would be putting a Primrose speech to too severe a test. In the matter of Irish land, allot- ments, and education, the Government have done the very reverse of what was professed by the Tory party when out of office. Is that " moral " philo- sophy? If so, we must say that— A merciful Providence fashioned them hollow, In order that they might their principles swallow.

Of the making of books there is no end; bxit the French are trying to make an end of "book- makers." They have put a stop to " bookmak- ing " amongst Frenchmen, and now they have given English betting firms at Calais and Boulogne a fortnight's notice to quit. It is said that the various " bookmakers" at these places employ altogether from 80 to 90 clerks—a fact—if it be a fact—which is suggestive of a lively trade. How- ever, they have got to clear out, for it is thought that if they leave the country it will be for the country's good. It is well ; they order these things better in France.

It is clear that visitors to New Brighton require to exercise special care whilst walking on the sands. On Sunday evening, there was another accident; a lady narrowly escaped sinking in the quicksand in the immediate vicinity of the Rock Lighthouse. Her cries for help soon attracted attention, and fortunately she had only stepped off the verge of the solid ground, so that little difficulty was experienced in drawing her out of her perilous position. It is not unlikely that the tidal flow is having some effects upon the sands, so that what is firm ground one day may be unsafe the next. Whatever the cause, there is every need for feeling one's way.

The divine William says "Knowledge is the wing wherewith we fly to heaven "—or to the Town Council, which to some people is the same thing. Anyhow, men of knowledge do wing their way to the Council Chamber, and a pretty flutter they make. At the present moment the Corporation of Southport are engaged in laying out a second Marine Park. It was suggested by one Town Councillor, when plans were under consideration, that it would be a good thing to have a gondola on the lake, whereupon another Town Councillor —a man of knowledge—put a poser. "Why not," he asked, have two gondolas, and then they could breed ofl them ?" Why not indeed!

It is not creditable to the Baths Committee of the Warrington Corporation that they should abandon the scheme for new baths because the plans submitted to them are likely to involve a larger cost than was originally intended. If the plans are too ambitious, lot them be altered; but, if they do not go beyond what is really required, the Committee will do well to appeal to the Town Council as a whole, and we are greatly mistaken if they will not find plenty of support. Seeing that everybody admits the necessity either for enlarged or new baths, the Committee will write them- selvws down as incompetent if they do not proceed with the work.

The school authorities in the Ashton-in-Maker- field district have decided on a penny fee. We are told that "in the discussion which followed on the subject, it was pointed out that many parents would derive great benefit by their children re- ceiving their education free, or almost free, whilst others would feel keenly the parental duty which had been taken from them. As a loophole by which parents of the latter class can still show the interest they take in the welfare of their children, it was decided to ask them to become subscribers of sums from half-a-crown to ten shillings to the school fund." Isn't this a bit like humbugging the parents ? And where does the "free" education come in, if parents are to subscribe to schools, in addition to paying a penny fee?

INQUESTS AT RUNCORN. Mr. Worsley, the coroner, yesterday, held an inquest at Runcorn, on the body of John Jones, aged 53 years, who had resided at 71, Nelson-st., and who was employed at the works of Messrs. Haziehurst and Sons. At about two o'clock that morning Fred Johuson, the watchman at the works, found the deceased lying behind the boilers quite dead. The widow stated that deceased had been in very bad health lately, and had often coughed for ten and fifteen minutes, until he staggered as though he would fall. A verdict of death from natural causes i was returned.—An inquest was also held on the body of' John Stubbs, aged 15 months, son of James Stubbs, of Perry-st., who died on Wednesday from injuries caused through accidently setting hls clothing on fire in the absence of his .mother.—A verdict accordingly was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE NEWS.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE NEWS.

On Wednesday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L. Davies, a navvy named James Manley, of no fixed abode, was convicted of travelling on the London and North-Western Railway between Frodsham and Runcorn without paying his fare. In default of paying a fine of 20s. and costs, he went to gaol for 21 days.—On Thurs- day, before Mr. Handley and Mr. H. Reynolds, a la- bourer named Walter Leggett, was brought up on re- mand charged with stealing 1361b5. of brass belongin3 to the Ship Canal Company at the Old Quay. The pri- soner, who is well known to the police, was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial.—Patrick Casey, a re- turned convict, was also committed for trial on a charge of stealing a coat from the shop door of Catherine Dodd, Church-st.—James Green was charged with stealing 4s. from the till of the Rose and Shamrock Inn, Mersey-st., the property of Alfred Baker. A fine of 123. 6d. was im- posed, or 14 days.
