Miss Marie succeeded in winning first prize, and Mr. Stanway is to be congratulated on the possession of such an animal. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington —Advt.

HOLY TRINITY Y.M.C.A., RUNCORN. The members had their annual picnic on Wednesda?, when they had a drive to Delmere Forest in brakes pro- vided by Mr. Jackson. The weather was beautifully fine and the journey both going and returning was very pleasant, while the rambles through the forest were much enjoyed. Ample refreshments were provided. DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

-- Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at Weston Paint, on the body of David Thomas, a native of Bangor, who lived at No. 1 hut, Weston t'oint. The deceased had been missing since the 7th inst. On Saturday his body was found in the Weston Canal near the Iron Bridge by a man named George Cox. A verdict of" found dead" was returned. J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE ROW 011. Sankey Street, Warrington.—.Advt. TREAT TO WORKPEOPLE AT RUNCORN. The workmen and wives of Mr. Isaac Stubbs, mineral water manufacturer, of Runcorn and Northwich, had their seventh annual treat on Wednesday, and about 40 took part. Tne party were conveyed to Overton Hills on the hurries of the firm, which were fitted with com- fortable seats, and the weather being fine, a pleasant and enjoyable day was spent at Belle Monte in games and dancing. A capital luncheon and tea was provided at the expense of Mr. Stubbs. J.& Nr. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOLS. The annual reports of Her Majesty's Inspector of Schools have just been received. Mill Brow Infant School earns the highest possible grant amounting to 17s. per head, which was considered highly satisfactory.. The Greenway-road Schools are in very good order and have been awarded the total grant per child of 18s. The amount earned is more than the department will pay, there being a deduction of £l2 12s. 10d. under article 107 b. In the Boys' School drawing has been taken, for the first time and the award is good, earning a sepacate grant of £2l is. BASSINETTES.—J . S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st Warrington.—Advt.
MARRIAGE OF A RUNCORN GENTLEMAN.

On Thursday afternoon, at St. Pauls Church, Helsby, a fashionable marriage and one in which great interest was evinced took place. The con- tracting parties were Mr. Arthur George Guest, of Beechfield, Helsby, and Miss Cassie Davies, daughter of the late Mr. W. E. Davies of Rose Farm, Helsby and the officiating minister was the Rev. W. T. Vale, vicar of the parish. The bride who was attired in gray cash- mere with silver trimmings and grey feather bon- net, was attended by Miss Parker-, of Manchester, who wore an embroidered heliotrope dress and a rustic hat trimmed with heliotrope. The best man was Mr. Walter Guest, brother of the bridegroom. The bride was given away by her mother. After the ceremony luncheon was provided in the Church schoolroom. The presents to the bride were very numerous and valuable. ST. HELENS SCHOOLS AND FREE EDUCATION.

The effect of the new Free Education Act, which I, comes into force next Tuesday, will be of a vari- able character in St.Helens. At many of the schools, fees ranging from 3d. to 6d. have been charged hitherto, and the school managers in such cases have found that to abolish the fees altogether would entail a serious pecuniary loss. To meet this diffi- culty small fees will be charged. At. the Parish Church Schools no fees will be charged in the in- fant classes, but in Standards 1,2, 3, and 4 a fee of id. will be charged, and in Standards 5,6, and 7 the fee will be 2d. No family, however, will be charged more than two fees. The Church of England schools in Sutton, Ravenhead, and St. Mark's parishes will be declared entirely free. At Parr Mount and Peasley Cross schools the infants will be free, Standards 1,2, and 3 will pay Id. per week, and standards 4,5, and 6 will pay 2d. The British School in Waterloo-street will be free for the infants and lower standards, but a fee of id. will be charged in the higher standards. The National British and Colliery schools at Ilaydock will be declared entirely free. The tame course will also be taken in regard to the Catholic schools at Lowe House, Gerard's Bridge, Holy Cross, Sacred Heart, and Sutton.
EA.ELESTOWN AND NEWTON, AND THE EDUCATION ACT.

On Monday afternoon a conference of the man- agers of the various schools in the district; was held at the Town hail, Newton. Colonel McCorquodale, presided, and there were present the Revs. Canon Whitley, T. R. Matthews, E. W. Wittenbury-Kaye, Messrs. F. G. Gillespie, W. F. Gooch, C. B. F. Borron, Thomas Molyneux, J. Starkie, J. Roberts, Joseph Massey, Drs. Watkins and Handyside, and J. Good- ing (hon. secretary). The schools represented were Wargrave, St. Peter's, and Gas-street, Newton ; St. John's National, and Wesleyan. The Catholic Schools were not represented. The minutes of a previous conference were read and confirmed, after which, the Chairman briefly stated that the meeting _ _.

had been called to take inio further consideration the question of the effect of the Public Elementary Education Act, of 1891, upon the various schools, and he asked for an expression of opinion. A man- ager, raised a discussion on the grouping of the whole of the schools, as it was thought it would be more advisable to do this and the best course to adopt under the circumstances, and it was tesolved that this should be done. A discussion Lhen took place as to the scale of fees to be charged generally in each of the schools, and it was agreed to adopt the following scale :—lnfants, free; Standards 1. and 11., twopence per week; Standard 111. and up- wards threepence per week.
J.IW. Dur;roN's SinstmEn SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.
EARLESTOWN AND THE SIR RICHARD MOON
SCHOLARSHIP.

It is now well-known that Sir Richard Moon, the late chairman of the London and North-Western Railway Company has transferred £2,000 of London and North-Western debenture stock to the Univer- sity College, Liverpool, for the founding of two annual scholarships of £4O each, for the benefit of the Company's large mechanical woiks. in connec- tion with this we have been favoured with the account of a meeting held at the Viaduct' nstitute, Earlestown, for the election of officers in connection with the management of the Institute for the cur- rent year. The meeting was held on the 13th inst., and in the course of the proceedings, the Chairman (Mr. J. W. Emmett) made a statement with respect to a communication he had received from Mr. Houghton, the secretary of the London and North- Western Railway Company, that Sir Richard Moon, their late chairman had transferred to the University College, Liverpool, £2,000 worth of London and North-Western debenture stock, to be used for scholarships, or exhibitions for the young men em- ployed in the Company's works at Crewe, Wolverton, and Earlestown, desirous of pursuing the study and practice of engineering. The fund would be knoA n as the Richard Moon Scholarship Fund. The state- ment was received amidst expressions of applause, and several members of the Committee spoke of Sir Richard's generosity. For the present the fund will be applied to the following regulations. Two scholarships will be created, each of the value of £4O per year, tenable for two years. One scholar- ship will be for competition in the course of the summer terms of each session, and the examination will be held sometime in the month of May. ' Candidates will be • examined in Mathematics, Physics, and Engineering, and every "Richard Moon" scholar will be required to employ himself wholly in the prosecution of his studies, at University College, Liverpool, or with the approval of the College Senate, in some manufacturing work- shop or institution, in such a way, as will conduce to his advancement in the science or practice of engineering. It is also provided that candidates must not be less than 16, and not more than 23 years of age, on the day appointed for the com- mencement of the examination, and they must have been employed 12 calendar months con- tinuosuly at one or other of the Company's works, named above.

Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Dobson have as yet made no sign, but that they will seek the suffrages of the rate- payers is assured. The arrangements for the election are in the hands of Mr. H. J. Grice, the chairman of the Board and so far as the antiquated and miserable system of election will allow, he is making every effort to secure the comfort and convenience of the voters.

div.head: YOUNG THIEVES AT WIDNES.
div.p: YOUNG THIEVES AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Henry Moss (13), Major Cross-st., Richard Rowbottom (14). 4, Wareing-st., John Harrison (16), Major Cross-st., John Daniels (15), Lugsdale-road, and Henry Hodgkins (15), 26, Victoria-st., were charged with stealing three purses from the shop of Mrs Caton, Widnes-road. The five boys went into the shop for some ice cream, and when they left the purses were missed. Rowbottoni, Daniels, and Moss had each a purse when arrested. The magistrates said they did not wish to send the boys to jail, but they would bind their parents to bring them up for judgment within six months if called upon. UTTERING BASE COIN AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, a respectably-dressed woman, of no fixed place of abode, who gave her name as Ada Bedford, with two men named Frederick Lloyd, Edin- burgh, and Thomas Morris, Richmond-row, Liverpool, were charged with uttering base coin in Widnes on Saturday. Tbe female prisoner purchased goods at several shops in Widnes, and tendered bad half-crowns in payment, receiving change at most of the shops. One .of the shopkeepers discovered that the half-crown she had given him was bad, and he informed the police. The prisoners were arrested that night, Lloyd as he was waiting for the last train for Liverpool. Each of the male prisoners had in his possession some of the articles purchased by the female prisoner. Superintendent Noblett asked for a remand, as he said there was another charge which would be brought against the prisoners. Tne prisoners were remanded for a week.
WIDNES MAGISTRATES AND PAWNBROKERS.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, two boys named Thomas and George Kennedy, aged respectively eleven and sixteen years, and living at 38, Major Cross- St., was charged with stealing a coat, value 10s., from the house of Eli Ireland,and further with stealing a coat belonging to J. Outram. The boys pledged the coats (with others) at the pawnshop of F. Neil, Ann-st., and the assistant to Mr. Neil stated that the boys were in the shop pawning articles as often as ten or twelve times aweek. Mr. Timmins said he had an opinion that pawnbrokers should not take articles in pawn from children not known to be sent by parents. If a child took clothing to a pawnshop ten or twelve times a week,the pawnbroker must know the articles did not belong to its parents. It was a temptation to children to steal if they knew they could easily dispose of the articles. It was monstrous. The pawnbrokers of Widnes should come to some arrangement among themselves to put a stop to this. Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the Liver- pool and District Pawnbrokers' Association,of which Mr. Neil was a member, said he would inform Mr. Neil of their worships' views. The boys were each ordered to receive four strokes of the birch rod in each case.

PRESENTATION TO THE REV. A. J. JAMESON, OF WESTON. An interesting gathering took place in Weston Church Schoolroom on Wednesday evening, the occasion being the presentation to the Rev. A. J. Jameson, the curate who had charge of St. John the Evangelist Church, for the past two and half years. There was a good atten- dance of the congregation, and the chair was occu- pied by Mr. W. Arinstiong, who in his opening speech, expressed the great sorrow felt by the parishioners at Mr. Jameson's departure for Chester. He had taken the deepest and most active interest in all parochial affairs and during his stay amongst them he had formed the Young Women's Society, and the Mothers' Meeting, and the Sunday Schools were now full. The good work Mr. Jameson had done would have a lasting effect in the parish.—Mr, Aaron on behalf of the congregation, then presented Mr. Jameson with a handsome and valu- able timepiece, and a silver pencil case, both suitably in- scribed. He endorsed the chairman's remarks, and re- ferring to the Sunday schools, said he was glad that Mr. Jamesdn had taken such a great interest in that institu- tion which was the nursery of the Church and the train- ing ground for the nation. The sick and the poor of the township had ever had Mr. Jameson's watchful care,and he had won the goodwill of the people of all denomina- tions in Weston.—The Rev. A. J. Jameson, whoappeared deeply moved, said he was quite incapable of expressing his feelings to them. Their gift was unexpected, because he has only done his duty, and his chief regret was that he had not been able to do more. He had not worked for any praise but for love of Godand the welfare of the village. J. and W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. SAnkey Street, War rington.—Advt. COLLIERY FATALITY.

On Friday, a middle-aged married man named Thomas Dowd, of Fleet-lane, Parr, St. Helens, was injured at the Collins Green Colliery by a fall of roof, a large wound being inflicted on his back. He was removed to the Providence Hospital,St. Helens, and attended by Dr. Jackson, but died in the insti- tution on Wednesday* night. J. aW. DovroN's SUMMER SLLN now on. Sankey! Street, Warrington.—Advt.

AN ARTFUL BUT UNSUCCESSFUL IMPOSTOR. On Saturday evening, about eight o'clock, an elderly man of clerical appearance called at a house in the centre of Warrington, and said he had been sent by Mr. for that gentleman's "coat and Papers." The householder had gone to spend the evening at the Public Ilan, and the caller was evi- dently aware of that fact, having probably seen him enter the building. At any rate, he knew the householder was from home, but the wife, who looked upon the man's statement with some suspi- cion, refused to entrust him with the coat and papers, and he took his departure. She subsequently went in search of her husband, and ascertained that the man who had called upon her was an impostor, and that, he had not been sent for the coat.

DEATH OF AN OLD NEWTON RESIDENT. At the age of 73 years, John McLaren, farm bailiff at the Liverpool Reformatory Farm School, died on Wednesday morning,after a very short illness. Mr McLaren is one of Newton's oldest inhabitants,hav- ing resided in the neighbourhood for over 30 years. As farm bailiff he has been employed at the Re- formatory since its institution, and by his genial manner has endeared himself to the inmates of the school, who looked up to him with the respect due to his ability and kindliness of heart. He lived a very quiet life, taking no part whatever in any public matters. lle was onlyill three weeks, dur- ing which time he was attended by Dr. Viri.itkins.
but from the first no hopes were entertained of his recovery, and he died as stated. Jc. W. Durrox's SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. - - - SUDDEN DEATH AT EARLESTOWN.

_ On Monday an old man named William Moses, 71 years of age, a joiner, of 2, Chemical-street, Earles- town, died very suddenly. He had been in ill health since Christmas last, and complained of pains in the chest,during which time he had been attended by Dr. Handyside, but he had not visited for the past six weeks. The deceased got up on Monday morning and ate his breakfast as usual, and after- wards went out for a walk. He returned at 12.55 p.m., and immediately he entered the kitchen he fell, as if in a fit. The housekeeper, Jane Hudson., called for assistance, and Bernard Dolan and Nlargaret Burke went to her aid, and together they lifted him up, but he died immediately. Dr. Handyside was sent for, but Moses was dead when he arrived. A certificate has been given by the doctor, to the effect that death was due to syncope and failure of the heart's action. div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION.
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS ELECTION.

The annual election of members of Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners takes place on Thursday next. The retiring members are six in number, viz., Messrs. James Dobson, James Prit- chard, E. Imison, W. Mellor, J. W. Lightburn and W. R. Wass, and there are therefore six places to be filled. Mr. Mellor and Mr. Imison do not intend to offer them- selves for re-election, and it is a matter of regret that two gentlemen who have served the ratepayers for so many years, should decline to again ask them for their suffrages. Mr. Imison has for several years been the chairman of the Finance Committee and in that capacity he has done most important and valuable work. A depu- tation of the temperance party waited upon him on Wednesday evening and expressed a strong wish that a gentleman of so original and independent a mind should consent to again become a member of the Board, but Mr. Imison's decision was unalterable and the deputa tion retired disappointed. Of the other retiring members, Mr. Wass issued his address early in the week and may be perused in our advertising columns. Mr. Was promises to de- vote the time necessary to the position of Commis- sioner and announces that he is in earnest sympathy with all questions affecting the health, welfare and prosperity of the town. He mentions particularly baths, recreation grounds and a highway bridge connecting Runcorn and Widnes and puts in the important and commendable proviso that he would not unreasonably increase the rates, or impose a heavy burden upon the present and future ratepayers. Mr. Lightburn issued his address yesterday, and the copy which appears in our columns will well repay perusal. He draws attention to a record of work done, which would do credit to any public man, and mentions a work for the consideration of the future Board of the most vital importance to the future growth and pros- perity of the town. We refer to the extending of the boundary of the Commissioners district, upon which hinge other and highly important advantages to the town and neighbourhood. This extension of the boundaries, he says, unlike the Temperance Question over which the Law gives the Commissioners not the , least control, is essentially a work for the Board, and ought to receive the attention its vast importance demands. The temperance party was the first in the field with their candidates, Mr. Daniel Bisbrown and Mr. Thomas Lea, and they are prosecuting the election canvass with vigour. The Women's Temperance Society have volun- teered their aid and several of the members are engaged in the attempt to allure the voters to the polling booth in favour of their chosen champions. The evils of the drink traffic are referred to with considerable force, and the candidates pledge themselves to bring forward and support measures to secure the greatest comfort and convenience of the ratepayers. They are strongly in favour of the proposal to unite Runcorn and Widnes by a cart-road, promise to support any well considered scheme for providing baths, and are strongly of opinion that all contracts for town improvements should be car- ried out by local firms. Another new candidate for local honours is Mr. Isaac Stubbs the mineral water manufacturer, who issues an address that may be read in our columns. He comes forward on the appeal of an influential section of the ratepayers and promises to use his energy, and ability and knowledge for the advancement of the interests of the town ; which he with truth states are susceptible of much improvement. Mr. Stubbs promises to give special

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of the Widnes School Board was held on Tuesday, at the Town Hall. The following members were present :—Mr. T. S. Tim mis (chairman), Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell, Major Wareing, and Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, C. E. Bar- low, and B. Brown.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

The Committee reported that during the month of July the number of applications for payment of fees was 136. The fees Ix ere recommended to be paid in 126 cases, and 10 were refused. There had been 79 persons sum- moned before the Committee for neglecting to send their children to school.—Mr. Deacon, in moving the adoption of the minutes of this Committee, said that they were obliged to prosecute a man for assaulting an attendance officer whilst in the execution of his duty. He had been proseCuted previously for not sending his children to school. He was fined 203. for the assault. The District Education Committee authorized the prosecution for the assault, as they had not time to wait for the Board meet- ing, and he (Mr. Deacon) hoped the Board would agree with what had been done.—The Chairman said they were perfectly right in prosecuting the man. Their officers must be protected in doing their duty.—Major Wareing thought that they ought to have some compen- sation for the damage done to the officer's clothing.—The minutes were then adopted.

div.head: TME \VAT TO MARRIAGE..
div.p: TME \VAT TO MARRIAGE..

Mr. Barlow asked that the minutes of the School Man- agement Committee be allowed to stand over for another meeting, as the Committee had not completed their ar- rangements with regard to the changes in the teaching staff.—The Chairman (referring to the numerous resigna- tions in the minutes) said :Arc' they all getting married ? —Mr. Barlow : Yes, I think so.—The Chairman : Girls have nothing to do if they want to he married but get under the School Board. (Laughter.)

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Clerk then read a letter from the L.eds School Board, asking the Widnes Board to join them in petition- ing for power to be grantel to the teachers to remove the children from one standard to another at their own discretion.—Mr. Deacon : What is the exact point they wish to bring, before us ?—The Clerk said that at present the children were removed from one standard to another by the inspector, but the Leeds Board wanted their teachers to have that power.—The Clerk was ultimately instructed to write to the Leeds Board regretting their inability to combine with them.—A letter was read from the School Attendance Committee of the Chorlton Union with regard to truant school accommodation in Lanca- shire,and asking the Board to petition with them for help from the County Council to provide more truant accom- modations.—Mr. Deacon said he thought this was very desirable.—The Clerk said he had prepared a petition for the purpose.—The matter was then left with the District Education Committee.—This was all the business.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present Messrs. Mclntyre (chairman), J. Baguley, E. Aaron, T. Lewis Edwards, Brandreth, Hewitt, IL Knowles, J. Whit- low, J. Weir, J. Ashton (clerk).

div.head: NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
div.p: THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR.
Mr. Aaron gave notice that at the next meeting of the\ Authority he would move the reappointment of Mr. Farrington as nuisance inspector at the same salary.
SCARLET FEVER.
Dr. Adams reported an outbreak of one case of scarlet fever, and two cases of diptheria, and said the usual precautions had been taken.
XECKWICK BROOB.

The Cleik said he had served Messrs. Earp and Co., tanners, of Preston Brook, with a copy of the notice that proceedings would be taken with regard to the pollution of Keckwick Brook and Mr. Earp had acknowledged receipt.
FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME.

Mr. Edwards asked when notice had been given to the Frodsham Gas and Water Company, that their powers as to water supply had ceased. The Clerk replied that notice was given, he believed, in the late Clerk's time, but it was a question he ought to have had notice of, as it was not in the minute book he had with him. In reply to further questions, the Clerk said the Public Health Act overrode the Frodsham Water Act, and if the Company did not do the work in a certain time the Authority could do so. Mr. Edwards quoted the follow- ing clauses from the Company's Act. " The powers of the Company for the compulsory purchase of lands for the purposes of this Act, shall not be exercised after the expiration of three years after the passing of this Act in respect of lands required for the gas undertaking, and seven years in respect of lands required for the water undertaking."- -" If the waterworks authorised by this Act are not completed within ten years from the passing of this Act, then on the expiration of that period the powers by this Act granted to the Company for executing the same shall cease to be exercised, except as to much thereof as is then completed, but nothing herein shall restrict the Com- pany from altering or renewing any of their works from time to time as occasion requires. for supplying water within the limits of this Act."—The Clerk said these clauses were fully considered at the time.—Mr. Edwards gave notice that at the last meeting he should move that the resolution passed at the last meeting with regard to Frodsham Water Scheme be rescinded.-.-The Clerk said unless they were going to take away the powers of the Frodshain Committee that notice would be given to the Frodsham Committee.—Mr. Edwards replied that the Authority was supreme ; the Parochial Committee was simply an inquiry Corn mittee.—The Clerk said it was nothing of the sort. The Committee could not spend money but every other power of the authority was dele- gated to the Committee. He quoted from the Public Health Act to show this. Mr. Edwards should have the resolution rescinded at a meeting of the Committee.— Mr. Edwards said his moti4n would be to rescind the resolution of that Authority approving of the recommendation pf the Parochial Committee. At the meeting of the Committee there was only the mover and seconder in favour of the proposal and that was how 23.000 of public money had to be spent. There had not been even a ratepayers' meeting.—Mr. Lewis suNested that Mr. Edwards as an overseer should call a meeting of ratepavers.—Mr. Aaron: Very good suggestion. (Mr. Hewitt: hear, hear.)—Mr. Edwards persisted in giving his notice and also moved that Mr. Timmins be requested to send in his bill of expenses incurred up to the present. —The Clerk: That is a matter you ought to bring before the Frodsham Committee. I shall rule that that must be done.—Several members approved stating that other- wise the Committee might as well be dissolved.—The discussion then ceased, but at a later part of the proceed- ings the Clerk read the followine clause, under which notice had been given to the 'Frodsham Water Com- pany, thowing that the Authority could do the work: Before commencing to construct waterworks within the limits of any water company empowered by Act of Par- liament to supply water, the local authority shall give written notice to every water company within whose limits of supply the local authority are desirous of sup- plying water, stating the purposes for which, and (as far as may be practicable) the extent to which water is re- quired by the local authority. It shall not be lawful for the local authority to construct any waterworks within such limits if and so long as any such company are able and willing to supply water proper and sufficient for all reasonable purposes for which it is required by the local authority; and any difference as to whether the water which any such company are able and willing to lay on is proper and sufficient for the purposes for which it is required, or whether the purposes for which it is re- quired are reasonable, or (if and so far as the charges of the company are not regulated by Parliament) as to the terms of supply, shall be settled by arbitration in a man- ner provided by this Act.

div.head: PUTRID BONRS AT FRODSHAM.
div.p: PUTRID BONRS AT FRODSHAM.
Mr. H. C. Chapman, of Sandon, Frodsham,wrote com- plaining of a nuisance from putrid bones at Frodsham Railway Station, and the Inspector was instructed to in- vestigate the matter.

FRODSHAM SEWER TAVS. The Inspector stated that there had been no necessity for him to prepare a report respecting these tanks, as the suggestions he had given to the engineers in reference to them had been carried out by the Ship Canal Company in a satisfactory manner.
DEFECTIVE SEWER IN DARE-LANE, HELSBY. A report of the Committee appointed at the last meet- ing to inspect this sewer was received and adopted.

NEW HOUSES AT HYLSBY. A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. W. Musgrove, of Helsby, for four new houses erected by him at Helsby, the water supplied thereto being returned by the analyst as first class. IMPROVEMENT OF A PUBLIC PUMP AT SUTTON. The Inspector reported that he had applied to two contractors for tenders for this improvement, but he had only been able to obtain one, and it was decided that he endeavour to get two others and submit the same to the next meeting. NUISANCES AND UNHEALTHY DWELLINGS AT WESTON POINT.

The Inspector reported a nuisance as existing at Weston Point arising from an offensive ditch, and direc- tions were given for final notice to be served. It was also reported that certain dwellings at the same place were in an unhealthy condition, and at the suggestion of the Inspector, the matter was referred to the Medical Officer of Health for his report thereon. Nuisances arising from overflowing privies, Sze., at Weston Point were also reported, and the usual orders were given relative therao. DEFECTIVE SEWER AT STRETTON. • A communication was read trom the Surveyor to the
Daresbury Highway Board, relating to a defectivesewer at Stretton, and the Inspector was directed to attend to the matter. NUISANCE ON PREMISES AT LUMB-lIROOK, APPLETON.

The Inspector applied for and obtained instrualOns to serve a final notice upon the owner of certain premises situate at Lumb-brook, Appleton, for the abatement of a nuisance thereon. This was all the business.
FATAL COLLISION ON THE MERSEY
NEAR RUNCORN.

On Tuesday, at Runcorn Burial Board Offices, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner for the fee of Halton, held an adjourned inquest on the body of Elizabeth A. Paton, who was drowned in the Mersey on the 6th instant through a collision between the fiat Argyle and the coasting vesselJames.—llenry Brown, a sea captain, residing at 22, Waterloo-road, Runcorn, said he wit- nessed the collision. At the time he was going down to Liverpool on board the steamer Queen of the Mersey, which had eleven flats in tow, five on one side and six on the other. The Argyle was the last fiat. The captain of the James attempted to cross the steamer's bow, but when he saw that he could not manage it he tried to get past her stern. He thought the captain of the James had not noticed that there were six flats on one side, and therefore miscalculated the distance, and came in collision with the Argyle, which immediately sank. Witness did not hear that a woman was drowned until he reached Liverpool. He would not like to say that there had been any real negligence on the part of the captain of the James, but he was of opinion that if a proper watch had been kept the collision could have been averted.—William Ashton, of 8, Terrace-road, Widnes, said lie was captain of the James. He attempted to cross the bows of the steamer, but failed, and in then trying to pass the stern he came in collision with the Argyle. Had the steamer given way a little the collision would not have occurred. Asked by a juror if it was not the rule for a sailing vessel to give way to a steamer, witness replied that it was not. He heard someone shout that a woman was drowning, and he looked from stem to stern of his vessel but could not see anyone in the water. He then sailed on and ran the James aground.—George Turner, 18, West-st., Widnes, seaman, corroborate this evidence, and, in reply to a juror, said the captain was sober at the time. —After a long consideration in private, the jury returned a verdict g " Accidental death."

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. James Burchall presided and there were also present the Rev. S. K. Sylvester, 4ev. Dean Finegan, M.r. T. Stapleton-Bretherton, J. P.,Messrs. Johnson. Lowe, Middlehurst, Borrows, Waring, Ken- wright, Syder, Whalley, Davies, Goldsworth, and Mr. A. F. Mann (clerk)._

AGED MARRIED COUPLES IN THE WORKHOUSE.—The Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Visiting Committee which included a recommendation, that accommodation be provided at the Workhouse for 12 aged married couples who may be desirous of living together. 1-I,i explained that the pro- vision of some such accommodation was forced upon the Guardians by the Local Government Board. After some discussion the subject was referred to the Building Com- mittee.

THE ALLEGED VACCINATION IRREGULARITIES AT ST. HELENS.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board dated the 24 August acknowledging the receipt of a copy of a communication from Dr. McNicoll, the public vaccinator of the St. Helens district, in explana- tion of the irregularities reported against him by the Board's Inspector after his recent inspection of public vaccination in the union. The Board had given the communication their careful consideration and stated that if the guardians desired to retain Dr. McNicoll's ser- vices as public vaccinator they would not, on this occa- sion, press forhis resignation, provided that he furnished the guardians with a written undertaking that he would in future, strictly comply with all the requirements of of his vaccination contract and the regulations of the Local Government Board. A copy of the undertaking should be forwarded to the Board with the Guardians' letter. In any case where a deputy was admitted to act fora public vaccinator in his occasional and unavoidable absence, the appointment of such deputy should be endorsed on the vaccination contract and the endorse- ment submitted to the Board, accompanied by particu- lars of the deputy's professional qualifications and the special certificate of proficiency in vaccination required under the regulations of the Ist December, 1859.—The Clerk added that he had forwarded a copy of the letter to Dr. McNicoll.—Dr. McNicoll wrote in reply on the 26th inst., stating that he was prepared at once to comply with the order given in the letter from the Local Govern- ment Board asid would thereby undertake to carry out the agreements of his vaccination contract and the regu- lations of the Local Government Board both in the spirit and in the letter. Ho nominated Dr. Fred Knowles, M.R.C.S., and L.R.C.P., as his deputy.—The Guardians unanimously decided to accept Dr. McNicoll's explana- tion and that his services be retained. Dr. Fred Knowles was appointed deputy vaccination officer. ESTIMATE OF EXPENDITURE.—The Clerk submitted his estimate of probable expenditure by the Guardians for the half year ending March next. The total estimate was £21,442, with ten percent. added for contingencies £2,144 ; total 23,586. The actual expenditure last year was £23,481. The estimate was unanimously ap- proved...... _ _

- THE WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—The Rev. Dean Finegan tendered the thanks of the Widnes School Board to the Guardians for the satisfactory manner in which the arrangements between the two authorities had worked during the past fifteen years in regard to the payment of school fees.—The Chairman said he was sure the Guardians were glad to acknowledge the comp liment. This was the principal business.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AND FREE
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD AND FREE
EDIJCATION.

The monthly meeting of Runcorn School toard was held on Tue•day night, Mr. J. Pritchard pre- siding. Present Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. Dr. Gas- taldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. J. J. Howitt, A. Salkeld, and G. Mess (Clerk). The chief business was the consi4eration of the folloving motion of which the Chairman had given notice "That the fee grant be accepted and that no fees be charged in schools belonging to the Board on and after the Ist Sepiember, 1891. The Board went into Com- mitte to discuss the question, and the reporters were not called into the room until the lapse of an hour and a half.

The Chairman explained that the adjournment of the consideration of this question from the meeting held a week ago was in consequence of a printed balance sheet of the schools having been received showing that cer- tain items that had been received out of the rates amounting to £156 to make up the deficiency for the working expenses of the Board schools, and because he thought it was proper that the members should have some time to consider the subject, and also because there were certain members absent who would support the adoption of the Act. It was also suggested at the time that a conference should take place of the school man- agers. Up to the present no satisfactory arrangement had been made, and had they been able to come to some arrangement as to the provision of a certain number of free places with the denominational schools, he felt sure it would have, been satisfactory to the ratepayers at large. lie went on to state that the amount paid out of the rates in Ail of the schools amounted to 4s 10d. per scholar, and ~is they would have to further charge if they adopt,. Free Education, or between £3O and £4O out of the rates. It was evident that the denominational schools would not be able to give freeeducation, because they were not in a position to place the deficiency upon the rates. So should the denominational managers make a small charge of a penny fee or so: it ought to be con- sidered reasonable and acceptable without agitation. The deficiency of the Board schools was only a small one, but if all the children in the town were educated in the Board schools instead of as at present four-fifths in the voluntary schools, the deficiency would amount to something like £9OO or £l,OOO without considering any rent or building of schools. Speaking with reference to the 8111, he said it encouraged education, but it was not compulsory upon School Board managers to adopt it. There was no doubt that the aim of the Education Act was to abolish fees,and certainly to greatly reduce them, and if they were to make the schools free, it would pro- bably meet the requirements of the Act. The Chairman then moved the resolution of which he had given notice. The Rev. Canon Wood said it was quite a mistake to suppose that those who supported denominational schools supported them for denominational reasons. They supported them because they thought they were good for the town, and for both reasons. He bad hoped that the suggestion which came from him—that a confe- rence of school managers should be held—might have i resulted n the whole of the denominational schools see- ing their way to mike a larger number of free places in them. Then the parents who desired to take advantage of free education could send their children to any school they chose. He hoped, however, they would go on in the same friendly way in future as in the past. He se- conded the chairman's resolution.

Mr. Howitt said he had great pleasure in supporting it. He said he had been referred to as one who posed as a free educationalist from the first. and that was perfectly true. With regard to his absence from the last meeting, he said he was given to understand that the Board was practically unanimous on the subject. He had always been in favour of free education, and when he joined the Board he suggested that they should petition Parliament in favour of such a Bill. At the time the members expressed themselves in favour of such a Bill, but said that the time was inopportune. The time had come, and the Government had decided the matter to some extent for them. lie ;hoped the adoption of the Act would 1;)e unanimous, and that the schools in Runcorn mieht prosper in the future as they had done in the past. He was also pleased to learn that the Board had taken action with regard to the provision

of science and art classes. They were a success last year, and he hoped they would be a success again. Dr. Gastaldi supported the motion on the grounds as he said, that he had been the first to adopt free educa- tion in his schools. He would benefit by it, and there- fore he was not sorry that he had accepted it. He contended that its operation would increase the effici- ency of the education, and do away with the levy on the Guardians which new existed. Dr. McDougall also supported the resolution. The Chairman had made the remark that he (the chairman) was afraid that if he had pressed his motion at the last meeting he would have found some of the .members hostile to it; but so far as his knowledgewent, there was not one single member who would have opposed it, only for one reason, that it was possible that some arrange- ment might be made with denominational schools with' regard to a larger number of free places. The School Board would give 605 free places, and if they could have been able to provide 300 free places more, then he con- sidered for that reason the adjournment of that meeting was a very reasonable one. He contended that eventu- ally, if the free educati,na scheme was carried to a legiti- mate issue. the School Board rate would be 7d. in the instead of 4d. With regard to the £3O deficiency at present, it was so small that it was not worth while dis- cussing. _ _ _

Mr. 'Salkeld said he hoped that the school pence thus saved would not be spent in drink, but that the parents would put it away, and it would become a nice sum for the children when they came of age. (Hear. hear.) The motion was carried unanimously. It was also decided, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Elowitt, that the children have a holiday on Monday, and that the schools open free on Tuesday, the Ist September.
MR. 710 WITT'S RESIGNATION.

Mr. Hewitt said as that was the last meeting of the Board he would attend, he begged to thank them for the way in which he had been treated since he became a member. He was very sorry to sever his connection with the Board.

Dr. McDougall expressed his regret that Mr. Howitt found it necessary to resign his seat owing to having changed his residence. Dr. Gastaldi also regretted his resignation, and said he hoped his, successor would enter into his work with the energy and zeal with which Mr. Howitt had dene. The Rev. Canon Wood said he was sorry that Mr. Howitt was leaving them. He had always found him straightforward, and one with whom it was almost a pleasure to have a combat with. The Chairman also spoke in similar terms. Mr. Howitt said there was nothing he regretted more than giving up his seat on the Board. With regard to the discussions which they had had, he said he did not care a fig for a man who had not his own opinions. He appreciated their conduct towards him as a member of the Board, and said their actions had been based on principle and not on personalities. He thapked them for their kind expressions. The meeting then coneuded.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present, Messrs. J. Baguley, J. W. Baguley, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, Edwards, Brandreth, Hewitt, H. Knowles, 3. Whithiw, T. Lea, and J. Ashton (clerk). THE LUNATICS' purl

A letter was read from the Lunacy Commissioners stating that Mr. Phillips, one of the inspectors, had visited the Workhouse and found everything well con- ducted. He, however, suggested that three meat dinners should be provided instead of two as at present, and that the inmates in the lunacy department should have a bathe once a week instead of once a month. The subject was referred to the Medical Officer.

MB. 11. G. LINAKER. A letter was read from Mr. H. G. Linaker, threatening legal proceedings, unless his claim for services rendered were settled at once. The Clerk was instructed to reply that the matter would be considered after the audit on the 30th September.
VACCINATION OFFICER WANTED. The Clerk was instructed to advertise for a Vaccina- tion Officer far Runcorn, in place of Mr. Coleburn resigned.

div.head: LEGAL EXPENSES.
div.p: LEGAL EXPENSES.
On the motion of Mr. Edwards, seconded by Mr. Lea, it was resolved that the Clerk prepare a return of all the legal expenses incurred and paid for by the Union for the last six years.
MR. AARON AND THB COUNTY COUNCIL AGAIN.

Mr. Brandreth moved the passing of accounts amounting to £1,902, which included £1,648 55., half of the county call for the past half year.—Mr. Aaron ob- jected to the payment of the county call until they had received a balance sheet from the County Council. There was no telling what extravagant use would be made of the money, seeing they had increased the cost of the sur- veyor's department from £5OO to £1,890.--The Clerk said they had had a balance sheet for the year ending March, 1890.—Mr. Aaron: Not for 1891.—Mr. Knowles: They don't give no returns as quick astha.t.—Mr.Aaroa : 'When the magistrates had the power, we always saw how the money was spent. There has not been a ba- lance sheet received since the County Council was formed, and I propose that the call be not paid until we re- ceive a balance sheet for 1891.—Mr. Brandreth : Begin at your township meeting by refusing to pay the Guar- dians' precept until they give a statement.—Mr. Aaron: If the Guardians did not receive their call the overseers would soon be summoned. Their Clerk gives a state- ment of the income and expenditure each half year, but here is a call for £l,OOO more than usual, and not a word of how it is to be spent. I move that the call be not paid.—Mr.Weir seconded.—The Chairman: I cannot entertain the amendment. We don't want to look ridi- culous.—Mr. Edwards: It ought to be put to the meet- ing.—The Chairman: Very well, gentlemen, if you wish to knock your heads against a stone wall.—The amend- ment was lost by nino votes to two, and the accoanta were passed.

div.head: RUNCORN SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES'
div.p: RUNCORN SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES'

The Committee of the Science and Art Classes met on Monday evening in the Town Hall, Mr. F. Wiswall in the chair. The Honorary Secretary, Mr..' John Poole, reported that the classes had been very successful and that 61 students entered for 7 sub- jects. Out of this number 48 presented themselves in May last for examination, 37 of whom passed successfully. The Chairman said great credit was due to the teacher Mr. Thos. A. Cook,of Northvrich, who had conducted the classes and obtained such excellent results. He was glad to be able to say that the classes on an extended scale would be continued during the coming winter season, though under another committee,as it had been arranged that the members of the School Board, along with representatives of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, should act as a committee fur carrying on evening classes, for teaching special subjects under the Technical Education Act. He trusted they would be as successful in the coming session as they had been in the past. A unanimous vote of thanks was given to Mr. John Poole for his services as honorary secretary. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
CHARGE AGAINST A CONSTABLE OF ASSAULTING A CHILD.

At the magistrates' court on Monday, Walter Brown was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Pier- point-st., on the 18th inst. P.C. Clough deposed to the facts of the case. The defendant accused the constable of "Laying on" to a little girl named Weaver with a stick, and requested that she might be called and that her body might be examined to prove her ill-usage: The girl was sworn and said the constable came up to her and struck her six or seven times on the back for nothing and did not say what it was for.—Alderman Harrison said this was incredible.—P.C. dough: Your worship, she is telling untruths.--The girl was taken out of court akthe request of the Bench, and examined by Mrs. Knight,who subsequently deposed that she had one mark on her body, which was yellow, and not on the back.— P.C. Clough said onthe day in question he was looking after some young men who were playing at pitch and toss, and the girl ran to warn them that he was coming. He pushed her and told her to go home or he would have to lock her up.—Alderman Harrison: She was acting as a sort of agent for them.—P.C. Clough: Yes, sir.—The Mayor: Well, you thought so.—Chief Constable Hunt: Did you knock dust out of her clothes? If you did say so.—P.C. Clough: No sir, I did not.—The defendant was fined se.
A " FAMOUS " Youiu.

At the Police Court, on Tuesday morning, the lad John Warrington, was charged with absconding from the Union on the previous morning, taking with him some clothing, the property of the Guarthans.—Mr. Curry, porter, stated the facts of the case. " The prisoner had been in the house since the 11th August, and yesterday he applied to the Master for a day's leave of absence. His application was refused, and he told him he should "go over the wall." Subsequently witness saw the lad trying to escape and he brought him back. Warrington, later on, got out, but was apprehended.—Mr. R. Gar- net (the presiding magistrate) : What do you want to do with him 2—Mr. Currey: He is no good in the house.— After some consideration, the Bench decided to order the lad's return to the workhouse.

div.head: MORE RAILWAY STATION ROWDYISM.
div.p: MORE RAILWAY STATION ROWDYISM.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, Thos. Moran and Robert Potts were charged with being drunk and disorderly at the Central Station, the previous night and assaulting David Pugh, ticket collector, on the same occasion. Pugh said that on the arrival of the 650 p.m. express from Manchester, he collected tickets from the train, and found the prisoners in a third-class compart- , ment with tickets from Manchester to Warrington. He requested them to come out as they had reached their station,and Moran helped him to get Potts out, he being asleep, but as soon as he had done so struck witness vio- lently. got hold of his vest and tore it, and said he would kill him. Potts also struck him and knocked and pushed bim away. A porter named Ranson came and took Potts away. It was stated that Ranson had been injured and could not walk, therefore could not appear. A railway constable having given evidence, P.S. Chandler 'deposed to the abusive and threatening language to Pugh. Four or five of them had to carry Moran part of the way to the Police Station. His language was fearful.—Moran was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and 103. and costs for the assault, and Potts 53. and costs in each case ; in default they went to jail as the alterna- tive.

A LODGING-HOUSE AFFRAY. Eliza Anderson, a married woman, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st. the previous afternoon. P.C. Corbett deposed that he was called to eject the defend- ant from Preston's lodging-house in Bank-st., where he found her drunk. A very serious fight was going on in the house, and Mr. Preston was bleeding from the head and the defendant from the mouth. Both witness and Mr. Preston and her husband asked her to go away, but she was very determined ,and said she would ram a knife into Mr. Preston before she went out. Witness, P.C. Barlow, and Mr. Preston had to take her forcibly into the street. Mr. Preston was now ill in bed in conse- quence of the blows she had given him, and he could not get up.—P.C. Barlow corroborated as to the prisoner's conduct.—lnspector Spinks said on Thursday the 20th Inst., it was reported to the police that a man had been robbed at the lodging-house of £2 103. 7d. Preston had since been brought up and fined under the lodging-house bye-laws, and since then a great deal of bickering had been going on.—Sergeant Monaghan and he (the inspec- tor) went to the house on Saturday to investigate as to the robbery, and the inmates had been charging one another and the police had to go several times to quell the disturbances. Preston was very badly injured in the forehead. He said the prisoner had struck him with a cup and she admitted this, but stated that he struck her with a fork on the shoulder, where she had three wounds which might have been produced by a fork.—The prisoner was remanded till Saturday for the appearance of Preston.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATuanAT.—Before Aldermen Burgess (in the chair) and Chandley, Councillor Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes.
6E- S—E RTER .—Georm.b Wilson' and Henry Letts were charged with being deserters from the Durham Light Infantry.—The prisonars pleaded guilty.—They were sent to Strangeways Gaol to await an escort.

Mosnay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb), and Aldermen Sutton, Harriscn, and Greenall. DRIINIC LNDDISORDERLY.—EIiza Smith,is Buttermarket- st., on Saturday afternoon, a month's hard labour.—John Mulcrow, in Winwick-st., on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Joseph Elliott, iron worker on the Ship Canal. was • charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bank Quay Station, on Saturday night, He came to the station about nine o'clock and asked for a ticket for Moore, and was told there was no train for Moore, but that he could book to Dareshury. He was in an advanced state of in- toxication and became very violent,and used threatening and beastly language to the booking clerk. He refused his name and address, and was taken to the police station, being very violent all the way, and it taking two officers nearly three quarters of an hour to get him there. He threatened to shoot a station official when he had" done his time."-20s. and costs, or a month's hard labour.— Annie Dooley. drunk and disorderly, on Town Hill, on Saturday night, 103. and costs.—Emtna Robinson, from Manchester, in Bewsey-st., the same night, discharged. —Sarah Ann Garland, in Sankey-st., at 12.40 on Sunday morning.—She was discharged.—Michael Callaghan, in Bridge-st., on Sunday nigha month's imprisonment. Samuel Parker, in Naylor-st., on Saturday night, also in the same street on the 16th inst., 10s. and costs.—John Derkin,in Friar's-green, early that morning. 7 days' hard labour. P.C. Turner,not a big constable.proved the case, and was complimented by the Mayor for tackling such a big fellow as the prisoner at one o'clock in the morning. —Thomas Kearney, in Jolley's Yard, on the 15th inst., 3s. 6d.—Michael Davitt, in St. James's-st., on the 15th inst., ss.—John Dutton, in Winwiek-st., on the 20th inst. —The Mayor; Is is not time you turned over anew leaf? 32 years ago you were fined ss. and costs.—He was now fined ss.—Alfred Guest,in Naylor-st., on the 16th inst.,ss. and costs.—Bridget and Mary Toole. in Bakehouse Yard, on the 15th inst.—Bridget 2s-. 6d., and Mary ss. FIGHTING.—SamueI Heaton and Thomas Burke, for fighting in Cairo-se., on the 17th inst., were each bound -over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months..

Robert Pearson, for fighting in Wilderspool Causeway on the lath init.' was similarly dealt with. CHARGE OF WIFE ASSAD/LT.—Joseph Oakes was charged under a free warrant granted to his wife Margaret Oakes with assaulting her. The complainant did not appear. Mr. Browne, solicitor, on behalf of the defendant, repre- sented that she had admitted to him that she was not blameless and she did not wish to press the case, and the defendant did not admit assaulting her. The defend- ant was dismissed on payment of costs, Alderman Harrison strongly protesting against the conduct of the complainant in not appearing after being favoured with a free warrant.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF SoNs.—John Flannighan,tanner, Hopwood-st., and Thomas Knockton, labourer, Erwood- st., charged with non-contribution for maintenance of their sons in-St. Anne's Industrial School, had an order for is. 6d. a week made against each of them.—John Dumbill. striker, Chorley-st., charged with a like offence as to Blakeney reformatory school, was ordered to pay Is. a week.

FURIOUS Drerviso.—Wm. Rowbottam, cattle dealer, of Northwich, for furiously driving on Monday night in Wilderspool Causeway, was fined the costs, lie. JUVENILE CARD PLAYERS.—Harry McCormick, Peter Knight, John Ede'sten, Harry Martin, and Herbert Apple- ton, boys, were charged with playing cards for money in the New-road on the 16th inst., and discharged with a caution.
TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. M.
Crosfield.

MISCELLANEOUS.—WiIIiam Lythgoc, a youngman, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly the pre- vious evening and was fined ss. including costs.—Two lads, named Albert Bate and Andrew Carrington, were charged with having stolen a quantity of sweets valued at 3s. 6d. from the shop of Caroline Ratcliffe in Lyth- goe's-lane. They both pleaded guilty to having taken sweets,though not the quantity they were charged with. It was ordered that each of them should receive six strokes with the birch-rod, six strokes that evening, and six the next morning.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman), Councillor John 14'airclough and Mr, John Geddes.

DRUNK AND DisoanariLY.---William Coates, drunk and disorderly in Bank-st. the previous morning, ss.—Annie Quinn, in Buttermarket-st. the same day ss. and costs. —Elizabeth Hewitt in Buckley--st., the same day, whose hands the officer proving the case said were bleeding in consequence of her smashing some windows, ss. A DRUNKEN Rumaii.—George Banks, of B ollins Green, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Tues- day night in Winwick-st., and assaulting and beating Mary Ann Travick, of 3, Rose-st.—The complainant said the defendant had been guilty of conduct near her door which amounted to indecency, as her daughter passed, and witness went to the door and remonstrated with him, upon which he used scandalous language. She followed him to see if she could see a constable, and he struck her with his fist.—The defendant said he merely pushed her because she "raised the place" about him and "blackguarded him all to pieces" through the street.— Mr. Bennett, hairdresser, said he saw the defendant knock her down opposite .his shop.—He was tined 10s. and costs, in default 14 days' imprisonment.
THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Alder- man Wright, Councillor James Fairclough, and Captain Ridgway. . .

DRUNK AND DISORDERir.John Armstrong was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., the previous afternoon. A constable said he was called into Mr. Alderman Chandley's office in Bridge-st. to eject the defendant as he was abusive to Mr. Cliandley, who was his employer, and would not go out. He was drunk and fell down when ejected.—Alderman Chandley, who was seated at the solicitors' table,made an unsworn statement corroborating the constable's evidence.—Alder- man Sutton: Would you taks him back, Mr. Chandley, if he prdmised to behave better P—Alderman Chand ley : No, certainly not.— The defendant was fined 55., in default seven days.
FILIDAY.—Berore Mr. John White (chairman) and Alder-
man Harrison.
VAGRANCY.—James Cu mmi ngs. charged with sleeping behind the furnace at Dallam Forge the previous night, was dismissed on promising to leave the town, unless he got. work. _ _ _ .

- NON-MAINTENANCE OF A SON.—Edward Whitehouse was charged with not contributing to the maintenance of his son Joseph on board the Clio. He was ordered to pay 2s. a week. AN ABSENTEE FROM Wonx.—Ellen Ogden was charged with disobedience of an order of the magistrates to return to her work at Mr. Edmund Mills's fustian-cutting fac- tory. The defendant hung down her head continuously, although requested to look up.—Alderman Harrison re- marked that the defendant wanted them to look at her hat.—Mr. Mills said she came to work at breakfast time and went away when she liked. She was off eight hours a day.—Alderman Harrison: Her demeanour in court proves that she does not intend to behave any better.— Mr. Mills said he would not like her to go to prison, if she would do anything like, but others took example by her and stopped away.—The defendant was ordered to be sent to prison for 14 days, provided she did not return to work in a week.

CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Joseph Lightfoot, a boy, was charged with cruelty to a horse by workinoblt while in an th unfit state on the 15th inst. and ElizabeLightfoot, his mother, was charged with causing the horse to be so worked.—lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said the horse was lame and suffering from disease of the joints, had a wound the size of a five shilling piece under the saddle; and had also a running tumour.—They were fined ls:and costs each.—T. Scattergood, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on the 21st inst., and Wm. Gilboddy, was charged with causing the same to be so worked.—lnspector Dowty said the horse was drawing a spring cart and there was a large running wound under the girth, which was rubbing against it.—Gilboddy said he took the horse to Mr. Ferguson, veterinary surgeon, and he told him it was fit to work if he kept the strap from rubbing the wound.—lnspector Bowen corrobo- rated Mr. Dowty'sevidence.—Gilboddy said he was only using the horse to take the cart to be repaired.—Mr. Whitehead. tea dealer, of Market-st., owner of the horse and cart, made an unsworn statement from the body of the court that it was_quite possible to keep the belly band from rubbing the wound. He asked the Bench to examine the horse.—Scattergood was fined the cost of the summons and Gilboddy. 10s. and costs. A WOMEN'S QUARREL.—Margaret Flannaghan, of Orford-lane, was charged with assaulting Mary Hart, keeper of two lodging-houses in Stanley-st., and wife of Thomas,Hart, forgeman, on the 20th inst. Mr. R. Davies appeared for the prosecution.—The defendant, it was stated, had used offensive language to the complainant and threatened to jump on her and,,pull her liver out if anybody would hold her (the defendant's) child and on a man doing so struck Mrs. Hart two violent blows on the head.—The defendant pleaded that the complainaut had previously thrown beer at her at the Star and Garter public-house, but admitted having first used an offensive expression to her.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months; in default a month's imprisonment.

div.head: DARESBUItY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBUItY PETTY SESSIONS.

TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. Parr, Long, and Nield. DRUNK AND DISORDRRRY.—Thos. Hardy, at London Bridge, on the 16th inst., ss. and costs.—Jane Yonge, at Appleton, on the 15th inst., who it was stated had knocked her husband down in the street, he being drunk at the time, 2s. 6d..a,nd costs.—John Miller, at Stretton, on the 28th ult., 53. and costs.—Ellen Percival was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Appleton, and it was stated had been abusive to a constable and a busman, but her defence was that this was not true, and that she only remonstrated with the busman for giving her 2d. instead of 10d. change out of a shilling. ss. in- cluding costs.—John Curley, drunk and disorderly at Appleton, on the 16th inst., ss. including costs. DRUNK.—EIIen Bower,drunk at Little Legh,on the 2nd inst., 10s. and costs.

ASLEEP ON THEIR CARTS.—Samuel Thompson, asleep in charge of a cart and two horses at Walton Superior, on the 6th inst., ss. and costs.—John Challinor, asleep on the night of the 28t1) ult., while in charge of a lurry and two horses, 2s. 6d. and costs.—Reuben Wilson, asleep on the night of the 4th inst., in charge of a lurry and two horses, who, the constable proving the case said was wrapped up as if he was in bed, 25. 6d. and costs.
ALLOWING CITTLE TO STRAY.—William Brocklehurst, for allowing a cow and a heifer to stray in Budworth- road, Little Leigh, on the night of the 4th inst., was fined 2s. and costs.

DRIVING A LOCOMOTIVE DURING PROHIBITED HOURS.— Robert Mitchison for driving a eqrtain locomotive on the highway at Appleton, at 7 20 on the 25th inst., this not being within the hours prescribed by the County Council regulations, was fined 205., and Bs. 6d. costs.

A Doc; CASE.—James Croft was charged with allowing his dog to be at large unmuszled at Grappenhall, on the 7th inst., also with keeping the dog without a license.— The constable who appeared against the defendant said when he went to serve the summons they threatened to throw bricks at him.—The defendant's son exclaimed that this was untrue, and he afterwards swore in corro- boration of his father, that the dog was a young pup of his own.—The Bench dismissed the defendant on the first charge, but on the second fined him 7s. 6d. and costs. A PUBLIC-HOUSE DISPUTE.—AIfred Brody, landlord of the Walton Arms, Walton, was charged with assaulting Enoch Wood, Ship Canal labourer, on the sth inst, and Wood was cross-summoned on a charge of assaulting Brody on the same date. Wood was also charged with being disorderly, and refusing to quit the Walton Arms. Mr. Herbert Woods appeared for Wood, and Mr. A. Browne for Brody.—Wood stated that on his going into the Walton Arms, Brody came into the room and ordered him out. He immediately went out, and on his getting into the passage Brody struck him and knocked four teeth out. Witness said he would make him pay for that, upon which Brody said " Dost tha want any more ?" and I struck him again, and the blood "fled" all over the place. If witness had been able he would have given him what for. (Laughter.) Witness went straight out of the house and for a policeman, but he was not in. Brody always got a roan into a sly place to hit him; he dare not strike him in public. He closed the door to strike him. Brody told him he had had sufficient drink and could have none there, but he had had none. Wit- ness did not fall against the door. He used no filthy _ language to the servant. Here Wood caused some laughter by exclaiming to Mr. Browne in reply to his I

questions, "You wasn't there." He denAd striking Brody.—Thomas Whitfield corroborated. He created some amusement by admitting that he had had some drink that morning,and adding that he would have some more when he got out, all being well.—Mr. Brody said when Wood came in he refused to serve him as he had had plenty of drink, and was all dirt, as if he had been 'lined in soil. He refused to go without being served, and used beastly language in the presence of his female servant. Witness allowed him plenty of time to go, and then tried quietly to lead him out, when he struck wit- ness, and then struck at him again but missed him. This was not the first time he had struck him. Wood had a bottle of bear in his pocket.—Jane McGregor corro- borated as to his bad language.—Both charges of assault were dismissed, but Wood was fined ss. and costs for being disorderly and refusing to quit. CHAIM OF ASSAULTING A CONSTABLB.—James Blain and John Miller were chargei with assaulting and beat- ing P.C. Gibbons, while in the execution of his duty, at Antrobus, en the Bth inst. The constable said he went to eject the defendants from the Wheat Sheaf Inn at 9.15 p.m., as they were fighting. Blain jumped on a form and struck witness three times on the head, and Miller struck him in the chest. Three witnesses corroborated as to the assault by Blain, but said they did not see Miller strike. Blain was fined ss. and costs and Miller was dismissed.
RWNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Major HazlehurstAand Mr. James Handley.

DISMISSED.—MendeI Blank, furniture dealer, Bridge- at., was summoned for obstructing the thoroughfare by allowing a cart to remain there. Mr. Humphreys de- fended. It transpired that the police had summoned for the wrong date, and the case was dismissed. RIVALFISH HAWKHRS.—MichaeI McGrath, Chas. Elli- son, George Duckett, jun., John Duckett, John Salt, and Joseph Chell, youths, were summoned for committing a breach of the peace in Granville-st., on the 18th inst. The youths am all fish hawkers, and they had a row about trade affairs. The Bench bound over George Duckett and John Salt, and dismissed the other cases.— John Duckett was then charged with assaulting Ann Chell, wife of a fish dealer. This arose out of the same dispute, and the case was dismissed on defendant pro- mising to pay the costs. DRUNKENNESS.—CharIes Evans, George Evans, Mary Alice Foster, and Peter Connolley were each fined ss. for drunkenness.

WARRINGTON V. BOLTON.—This return match was played at Bolton, in dull and threatening weather. Only a fortnight has elapsed since the first meeting, on which occasion Bolton were victorious. A late start was effected, and Bolton winning tae toss, elected to bat on a wicket which certainly did not improve. Walker and Bennett were the first pair, the former despatching J. J. Crosfield's third ball for a couple. Smith took up the attack at the opposite end, and after a couple of singles had been scored from him, he had the satisfaction of getting the professional caught by J. S. Crosfleld. Staton and Walker, however, put a different complexion on this state of affairs, runs coming rather freely, especially from Smith. The bowlers plodded on, and success awaited Smith at 28. for Staton was beaten by a good one, having made 15. The stand of the match was made by the next pair, both batting with a freedom that enlivened the proceedings, especially from a Bolton point of view. With the score at 84. Walker fell into a trap laid for him by Smith, having played good cricket for his 30. Ellis was out without scoring, and then another stand was made when Morton arrived. The century was hailed with cheers, but with 110 runs on the board Morton was finely caught and bowled by Smith. A similar performance got rid of Williams, and Cleaa being a trifle too eager was run out. With the scere at 130 for eight wickets the closure was applied. The visitors were first represented by R. Smith and W. H. Podmore,Ellis and Morton bowling. The start was indeed disastrous, as l'odmore, Smith, and Clarke all fell with but nine runs on the board. Meanwhile Lee had taken precautions that decided the fortunes of the day, and despite various methods of bringing about his dismissal, he maintained his end to the finish. Crosfield batted patiently for his 7, but the credit of the Warring- tonians making the draw is undoubtedly due to Lee. His 34 was an excellent display, made without a chance, and some idea of his brilliant strokes, considering the not too good nature of the wicket, may be found in the fact that six boundaries were included in it. Mary Ann Mack and Margaret Mack, mother and daughter,and Mary Murphy were summoned on similar charges, but the cases were dismissed.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of 53. was imposed in each case. Wenrinca TO COAL DHALBIL9.—Arthur Kidd,Farnworth, was summoned for a breach of the by elaws relating to the sale of coal, by not having metal labels attached to tne bags stating the weight of coal therein. Inspector Kilpatrick proved the case,and defendant said the labels had come off through wear and tear.—He was fined ss. and costs, and the Bench intimated that future cues would be more sevelely dealt with. &TAOS ASSAULT.—John Blain, of Victoria-st., was brought up on remand, charged with assaultineThomas Moran on Saturday last. The men lived together, and on Saturday night they had " words " about a grievance between them,ending in the prisoner knocking the prose- cutor to the floor, and while he was lying there biting his ear. The prosecutor thee went downstairs and the pri- soner followed him and struck him with a poker. The wounds bled very much and a doctor had to be called in. The prisoner was sentenced to one month's hard labour.

WA.RRINGTON 2ND V. BOLTON 2ND.—This match was played under most unfavourable circumstances on the Arpley ground. on Saturday. The weather was dull and threatening, and the wicket sodden with the heavy rains. The visitors won the toss, and of course elected to bat. The first wicket put on 14 runs, and both bats- men gave possible chances, but after the first pair were dismissed no stand was made, and the whole side were out for the poor total of 44, Bibby and Dutton both hav- ing a capital analysis, the former taking four for 20,and the latter five for 16. D. Smith and W. Wallington were the first to take up the defence for the home team. The first-named quickly got to work, obtaining 16 out of the first 23 runs by vigorous and judicious hitting. Wal- lington and Adamson took the score to 40 for the third wicket, the first-named being bowled in attempting to pull a straight one, and retired with 15 to his credit, the result of careful play. Unsworth was bowled by a beauty, , the first ball he received, four wickets for 40. Jolley hit his second ball to the boundary, and then the visi- tors' score was passed the same over. He was quickly bowled by a slow bowler, however, five wickets being , down for 49. Bibby and Adamson by careful play took the score to 70 for the sixth wicket, although the latter was helped by the indifferent fielding of the visitors. Bibby was eventually caught and bowled by Lee, his 18 being the result of good careful play. The venture finally reached 84, not at all a bad score,considering the'i state of the ground. Score :

div.head: DEATH 01? THE POSTMASTERGENERAL.
div.p: DEATH 01? THE POSTMASTER- GENERAL.

The Right Hon. Henry Cecil Raikes, the Postmaster. General, died at nine minutes past three o'clock on Mon- day afternoon, at Llwynegrin, near Mold. The life of the deceased gentleman was closly identified with the city of Chester. He was the eldest son of Mr. Henry Raikes. of Llwynegrin, Flintshire, and was born in 1838, at the Deanery, Chester. In the year 1865 his political career commenced, when. he made his debut as a candid- ate for Parliamentary honours and for the position of representative of the ancient city. He contested the two seats in the Conservative interest, his opponents being Earl Grosvenor (now the present Duke of West- minster) and the late Mr. W. H. Gladstone (the two Liberal candidates), and Mr. Fenton (Independent Liberal). The Liberal candidates were victorious at the poll, the figures. as the result of the contest, being as follow :—Earl Grosvenor, 1,372; Mr. W. H. Glad- stone, 913; Mr. Fenton, 626 ' • and Mr. Raikes, 574. Fol- lowing on this somewhat discouraging reverse, Mr. Raikes consented to stand for the town of Devonport, but was again unsuccessful; and on the dissolution of 1868 occurring he decided to again come forward for Chester against Earl Grosvenor, Mr. Hoare, of London (L.), and Mr. E. G. Salisbury (Independent). Earl Grosvenor again recorded the greatest number of votes, the total beirg 2,270 ; and Mr. Raikes secured the second seat with 2,18 votes, Mr. Salisbury receiving only 1,283, and Mr. Hoare 1,071 votes. In 1874 Mr. Raikes sought re-election against the Right Hon. J. G. Dc‘dson (now Lord Monk Bretton), and Sir Thomas Gibbons Frost (Liberals). The result of this contest was that Mr. Raikes headed the poll. The next contest in which the deceased gentleman figured was the memorable one of 1880, when the feeling between the political parties in the city was very great. The Con- servatives brought forward two candidates, Mr. Raikes and Colonel Sa.ndys : the Liberal candidates being Mr. Dodson and Mr. B. Lawley (now Lord Wenlock). The result of the election was an overwhelming defeat of the Conservatives, both- being beaten Hy over 1,000 votes. It will be remembered that a Royal Commission was appointed, re- sulting in the proof of wholesale bribery, and unseating of the Liberal members. When Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment of 1880 introduced strict measures of procedure, inclusive of the closure, the Conservative party regarded Mr. Raikes, who had acted as Chairman of Committees from 1874 to 1880, as an authority-, and were anxious to have his services in the House of Commons, and accor- dingly Mr. Tomlinson, one of the sitting members for Preston, vacated his seat for him, and Mr. Raikes was returned for that Lancashire constituency, which lie re- presented for several years, till a vacancy occurred in the representation of the University of Cambridge. The Liberals fought the seat with Professor Stuart, but Mr. Raikes commanded a majority at the poll, and repre- sented the University up till the present. The interment of the late Postmaster General took place on Thursday at Mold, in the presence of many of his old colleagues and friends. Mr. Gladstone was re- presented by the Rev. Stephen Gladstone, and Lord Salisbury by the Hon. Sidney Greville. A wreath was sent by the Queen.
