div.head: FAIRY TALES.
div.p: FAIRY TALES.
THE GOBLIN AND THE HUCKSTER.

There was once a regular student, who lived in a garret, and had no possessions. And there was also a regular huckster, to whom the house belonged, and who occupied thetground floor. A goblin lived with the huckster, because at Christmas he always had a large dish full of jam, with a great piece of butter in the middle. The huckster could afford this; and therefore the goblin remained with the huckster, which was very cunning .of him.

One evening the student came' into the shop through the back dcor to buy candles and cheese for himself; be had no one to send and therefore he came himself; he obtained what he wished, and then the huckster and his wife nodded good evening to him, and she was a woman who could do more than merely nod, for she had usually plenty to say for herself. The student nodded in return as he turned to leave, then suddenly stopped, and began to read the piece of paper in which the cheese was wrapped. It was a leaf torn out of an old book, a book that ought not to have been torn up, for it was full of poetry. " Yonder lies some more of the same sort, "said the huckster " I gave an old woman a few coffee berries for it ; you shall have the rest for sixpence if you will." "Indeed I will," said the student; "give me the book instead of the cheese. I can eat my bread and butter without cheese. It would be a sin to tear up a book like this. You are a clever man,and a practical man ; but you understand no more about poetry than that cask yonder." This was a very rude speech, especially against the cask; but the huckster and the student both laughed, for it was only said in fun. But the gob- lin felt very angry that any man should venture to say such things to a huckster who was a househol- der and sold the best butter. As soon as it was night and the shop closed, and every one in bed except the student, the goblin stepped softly into the bed- room where the huckster's wife slept, and took away her tongue, which, of course,she did not then want. Whatever object in the room he placed this tongue upon immediately received voice and speech and was able to express its thoughts and feelings as readily as the lady herself could do. It could only be used by one object at a time, which was a good thing, as a number speaking at once would have caused great confusion. The goblin laid the tongue upon the cask, in which lay a quantity of old newspapers.

"Is it ietilly true," he asked," that you do not know what poetry is ?" "Of cours? I know," replied the cask: "poetry is something that always stands in the corner of a newspaper, and is sometimes cut out; and I may venture to affirm that I have more of it in me than the student has, and lam only a poor tub of the huckster's."

Then the goblin placed the tongue on the coffee mill; and how it did go to be sure! Then he put it on the butter tub and the cash box, and they all ex- pressed the same opinion as the waste-paper tub; and a majority must always be respected. "Now I shall go and tell the student," said the goblin; and with these words he went quietly up the back stairs to the garret where the student lived. He had a candle burning still, and the gob- lin peeped through the keyhole and saw that he was reading i%the torn book, which he had bought out of the shop. But how light the room was! From the book shot forth a ray of light which grew broad and full, like the stem of a tree, from which bright rays spread upward and over the student's head. Each leaf was fresh, and each flower was like a beautiful female head; some with dark and sparkling eyes, and others with eyes that were wonderfully blue and clear. The fruit gleamed like stars, and the room was filled with sounds of beau- tiful music. The little goblin had never imagined, much less seen or heard of, any sight so glorious as this. He stood still on tiptoe, peeping in, till the light went out in the garret. The student no doubt had blown out his candle and gone to bed; but the little goblin remained standing there nevertheless, and listening to the music which still sounded on, soft and beautful, a sweet cradle-song for the student, who had lain down to rest. "This is a wonderful place," said the goblin; "I never expected such a thing. I should like to stay here wfth the student ; " and then the little man thought it over, for he was a sensible little sprite. At last he sighed, "but the student has no jam !" So he went downstairs again into the huckster's shop, and it was a good thing he got back when he did, for the cask had almost worn out the lady's tongue; he had given a description of all that he contained on one side, and was just about to turn himself over to the other side to describe what was there, when the goblin entered and restored the tongue to the lady. But from that time forward, the whole shop, from the cash box down to the pinewood logs, formed their opinions from that of the cask; and they all had such continence in him, and treated I him with so much rewect, that when the huckstet 'read the criticisms on theuricals and art of an evening, they fancied it must all come from the cask. But after what he had seen, the goblin could no longer sit and listen quietly to the wisdom and understanding downstairs; 80,88 soon as the evening light glitrmered in the garret,he took courage,for it seemed to him as if the rays of light were strong cables, drawing him up, and obliging him to go and peep through the keyhole ; and, while there, a feeling of vastness came over him such as we ex- perience by the ever-moving sea, when.the storm breaks forth ; and it brought tears into his eyes. He did not himself know why he wept, yet a kind of pleasant feeling mingled with his tears. "How wonderfully glorious it would be to sit with the student under such a tree ;" but that wasout of the question : he must be content to peep through the keyhole, and be thankful for even that. There he stood on the cold landing, with the au- tumn wind blowing down upon him through the trap-door. It was very cold; but the little crea- ture did not really feel it, till the light in the garret went out, and the tones of music died away. Then how he shivered, and crept downstairs again to his warm corner, where it felt homelike and comfort- able. And when Christmas came again,and brought the dish of jam and the great lump of butter, he liked the huckster best of all. _ _ _

Soon after, in the middle of the night, the goblin was awoke by a terrible noise and knocking against the window shutters and the house doors,and by the I sound of the watchman's horn ; for a great fire had broken out, and the whole street appeared full of flames. Was it in their house, or a neighbour's? No one could t,41, for terror had seized upon all. The huckster's wife was so bewildered that she took her gold ear-rings out of her ears and put them in her pocket, that she might save something at least. The huckster ran to get his business papers, and the servant resolved to save her black silk mantle, which she had managed to buy. Each wished to keep the best things they had. The goblin had the same wish ; for, with one spring, he was upstairs and in the student's room, whom he found standing by the open window, and looking quite calmly at the fire, which was raging at the house of a neigh- bour opposite. The goblin caught up the wonder- ful book which lay on the table, and popped it into his red cap, which he held tightly with both hands. The greatest treasure in the house was saved; and he ran away with it to the roof, and seated himself on the chimney. The flames of the burning house opposite illuminated him as he sat, both hands pressed tightly over his cap, in which the treasure lay; and then he found out what feelings really reigned in his heart, and knew exactly which way they tended. And yet, when the fire was extin- guished, and the goblin again began to reflect, he hesitated, and said at last, "I must divide myself between the two; I cannot quite give up the huck- ster, because of the jam." And this is a representation of human nature. We are like the goblin; we all go to visit the huck- ster "because of the jam."

CHARGE OF PERJURY AGAINST A WARRINGTON WOMAN.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday' Ellen Greenough, married woman,of St. James's-st., Latchford. Warrington, was brought up on remand charged with committing wilful and corruptperjury in the DaresSury Police Court on the 30th of June last. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, for the defence. Mr. Browne said that on the date in question he appeared there in an affiliation case in which Elizabeth Gleave,single woman, of Stockton Heath, the present informant, was the complainant, and Henry Greenough, the son of the present defendant, was the defendant. The ground on which Elizabeth Gleave made her application was that money had been paid by Mrs. Greenough within 12 months of the birth of the child, which took place on September 7th, 1888,for its maintenance. Eliza- beth Gleave then swore that the present defendant had paid her for 2i years the sum of 2s. a week for the maintenance of the child, and Mrs. Greenough swore point blank that she never gave a single half- penny for the child, but that what she gave was for washing done for her son. She also denied cer- tain allegations for the prosecution that she gave some slippers, stockings, and other articles for the child. The Bench on this evidence refused to make an order against Henry Greenough, and he (Mr. Browne) thereupon applied for a summons for per- jury against Mrs. Greenough, which a magistrate not now present granted on the following day. The evidence he should now call was so strong and cogent that he thought the Bench would have no alternative but to conclude that there was a prima facie case for the committal of the defendant to the Chester Assizes. He would call witnesses to prove that Elizabeth Gleave had received 2s. a week many a time and that this was for 18 months before she and her mother commenced to do any washing, and that when washing was done for Mrs. Greenough it was only of four or five collars a week, for which only a penny per collar was charged. It would also be proved that vegetables were presented for Mrs. Gleave, on her sending for the 2s. for the baby, and that Mrs. Greenough told Mrs. Dolman that she had already paid £l3 for the child and would pay no more.

Peter Edgar, assistant magistrates' clerk, deposed to taking some notes of the evidence in the case heard on June 30th, and to Mrs. Greenough denying that she had paid any money for the child but stating that she fre- quently gave money, sometimes over 25., and vegetables for washing done for her, that the sums paid varied according to the washing done, and that she gave no slippers or socks for the child. It was impossible to take everything down, and he could not remember her swearing that she never gave a coat and cape for the child.—By Mr. Riley: She swore that her son knew nothing about the payments, and he had never author- ised her to make them.

Elizabeth Gleave was then sworn, and said she was a single woman in service at Grappenhall. She deposed to Mrs. Greenough swearing that she had never paid 2s. a week for the child, and to receiving exactly 2s. a week from her on calling herself, fr im the birth of the child until Christmas last, and on Warrington walking day, 1890, a pair of slippers for it, sent through her brother Frank. At Mrs. Greenough's request she took the child to her, and she gave her some laced shoes for the child. Henry Gmnough, she believed, resided in St. Helens. and after the second of May, on which date she applied for the summons in bastardy, but before it was served Mrs. Greenough called upon witness's father and mother to see if she had been making enquiries about her son, "as there was nothing else black against him unless the child." Witness's father told her that if they did not get some money smoothly they would have it roughly. Witness had taken collars to Mrs. Greenough's, four or five a week, which had been washed for her son, for which id. a piece was charged, and received in addition to this the 2e, Witness also deposed to Mrs. Greenough proposing tohave the child christened, and to her send- ing by Frank Gleave a coat and cape and a pair of socks for the child.—By Mr. Riley: She could not tell on how many occasions within twelve months of the child's birth money was received. . She could not fix the date of .any payment. Whether any washing was done or not the 2s. was always paid. Ann Gleave, wife, of William Gleave, of Stockton Heath, and mother of the last witness, deposed to the alleged perjury, and to seeing Mrs. Greenough about the child four months before its birth. She nearly fell to the floor when witness told her her son was the father. She asked her to come again to see him, and she went frequently, but she always said he was not in, and that she had not told him. When the child was born Mrs. Greenough gave her 3s. for it and promised to come and see it, but did not. She afterwards promised to give 2s. a week and more when work was plentiful, and gave her a nighelamp and three feeding bottles. She paid the 2s. regularly up to last Christmas,and gave her holland and union twice for the child. The 2s. was never for the washing. She always received vegetables for that.—By Mr. Riley: Mrs. Greenough was always very kind to her. She was an extremely good-natured woman. She said when witness first complained to her "I never knew him going with anybody,it is work and bed, bed and work." Annie Gleave, a child, daughter of the last witness, deposed to going frequently to Mrs. Greenough's for Amy's (the baby's) money and always receiving 2s. dur- ing last-year, but was not clear as to the exact periods. Frank Gleave, a boy, her brother, also deposed to bringing payments oi two shillings, and slippers sad a coat and cape for the baby. . _ _ _ .

Martha Percival, aged 13, deposed to accompanying Annie Gleave one Saturday night last summer, she did not know in what month, to Mrs. Greenough's and to Annie receiving 2s. The Case, which had lasted about three hoursand three quarters was then adjourned to the Warrington Occa- sional Court till the following morning. On Wednesday morning the hearing was resumed there before the same magistrates. Mrs. Ellen Dolan, oil and colour dealer, Wilderspool- road, deposed to Mrs. Greenough telling her since Christ- mas last that she had paid £l3 for the child and would pay no more. She had quarrelled with Mrs. Greenough because of the manner in which a lodger of witness's had been taken by her from witness.—Mr. Riley: You feel very indignant still.—Witness: I haye my own thoughts.—By Mr. Browne: Witness had not the slightest ill feeling against Mrs. Greenough, and gave evidence _against her will. - _

Hannah Maria Brereton deposed to holland, flannels, pianofores, bonnets, a coat and cape, Sm., being sent by Mrs. Greenough for the child. The bonnets, coat and cape were sent on Stockton 119ath walking day. She did not know whether that was Warrington walking day. She had seen slippers and boots brought for the child, and the children brought money and vegetables several times.

Arthur Jenkins, assistant to his father, a bootmaker,in Bridge-st., testified that Mrs. Greenough purchased on June 24th, 1890, a pair of child's slippers at the shop. This closed the case for the prosecution.

Mr. Riley then addressee the court at consider- able length. He said as to the evidence of pay- ments it was shown by that tof the prosecution itself that the payments were not made with the authority of Henry Greenough, and had it been proved otherwise the evidence would not have been material because for it to be so the pesetas must have been made within 12 months of the birth of the child. As to payment of money within 12 months there was no corroboration. He cited a case to show that to establish such a charge of perjury as this proof of false swearing as to a particular payment on a particular date must be furnished by two witnesses and it must not be merely shown that payments were made extending over a certain period. Mrs. Gleave and her daughter on almost the only vital points disagreed most markedly. The case was not one in which their worships could reasonably believe that a jury would convict. The magistrates after about half-an-hour's considera- tion, dismissed the case. THE LEWISHAM ELECTION.

Mr. RATCLIFFE asked the Clerk how the Board of Guar- dians stood with regard to school fees after the passing of the recent Education Act.—The CLERK said it seemed to him, from his reading of the Act, that so long as there were schools within the Union which charged fees they could not alter their course. It was for the manageraof schools to take action under the Act. It was entirely,at their own discretion whether they took action under the Act, of whether they deferred it to some future period; in fact it • was a permissive Act. So far as the Guar- dians were concerned, so long as fees had to be granted, inquiries would be necessary, and with regard to the appointment of relieving officer they were to make that day, he should recommend that they divide the salary of £lOO in some way, such as, for instance, LW for relieving officer and £5 for inquiry officer.—Mr. RATCLIFFE asked what they would do in the event of the being abolished in Newton district.—The CLERK said they would not then need an inquiry officer, and they could then increase the salary for the relieving officership to £loo.—Mr. ReircLurs moved that £95 be paid to the relieving officer and £5 as inquiry officer. For his part, if the office of inquiry offi- cer was not needed, he should be disposed to leave the relieving officer's salary as it was.-Mr. HEATON pointed out that they had advertised for a relieving officer at £lOO a year.—The motion of Mr. Ratcliffe was then agreed to. APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICER FOR NEWTON. The next business was the appointment of a relieving officer for the Newton district but before proceeding to it the Clerk read two letters. The first was froni3b• Local Government Board stating that they deemed Mr. Caldwell, the late relieving; officer, unfit for the office, and that they had formally removed him from the office. The other letter was from Mr. E. J. Mitchell, of Bewsey. street, one of the candidates for the vacant office.!) It was to the effect that he had heard with astenishment thatit had been stated he was betting and boasting astir his chances of election,but this he added,was a" wicked and infamous lie without the slightest foundatiop." It will be remembered that there were orig,inally,6s applicants for the post of relieving officer, but at a meeting held last week the number was reduced tosix, who were requested to appear before the Board at their meeting on Wednesday morning, namely Messrs. ArOur Frost, Newton; Thos. Bowes, Earlestown ; Fred Davies, Penketh ; Geo. Clarke, Earlestown • Frank Herbert Aukland and Edwin J3lin Mitchell, Bewsey-st., War- rington. On a first vote the result was as followi: Frost. 12 ; Bowes. 19; Davies, 7; Clarke, 5 ; Aulclatul, 9: Clarke and Davies were consequently struck out. Second vote : Frost, ten ; Bowes, 15; Auklandi• 9' * Mitchell, 6. The two last-named being now left out the final .vote lay between Bowes and Frost, and as there were 15 votes for the former and eleven for the latter Mr. Bowes was consequently appointed. This was the only business of public importance.

AN OLD FRIEND" OF THE HOME
SECRETARY.

Hugh Titus Crawford was remanded on Wednesday, at the Marylebono Police Court, on the charge of obtaining £2lO from Jane Cirosutt, a widow, by false pretences. It was stated that the prisoner, who is the son of a Cheshire gamekeeper, has had an extraordinary career, and has been several times in prison. He represented himself to the widow as a detective, said he was about to come into a large fortune, and that the Home Secre- tary, who was an old friend, would be pleased to 'give away his bride—Mrs. Grosutt's daughter. The widow, believing his statements and that his interest in her family was sincere, gave him the money. The prisoner was remanded.

THEZOLLY--Under the form holm, the name ot the holly enters into many of our early English place-names, such as Ilohnwood, and no one has ever doubted the iunigenous character of the species, which is still represented by ancient trees in the oldest portions of our English forests. On the poor, sandy soil of the Millstone Grit, in the old forest of Kingswood, now better known as the Bristol nal-field, the hogies flourished so luxuri- antly that chatty old Aubrey suggests that they derive benefit "from the effluvia of that mineral. The Speech House in the centre of the Forest of Dean isPsurrounded by ancient hollies, boughs cut from which used, down to within the last 50 years, to take the place of the Testament in every oath sworn in the Verderer's Court. Evidence has been brought forward to show that this speech-house is a most ancient rendezvous, and that the holly was planted as a sacred tree round the villages of the Kelts even on the bleak downs of Cornwall. Holly forms a great part of the undergrowth in the older parts of Epping Forest, where its evergreen foliage excited the admiration of Peter Kahn, the pupil of Linna3us, who visited England in 1748, and who expressed his regret at the absence of this beautiful tree from Sweden. The New Forest also is noted for its hollies. One of the largest individuals in the kingdom is probably that at Claremont, SO feet in height, which, considering the extremely slow growth of the tree, may be a relic of the primeval forest of North Surrey. The holly will grow in any soil in which water is not absolutely stagnant; but it prefers a rather dry sandy loam, and, whilst it not only " outdares cold winter's ire," but seems to flourish in the bleakest situations, it does not do well under the shade of other trees. It is generally from ten to forty feet in height, and not more than two or three in girth; but hollies at Bleak Hill, Shropshire, are stated to attain a circumference of 14 feet. The slow-growing, even, and hard-grained wood is, except at the centre, as white as ivory, and is valued for turning and inlaying. It strains well, and is therefore used in place of ebony for the black handles of teapots, while for engraving it is perhaps second only to boxwood. —From Familiar Trees. AN bum LEGEND. —As might be expected, the whole locality of Ross Island, Killarney, is rife with memorials of the great O'Donoghue of Ross, lord of the lake and its islands. Whatever may be the historic truth relating to this great chieftain, it has long since become obscure, and now only lives in a legendary form. The Halls tell the story with their usual charm of narration. "In ages long passed O'Donoghue of Ross was lord of the lake, its islands, and the land that surrounded it. His sway was just and generous, and his reign pro- pitious ; he was the sworn foe of the oppressor; he was brave, hospitable, and wise. Annually, since his death, or rather disappearance, he is said to revisit the pleasant places amongst which he lived. Every May morning he may be seen glid- ing o'er the lake, mounted on a white steed richly caparisoned, preceded and followed by youths and maidens, who strew spring flowers in his way, while sounds of unearthly sweetness glide along the waters, and become thunder as they make their way up the surrounding hills. Although he appears in stateonly on May mornings, he is seen on various other oc- casions; and lucky is the child of earth by whom the immortal spirit is encountered, for, be he peer or peasant, good fortune will be sure to wait upon him; and, therefore, many are they who peer with longing eyes along the lake at sunrise or in twilight to catch a glimpse of the chieftain, and listen with eager ears for the music that heralds his approach." Another writer gives the legend in a somewhat different form, telling us that the prince is doomed to dwell beneath the waters till by an annual, or some say sentennial, ride over the surface of the
lake the silver shoes of his white horse are worn

out by coming in contact with its waves. "As he approaches his ancient residence everything returns , to its former state of magnificence—his castle, his library, his prison, and his pigeon-house are reproduced as in olden time."—From Our Own Country. ' GENERAL SHERBRoKE As A PRIEsT.—Sir F. H. Doyle relates of General Sherbroke that in the Peninsular War he came once upon some baggage- waggons, and the baggage-drivers were walking past a sick officer, left helpless upon the road, with the utmost indifference to his fate. Sherbrook seized the trunks that were in the transit—includ- ing some of his own—and flung them right and lett into space seating the officer on the waggon in their stead. space, he arrived at his destination be took the sick officer into his own quarters and watched over him with the utmost tenderness until Ve died. In due time it became necessary to read te funeral service over his body. Sherbroke dressed himself in full uniform, and began his task with the solemnity of an archdeacon. He arrived safely at" Ashes to ashes ;" but then, unluckily, IlOnle impish little Spanish urchins came upon the sciene, laughing and jumping and chasing each eater up and down the churchyard. The soldier- *est's temper went like a rocket; he began pelt- . the lads heavily with stones, interpolating into Eg a Prayer Book this kind of unolerical language; ,IgYou st—d young blackguards, I'll teach you to iiin whilst I read the funeral service over a British officer I Take that—and that—and that I" accom- , . ying the pelting with a volley of curses. : ring thus discharged his wrath, the archdeacon is red resumed his functions, and the service went on, "Dust to dust," ftn, just as if nothing had happened. i Tsts object sought in the Persian towers of silence is to shun, so far as possible, contaminating earth and air' and water. The towers are, in all places, v.strueted on one rlan. That near Tehran is a 'y• sample. . . . It is built on a crag overlook- tpg, the plain of Tehran and is about six miles distant from that city, and is near the ruins of Ra. The exterior is a round wall about 20 feet high, covered with white plaster. The interior is eon. structed with a floor of masonry, about six feet below tha top of the wall. This upper section of NAB serves as a parapet. The floor is made with rehes in the mason-work large enough to bold a body, and about one foot deep. In these the dead bodies are placed, so that the face of the dead shall be towards the north. In the centre of the pave. tient is an opening or pit. The niches are made in rows about the pit. When the flesh has been plucked by the vultures, the bones are burned in the niches, and whatever remains is thrown into the pit.--James Bassett. Aimee PHENOMENON.—A correspondent writes from Venice to the Frankfurter Zettung, that one or two days before Christmas a singular phenome- non was seen at Saville, near Udine, which recalls accounts of the mirage sometimes presented near Messina. The sky was partially covered by clouds In which the surfaoe of a calm sea was discerned, with boats passing over it, and even a steamer tatting its way. Presently houses came in view, then large, beautiful buildings, palaces, and churches, and, as the features became more defined, the cathedral of St. Mark, with the Piazza and tower, were plainly presented, and the neighbour. ing canals. The spectacle faded gradually away, having made a great impression on all who saw it. By permission of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, the mem- bers of the Warrington Habitation of the Primrose League held their annual demonstration and fete at Grappenhall Heyes, on Saturday. Notwithstand- ing the unfavourable state of the weather there was a large gathering of local Conservatives. Amongst those present during the afternoon were— Mr. and Mrs. Parr, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., Lady Greenall, the Misses Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. E. Greenall, juur., Mr. A. Lister-Kaye, Mr. R. I. Wynne-Jones, Mr. S. Rey- nolds, Alderman and Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Reynolds (ruling councillor), Mrs. Clare (hon. treasurer), Mrs. W. Jones, Mrs. H. Greenall, Captain Hutchinson, Mr. John Hampson, Mr. A. Woods, Mr. John Rob- erts, and Mr. C. H. Wood (honorary secretary). An admirable programme of athletic sports had been provided by the executive, and was successfully carried out by the following officials :—Handicapper. Mr. J. E. Warren; starter, Mr. Walsh; judges, Messrs. R. 1. Wynne-Jones, S. Reynolds, and A. Woods; referee, Mr. John Roberts; secretary, Mr. C. H. Wood, assisted by Mr. G. Griffith. The results were as under :—Hundred yards flat race, 59 entries: 1, E. Osborne (10 yards) ; 2, F. Smallman, (10 yards) ; 3, W. C. Litton, (9i. yards). Two Hundred and twenty yards flat race, 47 entries: 1 F. Smallman (19 yards) ; 2, E. Osborne (19 yards) ; 3, G. N. W. Lake (19 yards) ; Four hundred and forty bards flat race, 31 entries: 1, J. H. Fair (scratch) ; 2, H. H. Evans (9 yards) ; 3, J. R. Warburton (17 yards). One mile bicycle race. 28 entries: 1, W. Leatherbarrow (35 yards) ; 2, W. Bamber (70 yards); 3, E. S. Hayes (85 yards. One mile flat race: 1, A. Pierce, a boy (two laps) ; 2, F. Brown (155 yards) ; 3, J. Barlow (135 yards). Pending the hearing of an objection lodged against Brown, the second and third prizes in this event were withheld. Amongst other amusements in which the visitors indulged were fishing, cricket, and dancing ; and the St. James's Amateur Minstrel Troup, gave several amusing enteitainments during the afternoon and even- ing. At half-past four o'clock a meeting was held in the entertainment marquee, under the presidency of Mr. J. Charlton Parr. The CHAIRMAN moved, Mr. J. W. D. BARRON Of Man- chester, seconded, and Councillor Muir, of Warrington, supported a resolution approving of the works of the present government, which was carried.—Mr. JOHN ROBERTS moved that the best thanks of the Habitation and of the Conservatives of Warrington be given to Mr. Parr for his kindness in granting the use of his park and grounds that afternoon. The vote was seconded by Mrs. CLARE, and heartily accorded.—On the motion of Mr. WYNNE JONES, seconded by Mr. A. WOODS, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. C. H. Wood, the hon. secre- tary, for the zeal, ability, and trouble he had taken to make the demonstration a success.—Mr. JAMES SMET- HURST proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs Reynolds for her services as Ruling Councillor. He mentioned, as an in- stance of the energy which was being displayed by the officials of the Habitation, that between 300 and 400 members had been enrolled this year.—Mr. DICKENS seconded the vote, and it was accorded and acknow- ledged. Mrs. Parr next distributed the prizes won at the sports, a vote of thanks being subsequently passed to her,on the proposition of Mrs. REYNOLDS, seconded by Alderman HARRISON.—This brought the formal proceedings to a close, and most of the visitors spent the remaining time in dancing on the lawn to the strains of the Walton Brass Band.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET

After settling accounts with Kent, the Lancashire Eleven went to the Oval, won the toss, and went in on a very peculiar wicket. The side were all out for 125, towards which Messrs.Crosfield,Smith,and Briggs contri- buted 97. Nothing more need be said as to the general display. The Surrey men had to go in on Saturday on a wicket that certainly had not improved, and they made on the average a wretched show, although they just topped the Lancashire total. The visitors lost six wickets in their second venture for 107 runs, and then Mr. Hornby declared his innings closed and put Surrey in with twenty minutes to play. The object he had in view was not very obvious, but it afforded some little excitement owing to Lockwood and Henderson being silly enougll to attempt to make runs and losing their wickets in consequence. The match was on the whole a tame affair, and neither side could claim an advantage.

With their victory over Sussex at Brighton Lancas- shire, so far as first-class matches are concerned,brought their season to a close. The batting averages of the players show as follows :—A. C. MacLaren, 44 2 ; Ward (A.), 29 11 ;S. M. Cresfield, 287 ; Smith, 235 ; Stlag, 20 19 ; A. N. Hornby, 16 6 ; Yates, 16 2 ; Briggs, 14 12 ; Baker, 14 10 ; Barlow, 14 9 ; A. T. Kemble, 11 11 ; Wat- son, 11 5; Mold, 10 7. The bowling averages stand : —Mold, 12 42 ; Briggs, 12 86 ; Smith, 15 8; Watson, 18 24 ; Baker, 26 1 ; Barlow, 70.

div.head: FOOTBAI.I.
div.p: FOOTBAI.I.

The fourteenth match of the tour of the English foot- ball team in South Africa, was played at Johannesberg on Saturday, and the visitors added another victory to their unbroken record of successes. Their opponents consisted of fifteen representing the combined Transvaal. From the severe defeat experienced by the Johannesberg clubs on Thursday it was almost expected that the game would be little more than a walk-over for the English- men. In this, however, spectators who thronged the ground were agreeably disappointed, the match being one of the best contested that has yet taken place. The Transvaal team, consisting of picked men from various clubs, made a most determined stand, and the visitors had to display all their powers and fertility of resource to prevent their goal being carried, the ball on several occasions being driven by the Transvaalers well within their opponents' camp. In the end, however, the Englishmen again proved victorious, defeating the home team by three goals to nil.

CYCLING. ' For the past few weeks almost all our well-known road " scorchers " have been busily training for toe annual road ride promoted by the North Road club. It was generally expected Holbein and Mills would fight their French battle over again on the course which a year ago was made more famous than ever by Holbein's marvel- lous performance of 338 k miles. Mills, it was known, was anxious to meet Holbein in this event, but for some time it was rumoured that if a very favourable opportu- nity occurred Hclhein would go for the record accom- panied only by his pace-makers, and if successful would abstain from competing in the great race of 1891. How- ever, on I,riday at midnight the little village of Henlow, four miles outside Hitchin, found not only Mills and Hol- bein ready for the start, but a crowd of other more or less notable road riders. A last hand shake from those left behind, just another pressure of the oil can, and a general running over with the monkey wrench, and the aspirants for long-distance fame were speedily mounted, riding away in the solitude and darkness of a dreary- looking night, the roads being muddy and very heavy. Hardly had the oil permeated the workings of Holbein's machine before he was placed hors de combat, a most untoward accident in the first few minutes causing the race to lose half its interest. Spencer, the Bradford rider, had slipped on the greasy road, and in falling brought down the champion, who cut lam thigh severely by catching the sharp edge of Lloyd's pedal. The news of Holbein's mishap was soon known by all the compe- titors, but beyond a muttered" hard lines" they had no time for sympathy, but were plugging along for Hunt- ingdon, which town was nearly 100 miles from the start.

Soon after leaving Lynn Mills west all to pieces, and turned up at Wisbech as back man on a tandem tricycle. With his retirement nearly all interest died away, as, barring accidents, Shorland was bound to win, whilst the wretched weather which had now set in rendered anything like an exceptional performance an impossibi- lity. NO MORE CROWNED HEADS.

Sir,—A Bishop (Strossmayer) has recently hazarded a prophecy. He says: In fifty years there will be no crowned heads." That was pod logic. "Don't prophesy unless you know." The prophet (bishop) re- ferred to might, judging from the great mental pro- gress we see on every hand, very reasonably conclude that in the near future the masses—the toilers, and pro- ducers of the necessities of life—will be supreme. Pageantry and domination, whether royal, military, or ecclesiastic,will, to say the least,be reluctantly tolerated. The drones will be deservedly turned out to starve, only the contributors devoid of "craft and subtlety," will be admitted into the industrial hive. The drones at the present time overawe the workers, keeping them in mental and physical subjection to their behests. Per- sonally I would thank the Bishop for his prophetic utter- ance. We should, I think be immensely benefitted should it be verified.
Ex. FARMER.
THE CHURCHES VERSUS PUBLIC-HOUSES.

Sir,—On reading over the speeches on the temperance question I harily know what to think of the consistency of the clergy and ministers in this movement. That inns or hotels are a necessity there is no question. In my rounds on business amongst some of them, I must say I have seen much that I dislike, oven coffee houses are not free from certain characters. Whether lessening them would make any difference is questionable.

For generations past no provision has been made in our places of worship, week days or Sundays, for the people to enter freely and take their seats. Churches and chapels are shut up and bolted and baired on week days, just as if they were prisons, and when open a rent is charged for seats, or an envelope put in each seat for a payment to be made—how much is left to each per- son—and a regular scat is provided. Another plan—an old one, and the worst of all—the favoured ones are set apart from year to year by appropriation, permitted to be cushioned, ac. What can be expected from this state of things—from those who ought to have known better—but that the working-people feel themselves shut out from having their minds and morals improved, and enter the public- houses Sunday and week day, where they are welcome. Nay,in my time I have seen numbers turned out of seats for intruding, and some out of the building altogether. Such proceedings have driven many to the public-house, and in the old Evangelical days, too, when controversy was all the rage. "Shall I not visit for these things ?" S.

THE SHUNTING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON Sir,—l have read with some amount of interest the letter which appeared in your issue of the 22nd inst. by one of the jury, who styles himself" Equal Justice." I earnestly hope his mind is somewhat eased by the expressions he made use of, and that he will cease to think any more about the coroner's summing up now that the case has been disposed of. Why did not "Equal Justice" unburden himself at the inquest. That would have been the proper place. The Coroner, no doubt very sensibly, came to the conclusion that the jury had exhausted the evidence, and that going over the same ground again was merely wasting public time. The writer being an eye-witness to the sad occurence, though not called upon to give any evidence, can testify to the signal having been given by foreman-shunter Knight, and also to the engine whistling, and there were several more at the inquest ready to do the same. "Equal Justice" has not been informed properly, or he would know the deceased man Buckley was deaf and could not hear. And, as regards the engine driver and stoker not giving evidence, that was no fault of theirs, both men attending on the two occasions. In conclusion I look upon the remarks respecting Inspector Wood as personal and unworthy any man who desires to see "equal justice" done. His excuse for going into,print is very thin, as I have the satisfaction of knowing a little more than he gives me credit for. Hoping you will kindly insert this in your next issue, I remain, yours truly
AN EYE-WITNESS.

div.head: SUGGESTED FEDERATION OF WARRINGTON
div.p: SUGGESTED FEDERATION OF WARRINGTON
SCHOOLS.

Sir,—The new Education Act comes into force on the Ist September next, and, taken in connection with the grants to be made by the County Council for Technical Education, it occurs to me that it offers an excellent opportunity for placing the education of the children of Warrington upon a sound workable basis without the necessity of a School Board. I would sug- gest the formation of a "Warrington Educational Committee " which should manage the schools placed under its care, and, I should hope, be able to establish a system of graded and free schools which meet all the requirements of the town for Free Education with a -.comprehensive system which will give the best results at a minimum of cost, and relieve many managers from the constant anxiety of making ends meet. The new Act , permits of a system by which one school may keep another in the matter of the grant, but this would only be possible in Warrington through the instrumentality of such a committee as I now suggest. It would prac- tically be a federation of the schools in the town under one management and I think with the best results educa- tionally. It would mean a giving up to a large extent of that individual management which now exists in favour of a broader, a more systematic and comprehensive system. There is to be a meeting of school managers on the 7th a September to copsider the new Act. 1 throw out the

suggestion to the managers of denominational schools whether it is not possible to come to some understand- ing by which we can secure to the town all the advant- ages that could be gained by a School Board, without its costliness and the religious strife it creates.—Yours faithfully,
F. MONKS.

A GREAT SANITARY REFORII: AN INTER- CEPTING DEPOT FOR PALMYRA SQUARE! Sir,—Would it surprise you and your readers to awaken some fine morning and find that, without any preliminary speech-making or flourishing of trumpets, the great sanitary authorities of Warrington had deter- mined to erect an intercepting depot on the vacant ground near the south-west side of the Wesleyan chapel in Bold-st. ! The thing is imaginable, and quite within the range of practical sanitation, and at the same time highly desirable. Goaded to desperation by the con- `inual sledge-hammering of Mr. William Di,ggle and his confreres, they will some day be compelled t 3 do some- thing to convince the people of Warrington that the smelling powers of these gentlemen are not to be de- pended upon, inasmuch as they seem to be capable of detecting horrible stenches where the noses of abler and more experienced men fail to discover any odour at all. And where could they do that something with greater advantage and success than at their own doors? A fully rigged depot, with its complement of perambulating "Dolly Vardens " placed in the locality named, would produce a profound and lasting impression upon the worshippers at the chapel, the habitues of the " gentle- men's " club, and other swells in that fashionable neigh- bourhood; to say nothing of the outsiders who would now and then come within smelling distance of its sweet influences. The cost would only amount to a few pal- try thousands of pounds sterling; but that would be a mere flea bite to the groat Corporation of Warrington, which, last year, generously expended £8,986 of the ratepayers' money in Parliamentary expenses and usury; and is now complacently sitting under a bonded debt of considerably more than a quarter of a million of money. But then consider the advantages that would accrue from so judicious an outlay. The members of the Council would then dwell together in unity as becometh brethren ; the oil of satisfaction would trickle down their well trimmed beards, and new leases of power would be granted unto them by their duly appreciating and ap- proving clients, while, oh, V•lessed change! the carping and piping voices of Messrs. Dixon, Diggle, and Co. would be heard no more at all in the Chamber of Wisdom. Moreover, the eyes of the men of the chapel and of the club, and of the aristocratic dwellers in our little Pall Mall, would be charmed by the beautiful outlines of the depot, and their ears soothed by the sweet music of the working of the apparatus! While the nasty air which now blows upon them from the pure hills of Cheshire would be cleansed and perfumed by the exquisite odours emitted by the depst and its grateful feeders the "Dolly Vardens." And, lastly, when Messrs. Burgess and his colleagues had gone the way of all the earth a grateful people would embalm their mortal remains and place them in suitable niches in the Museum, in order that, in ages yet to come, the inhabitants and wise men from the east might gaze with admiration upon the classic features of the great Sanitarians of Warrington in the nineteenth century.—Yours truly, CUI BONO.
TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION-.EIBO FOR NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS TOWNSHIP.

Sir,—Through Mr. Ormand's interest and action we now learn that the Commi-sioners are on the eve of re- ceiving the first grant from the County Council for Tech- nical Education. I venture to hope that the amount will be kept in the right channel, viz., a Technical Night School. By no means should the grant be allowed to dribble into the day schools for technical instruction. The object of the scheme is to help the apprentices to learn the other side of their trade, which they can not learn in the workshop. It is essential they should know the principles that underlie their calling, not with a view to make them better machines, but better men. Brute force can only command limited remuneration, but intel- lectual labour is without limit.

The apprenticeship of former times is gone; now a boy is dropped into a department to pick up his trade any way he can. It is no one's duty to teach him. He also has to conteni with the simplification and sub-division of work, where general skill is not required and less ac- required. Moreover, a person who devotes a lengthened period to get proficient at a trade, and that for a small rate of pay, has an unquestionable claim to the grant over and above those who might enter for Technical Instruction more with a view of satisfying morbid curiosity, or as a luxury of being created into half-inch characters.

Theory without practice and practice without theory is a muddle ; therefore it is hoped our Commissioners will be practical and give a higher culture of powers to the young and sa keep the grant on its original and legitimate lines of benefiting the staple industries, viz, building, engineering, glass, mining, and, if practi- cable, electricity and chemistry. In dress and mantle making, many are lost through being limited to "stitch stitch," with no prospect to cut, fit, &c. Such have a prior claim over such subjects as animal physiology, which will not teach a collier how to detect fire damp, or gas in mines, or the quantity of air a fan will pass. Hygiene will not tell a fitter why a compound engine is more economical than a single one, or explain to him how it is a pulsometer works without a piston and " ex- haust ; " "sound, light and heat" will not suggest to a joiner a suitable form of roof for a span of 30 or 60 feet, or what is the strength of a loaded beam. Therefore the grant should be spent to spread real practical Technical Education for the benefit of those who are committed to industrial pursuits. Possibly the time will come when preference will be given to those holding technological certificates. However, be that as it may, we are far behind and suffering from the non- intellectual employment of those forces that are at the command of mankind, and ought to be used for the benefit of mankind. Therefore workmen ought to keep a vigilant eye upon this subject.—l remain Ste., D. WILLIAMS 240, Earle-st., Earlestown, 28, 1891.

div.head: LICENSING QUESTION.
div.p: THE LICENSING QUESTION.

Sir,—l see, in your last week's issue, that the teetotal- lers have been at it again, and, in spite of all they say, trying to force the licensing Magistrates into their way of thinking,which,with a presumption peculiarly their own, they swear is the right way ! I pass over a great heap of twaddle in the speeches ; but pause at one made by a person whom I have often heard assert, and boast, that he had never taken a drop of alcoholic drink in his life ; and yet he has the calm assurance to condemn it! Aye and in the face of the evidence of eminent medical men ! Sir, I remember, some years ago, a great critic was de- tected in the act of condemning a work that he had never read! and he got a severe castigation for it. Whilst not wishing anything of the kind for this budding orator, I would say that he is in exactly the same ridiculous position.

The Rev. John Yonge's speech was a glorious climax to the meeting, and was received (according to your report) with " Loud applause." Sir, this proves to the hilt the assertion which I have often made, that when you have packed a lot of bigoted teetotallers together, you have got there the very finest samples of blind un- fairness which the country can produce. I grant that no Brewer, and no one interested in Breweries, should sit upon the Licensing Bench ; but neither would I have a professing teetotaller there ; for whilst the former would no doubt be fully alive to his own interests the latter would go " baldheaded " at his " favourite aversion," and a sense of being either just or fair would never enter his "faddy "brain. There are however, signs about, thank goodness, that the meddlesome presumption of these "Prophets of Evil" will receive severe checks, as witness the disturb- ance at Lewisham yesterday where the interfering im- pertinence of Sir Wilfred Lawson nearly caused a riot; the effect of which he couldn't face, but like most of his pop-valiant crew, he turned tail, and "incontinently bolted through a side door ! " I feel proud of those Lewisham men who resisted the impudence and "cheek," of this maddest of all those Apostles who preach the beautifully modest doctrine that a man's tastes must be entirely guided by the gas-blown opinions they pharisaically promulgate! • PLUTO. August, 25, 1891.
RENEWAL OF LICENSES.-THE DECISION OF THE MAGISTRATES.

,Sir,—Permit me to express the deep regret I feel that that the majority of the magistrates,on Tuesday, thought fit to ignore the wishes of the people as expressed in a large public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, on Thursday, the 20th instant. It may be said that this meeting represented only a section of the community. Let this pass. At any rate, when we note that the Rector of Warrington was in the chair, and all or most of the Nonconformist churches were in evidence by the presence of their ministers and laity, it seems to me that scant courtesy was done to such an eminently important part of the community by the hasty action taken by the majority of the magistrates in taking advantage of an informal and immature protest against the renewal of the licenses of seven houses. Surely we could have waited until the 22nd September to give the Council of the Temperance Federation time to mature its protest. Moreover it seems to me . that this Haste was the more unjust, as some magistrates were absent, not knowing that they would be called upon to vote. In fact it was thought that only the Liceusing Committee would have aoy 19cus staudt, a4cl tbil4 he full bench

div.head: EX A M USER. SATURDAY. AUGUST 29, P9l.
div.p: THE EX A M USER. SATURDAY. AUGUST 29, P9l.

would be called to confirm or rescind the action of this Committee on the 22nd September. This has been the usual course pursued, and I think it ought to have been acted upon on this occasion. Many of the houses objected to have been shown to be not required by the owners offering to give them up if two new licenses were granted in other parts of the town. So far these licenses have not been, and, I trust, will not be granted. In the meantime surely the magistrates would be more than justified in refusing to renew these licenses, that are shown even by the owners them- selves to be unnecessary. But, forsooth, the majority ef the magistrates, as it appears to me, took advantage of the unfortunate mis- take made by the Council of the Temperance Federation, in bringing a weak protest against the renewal of the licenses of seven houses, to hastily grant these licenses. Such hasty action will, I feel sure, bring the discretion of the magistrates into public condemnation, and will. I trust, hasten the time when the people shall have abso- lute control in settling the question of how many licenses shall be granted. At the present time the voice of the people can be heard only through the medium of public meetings, the press, and protests before the Bench. The magistrates have absolute power to grant or to refuse licenses according to their own discretion, or want of discretion. But absolute power tne ), without regard to the expressed wishes of representatives of an important part of the community, will surely arouse a feeling of distrust, and lead ultimately to the people de- manding that that power shall be taken away from those who misuse it, and be given to the people themselves who ought to know how many, if any, licensed houses are required. In conclusion, I wish to ask the folloWing questions : Is it not a fact that the majority of cases of crime brought before us are the results directly or indirectly of drunkenness?
Do not most cases of drunkenness occur in Licensed Houses ?

Are there not a multitude of men and wamen chained and bound by this sin lorarT e. in to be emancipated ? Does not every additional facility for drinking ren- der it more difficult for the slaves of this vice to break the snare ?

If these questions can be answered in the affirmative only, then it seems to me the majority of magistrates sitting on Tuesday only lightly considered their respon- sibility in granting licenses admittedly unnecessary.— Yours faithfully, E. J. GUEST.

Sir,—The bench of magistrates have decided, (by a majority, as I understand of nine to seven,) to renew all the licenses in the borough. I write to express the dGep senses of disappointment at this decision which will be felt, I believe, by a very large proportion, if not a large majority, of the ratepayers of this town. I am aware, of course, that this decision was ostensibly made in con- sequence of the at'sence of more direct personal evidence in support of this objection made to certain specified licenses. Personally, I regret the course that was followed on Tuesday last, and through unavoidable absence from this Committee, I had no part in deciding it. In my judgment it would have been better to have left the matter on this occasion to the "unfettered discretion" of the magistrates. They were fully aware of the expression of opinion given by pie meeting of last Thurs- day week, and also of the fact, which they de not yet seem properly to understand, that they have full power to reduce the facilities for drunkenness, if they choose to use it.

My own action in the Court, on Tuesday, was under- taken on the spur of the moment, in the hope of averting or mitigating a failure which I saw was at hand; and also because I don't like an unpleasant duty to be avoided by persons who have " positions to consider," 1 and devolved upon others of humble standing. But I greatly honour Mr. Drury for the stand he took, as I I believe, in loyal devotion to a cause he has deeply at heart, and in which he has long worked earnestly and well. I very much regret that the proper answer to one of Mr. Davies's questions to myself did not occur at the right moment. He asked why I objected to these especial licenses, and I could only think at the time of a very general answer. Almost immediately afterwards, however,it occurred to me that I ought to have said, what would as I believe have been perfectly correct, that I and those who acted both last year and now in the matter, objected to these particular licenses because two years ago the licensing magistrates themselves, or some of them, had caused inquiries to be made about these licenses, and even instructed their clerk to object to their renewal. This objection, as I believe, Mr. W. A. White made in open court, and the consideration of them was thereupon adjourned. At the adjourned meeting how- ever, it transpired that because the proper legal notice of objection had for some mysterious reason been over- looked, the objections failed. This. I imagine,would have been my proper answer, and I much regret having failed to give it. I submit, however, that the decision of the justices was arrived at from other than judicial reasons. No judicial consideration could possibly have overcome the objection that these licenses were not needed in the locality. No one, in his sober senses, cauld even for a moment contend that they are. He could not so stultify his own common sense and knowledge. It is to the great honour of Alderman Sutton that he abstained from voting on this question. It would have been to the similar honour of some other justices present if, for like reasons, they had also abstained. This is a matter of public action on the part of public men, and they must forgive me if, in the public interests, I seriously question the rightness of their action. It may suit the ideas of propriety, apparently cherished by a worthy alderman, to consider it improper to cast reflec- tions upon the action of the Bench : and I, at least, do not wish to do so in any unfair or discourteous spirit. But the justices are not infallible, and they must be wil- ling to have their acts discussed and described by their fellow-townsmen. I do not see how it is possible for men to act judicially on a trade question such as this, who are themselves in any way connected with that trade, even though only as occasional adviser or agent or servant. And I for one strongly object to decisions in this matte being in their control. Those who are working to deliver Warrington from its prevailing public drunkenness have a hard battle to fight. They have to fight against not only what Mr. Davies described as "the drinking habits of the people," but also they have to fight against a gigantic trade, firmly entrenched in every part of the town, which directly ministers to these drinking habits, and directly thrives upon their prevalence. lam personally obliged to Mr. Davies for his quite too flattering reference to myself when I entered the witness box, but I cannot al- low even his blandishments to prevent my expression of surprise at his very curious and questionable reasoning. I For Mr. Davies to" deplore," on the part of brewers and publicans, the too prevalent drunkenness, is something like Satan reproving sin. And for him to allege that not the brewers and publicans are responsible for the general drunkenness, but the vicious habits of the people, is to show a singular obliviousness to the usual sequence of cause and effect. But those who attend Brewster Sessions in Warrington are used to his very specious representations ; and they have often smiled at the philanthropic reasons he has advanced for the provision of new houses in new neighbourhoods, with " suitable " and "comfortable" accomodation for the manufacture of additional drunkenness. For another year, however, the Borough Justices have given all the licenses a new lease. They have thereby shewn themselves to be reluctant to remove unnecessary opportunities for the sale of drink. They have also, as I fully believe, shewn that they do not apprehend the real state of general opinion in the community. It must be the object of the churches and temperance organisations to elicit during the next twelve months so clear and unmistakeable an expressson of that opinion as shall leave no longer any doubt upon the subject. There are several points on which it might be profit- able to write, but hoping for your kind indulgence on another occasion, I will trespass upon it no longer now. —Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE. 13, Wilson-Patten-st., August 28th, 1891.
TERRIBLE RAILWAY DISASTER IN AMERICA.

Another terrible railway disaster has occurred in America—this time in North Caroline. Through the breaking or removal of a rail, a passenger train plunged over the side of a lofty trestle bridge and fell into the river Catawba, eighty feet below. Twenty or thirty dead bodies have already been extricated from the broken carriages.
THE CHILIAN CIVIL WAR.

The Chilian Government sent on Thursday to Washing- ton and London a despatch announcing the total defeat and subsequent surrender of the insurgent force which had landed near Valparaiso. Fighting was resumed on Tuesday, and the insurgents, being beaten and cut off from the fleet, were compelled to surrender at discre- tion.
THE SENSITIONAL SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON.

The body of the man who committed suicide by jumping into the Mersey from Warrington Bridge on Sunday, the 16th inst., was found floating in the river about 300 yards from the Iron Bridge on Saturday evening. It was removed to the Lower Seven Stars, Bridge-street, to await the inquest. The following description is given by the police : " Age, about 35; height, sft. Bin. ; dark hair, dark sandy .moustache and beard of about a fortnight's growth; dressed in a black worsted morning coat, a cloth vest with black stripe, a check tweed pair of trousers, a red, white, and blue striped cotton shirt, and striped cotton handkerchief, a pair of ribbed woolen socks, pair of lace-up boots with square nails in soles and heels. The clothing had been very much worn, and the deceased is supposed to have been a working-man."—The inquest on the body was held on Tuesday, at the Lower Seven Stars, Bridge-st., before Mr. ;W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner for South-West Lancashire.—John Smith, carter. 2, Packet-stage, stated that about half-past four on Sunday afternoon, the 16th inst., he saw a man mount the parapet of Warrington Bridge and jump into the river. On coming to the surface the man moaned and then sank. To the best of his recollection the body the jury had viewed was that of the man in question.—Her- bert Booth, Sankey-st., stated that on Saturday evening he was boating on the Mersey. When near the iron bridge at Arpley, he saw the body of the deceased floating in the river. He gave informe don to the police, and the body was recovered.—P.C. Rowbotham spoke to search- ing the body on Saturday night, but found no papers or anything of value upon it. The body was that of a work- man aged about 35. There were no marks of violence abut it. The body had not been identified.—The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide."

div.head: "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL" AND MR PARNELL
div.p: THE "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL" AND MR PARNELL

A special meeting of the shareholders of the "Free- man's Journal" was held on Thursday at the Imperial Hotel, Dublin, at the instance of Mr. Dwyer Gray, one of the principal proprietors,to consider the policy which the paper has recently pursued in supporting Mr. Par- nell, and to remove from office the Lord Mayor and other directors who have been associated for the last three years with the editorial staff in the management of the "Freeman" and other papers belonging to the company. Mr. Gray proposed a resolution disap- proving of the position taken up by the directors, and expressing the view that it was essential to make a change in the constitution of the Board by increasing the numberof directors, or, if necessary, by the removal of the present members. Mr. T. Harrington,M.P moved 'an amendment expressing perfect confidence in the present directorate. Eventually a vote was taken with the result that there voted by proxy for the amendment nineteen shareholders with 1,196 votes, and against the amendment by proxy 129 shareholders with 15,529 votes. There voted in the room for the amendment 32 shareholders with 1,366 votes, and against eight share- holders with 99 votes, the result being that there were 15,626 against the amendment and 2,562 for, leaving a majority of 13,666 votes against the amendment. The meeting was adjourned for a poll on the original motion to be taken.

It removes all ianpasant odour arising from decayed teeth or tobacco smoke.
