div.head: YACHTING FATALITY.
div.p: A YACHTING FATALITY.

A yachting party from London met with a sad acci- dent on Thursday on the river Yare, at Postwick Grove, near Norwich. They got into the dingy, when the mainsail of the yacht veered and struck the boat in which they were seated. A young lady fell overboard, and in trying to rescue her Arthur Greenfield was drowned. A panic ensued and the boat was upset, leaving several persons struggling in the water. Dr. Ruffer and another of the party made desperate attempts at rescue, but Muriel and Norah Greenfield were also drowned. GitEXT SA.NKEY SCLIOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, Captain Ridgway presiding. There were also present the Rev. E. S. Jackson, sir. J. Wright, and S. Sutton (clerk). The Clerk reported that the balance in the hands of the treasurer amounted to £36 Ss., and the cheques to be signed that day would amount to £24 ss. It would, therefore, be necessary to issue an)ther precept upon the overseers, and, upon the proposition of the Chairnaan, seconded by the Rev. E. S. Jackson, it was resolved that a precept for £9l 103. be signed and issued. Mr. Clarke, the head- master, reported that the percentage of attendance at the school was now 89. The Clerk remarked that he thought it was about the best percentage in the district. Mr. Clarke said it was one of the best, not only in the district, but in Lancashire. A communicittion was read from Mr. T. Rostron, lecturer for the Church of England Temperance Society, asking whether he might deliver lectures to the children upon certain days named by him. The Board was unanimously of opinion that it would be advisable to grant him the permission he sought, but instructed the Clerk to write to him asking that he might fix some dates after the Government examination in October. The Board then proceeded to the consideration of the provisions :of the Education Act, 1891, and an elaborate and carefully pre- pared report bearing on the matter was submitted by the headmaster. Mr. Clarke was afterwards compli- mented on the able manner in which this report had been prepared, and after some discussion, it was decided, on the proposition of the Rev. E. S. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Wright, that the infants and standards 1. 2, and 3 should be entirely free,and that standards 4,5, 6, and 7, should pay 2d. per week from the first of September, books to be provided free as usual.
.LTMALE.

FRBEMASONRY.—Pa,st Master Mr. John Lewis, Altrin- cham, member of the Earl of Chester Lodge, Lymm, has been nominated by the Provincial Grand Master of the Province of Chester, to the position of Deputy Provincial Grand Director of Ceremonies.

FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.—In consequence of the success of the parade of the United Friendly Societies of Lymm last year, the Rector has been approached with the object of holding another next month. With his usual courtesy the Rev. G. W. Guest has consented to place the church at the disposal of the societies, and promised to invite the clergymen whom the committee desire should preach.

BREWSTER SESSIONS.—At the Altrincham Brewster Sessions, on Monday, Superintendent Walker presented his annual report with reference to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beer retailers in the division during the past year. The following was the reference to Lvmm :—Fully-licensed houses, 13; beerhouses, on and off, 5; beerhouses, off, and grocers' licenses, 6 ; total 24; being ene to 208 of the inhabitants. THE STORMS.—Yesterday week a terrific storm of rain, thunder, and hail passed over Lymm. The rain has con- tinued more or less daily since, and on Wednesday the flood came out in the meadows. On Thursday owing to the facilities of the Ship Canal cutting, it practically dis- appeared. Great damage has been done to the crops, the corn having beaten down to an unprecedented extent and the potatoes, it is to be feared, are beginning to show signs of disease. SERVICE OF SONG.—A service of son., entitled "Signal Lights," was held at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lymm, on Sunday afternoon. The choir was conducted by Mr. Mairs. and Miss Shore was at the organ. A ser- mon was preached in the morning by Mr. H. Bancroft, jun., of Dunham Massey, and in the evening by Mr. Dockster, of Oakham. There vc as a large congregation at each service. The collections, which were in aid of the choir fund, realized a satisfactory amount.

MANCHESTER ANGLERS AT LYMM. About a dozen members of the Manchester Free Anglers' Association had a day's fishing in Lymm Dam, on Wednesday, by the kind permission of Mr. G. C. Dewhurst. Some excel- lent sport was had during the first hour or so, at the bridge separating the two dams but,after that two gentle- men in a punt on the lower lake had admirable sport all day, pulling out every two er three minutes. The mem- bers of the association had their lunch served from the Plough Hotel, as usual—for they had come for many years to Lymm, and afterwards the party was photo- graphed, also an annual custom. An excellent dinner was served in the evening, at the Plough Hotel, by the hostess, Miss Sumner, at the close of which the usual loyal toasts were duly honoured, as was also the pros- perity of the Manchester Free Anglers' Association. The sportsmen returned home by the 9.30 train.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.
BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

Last week 1 drew attention to a little episode which was transacted in High-st., Newton, result- ing in the spoliation of a young lady's white dress, by soot throwing. Since the publication of my note, I have not heard of a repetition of the silly practice, and perhaps the exposure has had a good effect. On Thursday night last week, however, I learned that the same game was curried on in Cross-lane, Earlestown, and I have now discovered the mode of procedure. To a short stick is fastened a piece of string, and attached to the end of this is a small hag tilled with soot. When an unsuspect- ing young lady, who offers a good mark for attack, happens to pass by, a sharp whisk of the stick is given, and the trick is done. Young ladies with white dresses will therefore perhaps be on their guard.

I wonder whether we have a nuisance inspector, or a surveyor, or a sanitary authority, or in fact anybody who can or will see to the proper carrying out of the sanitary arrangements, which are so necessary for the perfect health of the inhabitants. It is,l believe,the custom in all well regulated town- ships to deal with the nightsoil during the time when honest people are supposed to be in bed. Not so however in the township governed by the New- ton Commissioners. Mr. Gillespie made a great cry of the pollution of Newton mere, and the consequ- ent injury to health, and Newton mere is several hundred yards from his residence. What would he say I wonder, if he lived in a certain part of Earles- town, where the nightsoil men do not attempt to empty the buckets until nearly breakfast time, and even then they are pulled from their receptacle, and allowed to stand in the street several minutes before they are emptied? The stench is not what might be called agreeable, nor is it of any great benefit to the health of the district, and for this reason I hope the matter will be remedied at once.

I hear the managers of the various schoools in this district have had a conference in regard to the operation of the New Education Act. One of the managers present proposed that all the schools be free, but such a revolutionary motion was indig- nantly scouted, though a happy medium iras struck by a reduction of the fees.

Of course "half a loaf, is better than no bread," and I take it parents will have to be content with the terms that have been agreed upon. Infants, I undentand, will go free, first and second standard scholars will have to pay twopence, and the third standard, and above, threepence per week. This is a reduction certainly.and it remains for the parents to say whether they will accept it or not—or send in a claim for a full and complete recognition of the Act. The terms are not generous, when com- pared with the reductions that have been made at other places, and I think the managers might deal with the people in a far more liberal spirit. How- ever, as I have said, the parents have the remedy, and a spontaneous and general claim for free places cannot fail to bring about the desired result.

• The Haydock Cottage Hospital, in a small unpre- tentious way, is doing a great amount of good, and proving year by year its usefulness to suffering humanity. who may need shelter within its walls. Defrayment of all the expenses incidental to such an establishment, and closing the year with the handsome balance of over £7O, speak well for the management. There can be no two opinions about the need for such a building in Haydock, sufficient proof being found in the fact that out of 58 new cases, 42 had been caused by colliery accidents. Dr. Hayward, the medical officer, enters heart and soul into the affairs of the institution and there can be no doubt that its success is due in a large measure to his efforts.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A monthly meeting of this Council will be held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening next. The agenda of business contains the following am9ng other items :
ASSERTING THE EIGHT OF WAY.

The Street, Improvement, and Lighting Committee have passed the following resolutions :—"That the Town Clerk take the necessary proceedings against the owners of premises in Carlisle-st. and Warburton-st. for stop- ping up and obstructing certain passag(s or strects lead- ing therefrom " ; and "that the Town Clerk be in- structed to take such proceedings as he may deem ad- visable for the protection of the rights of the public over and along the public highway leading past Litton's Mill at Bank Quay, and that he be instructed to give notice to Messrs. Litton and Company to remove an ob- struction put up by them, and on their failing to do so to have the obstruction removed."
MR. DIXON AND THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.

Councillor DIXON has given notice that he will ask the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee the two following questions :—" Will the Chairman give the particulars of the plant said to have cost £2,160 ?" and also, " Where are the patent furnaces of Messrs. Bryan, Donkin and Co., which cost £132 95., and if the engine and boiler from Messrs. Marshall and Sons, which cost £174 6s. 4d., was for the special purpose of driving a fan or otherwise ?" Mr. Dixon will further move "That the resolution passed some time ago requiring an order from Mr. Alderman Burgess before any rate- payer or stranger can inspect the Longford Works be suspended during the months of September, October,and November, to allow all ratepayers to inspect the works when convenient during working hours, because of their present con( I ion!'
THE DEPUTATION' TO THE " CLIO."

The School Attendance Committee's minutes contain a report, signed by the Chairman, Mr. Fleming, of the deputation appointed to visit the ship Clio," which roads as follows :—" In accordance with the usual cus- tom, and by resolution of the School Attendance Com- mittee, a deputation was appointed to visit the Training Ship " Clio "on the 10th July. On getting on board we were received by the Captain Superintendent, who con- ducted us all over the ship. The Warrington boys (34) were all summoned on deck before us, and we were highly satisfied with their appearance and physique. The education received by them is of a first-rate character, and the technical instruction, such as tailoring, joiner- ing. shoemaking, &c., together with the nautical train- ing, is very much to be prised, and it gave us all very great pleasure to know such a useful institution was doing such noble work, in not only maintaining them hut fitting the boys for almost any position in the futures"
PICTURES FOR THE ART GALLERY.

At a meeting of the Museum, &c., Committee, the CHAIRMAN read an extraoet from a letter he had received from Miss Gaskell of Weyinouth, offering to lend a num- ber of pictures to the Committee, and to pay the insur- ance on them, and it was resolved that Miss Gaskell's offer be accepted, and that the Chairman be requested to convey the thanks of the Committee to her. A letter was also read from the Secretary of the Royal Academy, stating that the President and Council of the Academy were willing to lend a picture to the Museum for four months on condition that the cost of carriage should be paid, and the picture insured aganist all risks. It was resolved that the loan be accepted upon the terms stated in the letter referred to.

div.head: TNCHNICAL INSTRUCTION
div.p: TNCHNICAL INSTRUCTION

The Museum,Library, Arts, and Technical Instruction Committee had at recent meetings been considering the question of establishing technical education in War- rington, and their minutes contain several resolutions bearing on the subject. It is stated that, on the recom- mendation of the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee, it was resolved :—(1) That Messrs. Gibson and Sons' estimate of £l2 10s. for work at the Old Barracks be accented : (2) that the Sub-Committee be authorised to purchase necessary apparatus, and to have the labora- tory and class room fitted up. It having been reported that the Recreative Evening Schools Association had applied for a grant for technical instruction, it was re- solved that the Committee does not see its way to recommend any grant to the Association. A circular received from the County Council had been read, stating the conditions to be observed in applying for grants for technical instruction, and it was resolved that it be represented to the County Council of Lancashire that in the opinion of this Commit- tee it is very desirable that the distribution of the por- tion of the Technical Instruction grant awarded to this Borough should be administered by the Town Council, as the Local Authority under the Technical Instruction Acts. The following resolutions were also passed : That the County Council be accordingly requested to pay over to the Town Council the whole amount awarded to be applied by it in accordance with the provisions of the said Acts; and that the Chairman and Mr. H. Roberts be deputed to lay the above resolution before the Techni- cal Instruction Committee of tne County Council, and to endeavour to ascertain, as soon as possible, the amount of the grant which will be allotted for the pre- sent year. A letter from the Secretary of the school of Art, applying on behalf of the School for a share of the Technical Instruction grant, having been read the com- mittee decided that the application be considered at a future meeting.

div.head: PROPOSHD ABANDONMENT OF THE BATHS SCHEME.
div.p: PROPOSHD ABANDONMENT OF THE BATHS SCHEME.

It will be generally regretted that the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee have come to the conclusion that, "having considered the plans and tenders for new baths, they are of opinion that the cost of supplying the same is more than they are justified in incurring, and re- commend that the same be postponed for the present."

TSB LIMEHOUSE MURDER.—John Lewis was on Wed- nesday remanded on the charge of murdering Emily Adams in a tavern at Limehouse. A verdict of wilfui murder had been returned against the woman's husband, there being apparently little doubt at the time that he had killed her and wounded Lewis on &ding them to- gether in the public-house; but further inquiry showed that Adams was in Cardiff gall at the time the crime was committed, and it is now suspected that Lewis stabbed the woman to death, and that his wound was self-inflicted to divert suspicion. DEATH OF A CONVENT SUPERIORESS.

The remains of Sister Mary Anne, superioress of the convent of Notre Dame, St. Helens, were interred in St. Helens Cemetery, on Friday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of sympathising friends. The de- ceased lady was born in 1828, at Redingen, Luxem- burg ; entered the novitiate at Namur in 1849,and made her religious profession in 1851. She arrived in England in the latter year, and for some years was superioress of the convent at Islington, and afterwards at Mount- pleasant, Liverpool. She was subsequently superioress of the Southwark Convent, but for the last 23 years had had charge of the convent at St. Helens. She was of a most amiable disposition, and her loss is severely felt by a wide circle of friends. BATHING AT SUTTON RESERVOIRS.

At the Poirc(;-61-irt on Monday, Mr—..J. o:Swift made application on behalf of the London and Manchester Plate Glass Co., Limited, for the prohibition of bathing in certain reservoirs belonging to the company. He stated that the Waterdale reservoir and others j)ined the road and on the banks of some of them respectable houses had been built. A considerable number of com- plaints had been received of lateas to people bathing in the reservoirs at all times of the day. Similar protection had been granted with regard to other waters of the company and the nuisances formerly existing at these places had practically ceased. They intended putting up notice boards prohibiting trepassers and bathers if the order was granted.—The Bench acceded to the appli- cation.

NEGLECTING SCHOOL.-At the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, John Byers, of Lowton, was ordered to pay ss. and costs for not sending his son regularly to the Lowton Endowed Schools.—Byers said he had beaten his lad innumerable times for not going to school, but he did not seem to care for that.

div.head: MR. JUSTICE HAWKINS.
div.p: MR. JUSTICE HAWKINS.

The condition of Sir Henry Hawkins was not so favourable yesterday morning, he having passed a rest- less night. Yesterday's bulletin was to the following effect :—" Sir Henry Hawkins's condition remains about the same. There is no material change.—Signed, E. COOPER BENTHAM."
THREATENED STRIKE OF SALT UNION WATERMEN.

As the Salt Union continue to effect reductions in their working expenses, some of the men who have come up the Weaver have already fastened up the stsamers and barges on which they were engaged, and there is every possibility of a general strike. EXTENSIVE ROBBERIES BY A LETTER-SO RTER TWO THOUSAND LETTERS STOLEN.

At Bow-st. Police Court,. yesterday, Henry Rhodes, letter-sorter in the General Post Office, was charged with stealing money and postal orders. It was stated that when prisoner was arrested twenty-four postal orders were found upon him. When charged he admitted that he had been stealing for twelve months. When his lodg- ings were searched a box was found containing two thousand stolen letters. Prisoner was remanded.
THE FIGHT FOR THE "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL." RESULT OF THE POLL OF SHARE- HOLDERS.

Yesterday the" Freeman "shareholders resumed, the Lord Mayor of Dublin presiding. The poll having been taken, Mr. Gray's mstion disapproving the directors' Parnellite policy was carried by a majority of 94 share- holders, representing 12,940 votes. The Lord Mayor said he and his co-directors accepted the result as a vote of want of confidence. They would remain in office till their successors were appointed. Mr. Ennis proposed Mr. Gray's accession to the directorate. Mr. Harrington objected for insufficiency of notice. A long discussion followed, and after consulting with his brother directors, the Lord Mayor ruled that the election of the new directors could not be proceeded with at the meeting, on the ground of insufficient notice.
SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.

About noon yesterday an accident occurred in the Crop Pit of the Little Delph Mine, belonging to the St. Helens Collieries Company, by which James Pennington, aged forty-four years, a married man with six children, was killed, and Robert Campbell, a youth, aged nineteen years, was seriously injured. The two men were mak- ing an air hole between two brows, when with- out any warning, several tons of stone and dirt fell from the roof ,completely burying them. As soon as pos- sible a gang of seven men was got to work to remove the stuff, but as the place was very narrow this was a work of difficulty and danger. In about three-quarters of an hour, however, the efforts of the men were re- warded by finding Campbell doubled up beneath a prop which had fallen across the way, thus .forming him a shelter. It was found that his left leg had been broken, but otherwise he was uninjured. The searchers con- tinued at work, and shortly afterwards came upon the crushed and lifeless body of Pennington, which was taken up the shaft, and removed to his late home in Bath-street.

div.head: RUSSIAN GRAIN SCARCITY. FATAL BREAD RIOTS.
div.p: THE RUSSIAN GRAIN SCARCITY. FATAL BREAD RIOTS.

ST. PETERSBURG, FRIDAY.—Later news from private sources states that the excited populace of Vitebsk, on the 19th inst., were fired upon by troops after an in- significant number of the latter had been attacked, and several were severely injured. It appears that quite a revolt took place, and the troops had to take possession of the railway station by force. The populace attacked the railway officials, beat the few grain dealers,and plun- dered their houses. Two persons have died from wounds from ball cartridges.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS ELECTION OF MEMBERS. LAl:rigs AND GENTLEMEN. —The time has come round When I have the honour of again asking for your votes for ro-election as one of your Commissioners. Although my attendances at the Meetings of the Board in the past do not appear to be very highly commendable. I have kept myself well posted up and interested in all matters affecting the well-being of the Town. and can now see my way to give that public attendance to the business of the Board which I ought to do as one of your Representatives. I am in earnest sympathy with all the questions affecting the Health, Welfare, and Prosperity of the Tovria. namely. Baths, Recreation Grounds, and a Highway Bridge connect- ing Runcorn and Widnes. which have been before you for some time past; and shall be ready to support any proposal brought forward for the carrying out of any of these objects, when I can see my way to doing so without feeling that I am helping unreasonably to increase our Rates, or imposing a heavy burden upon the present and future Ratepayers. I place myself unreservedly in your hands, and in the full assurance that the sound good judgment which has guided you in the past, will not allow you to be misled on the pre- sent occasion by any attemptto introduce subjects which do not affect the Board of Commissioners, and that you wili support those who 'believe in the motto of "Live. and let live," so long as it is carried out honestly and legitimately. I have the honour to be, Your Obedient Servant. WILLIAM R. WASS. Runcorn, August, 1891.

ELECTION OF RUNCORN CONMISSIONERS 1891. TO THE ELECTORS OF RUNCORN. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The period for which I was elected a Commissioner for, the town of Runcorn in 1828 expires on the 2nd prox. I now offer myself for re-election on Thursday next and respectfully submit your support on that day. I base my claim for this support on perform ances in the past rather than promises for the future. The general value of promises may be tested by those made at previous elec- tions. In connection with the past I am reluctantly com- pelled to refer to myself. I have been Chairman of the Health Committee since Its formation with the exeep pf the period I was Chairman of the Beard. The Health Committee has at all times onerous and responsible duties to perform and this is especially true since the commencrment of the Ship Canal operations. I have taken an active part in nego- tiating for agood road to Weston Point, in the formation of Victoria-road, in the new sewerage scheme, in providing graving docks, in the construction of Baths (being the first Chairman of that Committee) and in the endeavour to obtain abridge for vehicular traffic over the Mersey at Runcorn. Though not so intimately associated, I have heartily co • operated with the Committee appointed to deal with Waterloo Bridge and its approaches. With respect to the future I may state that DEEP DOCKS are an absolute necessity for Runcorn. Docks that will admit the largest vessels, using the Ship Canal to enter, discharge, load, 8;,c., will be the means of bestowing commercial blessings on Runcorn and its neighbourhood. With Deep Docks a direct and good road to Weston Point is assured. Runcorn can materially assist in this matter by extending its boundaries. This extension of boundaries unlike the Temporomoo Quo.tion. over which the Law gives the Corn- ndissioners not the least control, is essentially a work for the Board and ought to receive he attention its vast importance demands. Relying on the deliberate convictions and active interest of intelligent electors, rather than on boisterous solicitations and vague promises am, Ladies and gentiemen, Yours very respectfully, JOHN W. LIGHTBURN. Runcorn. Friday. August 28, 1891.

WELSH NATIONAL INSTITUTIONS. On Tuesday afternoon a very largely attended confe- rence of representative gentlemen from all parts of Wales was held at Llandrindod to consider the proposals contained in the National Institutions (Wales) Bill, in- troduced into the House of Commons by Mr. Alfred Thomas, M.P., and backed by all the Liberal members for the principality. The bill proposes that a Secretary of state for Wales shall be appointed, a Welsh Education Department created, and a National Council formed, the latter to have, among other powers, authority to insti- tute a Welsh National Museum and to apply for a char- ter for a Welsh University. After hearing the various clauses explained by Mr. Thomas, M.P., and Mr. J. T. Dodd (the barrister who drafted the bill), the meeting, by a practically unanimous vote, adopted a resolution approving of the general principles of the bill. A com- mittee was afterwards appointed to arrange for a fur- ther meeting in London, when the beet means of pro- moting the bill in Parliament will be considered
